Chapter 19Symmetry, periodicity and constraints

So far we have solved every structure completely: with all nodes, all elements and all unknowns. The finite elements of chapters 7 and 12 have two troubles here. The first is size: a portal frame with four elements on each column and eight on the beam already has \(51\) unknowns, and symmetry can save us half of the work. The second is that the conditions between unknowns do not end with a support that forbids a single unknown: a support slides along an incline, a beam is rigidly attached to a column that belongs to another element. This chapter gives three tools for both troubles. With mirror and rotational symmetry we compute only a piece of the structure, with periodicity we use repetition, and with constraints we tie together the unknowns that the mesh does not tie by itself.

Each word of the title has its reason. Symmetry (simetrija) is a Greek word from syn, together, and metron, measure: what is symmetric has a common measure with another part, so that it can be made to cover it. Periodicity (periodičnost) comes from the Greek periodos, a going round, from peri, around, and hodos, way: what is periodic repeats, returning to the same state after each round. A constraint (vez) is a condition that ties unknowns to each other, as a rope ties one body to another so that it cannot move freely.

The chapter keeps four promises of earlier chapters. Chapter 5 promised the symmetry of frames, chapter 7 the symmetric and antisymmetric load, chapter 11 the conditions of symmetry on a plane, and chapter 12 the constraints between several nodes and the joining of different elements. The path is this: first we prove that a symmetric structure under a symmetric or antisymmetric load gives a symmetric or antisymmetric solution, then what this means on the plane of symmetry and how an arbitrary load is split. Next comes why this does not suffice for vibration and buckling. Then constraints: elimination of unknowns, rigid links, joining of different elements. At the end repetition and rotation, where the symmetry is not a mirror but a shift or a turn. Where none of the books we have gives a proof, we derive it ourselves and say so.

19.1 Mirror symmetry

For a spatial cantilever (lemma 7.36) and for a bridge (lemma 7.38) chapter 7 proved that a symmetric structure under a symmetric load gives a symmetric response. Each of the two proofs held for its own structure. Here we prove the same idea once, for every body and every mesh model. Why is this worth it? Because half a structure means half the unknowns, but only if we know when we may use the symmetry. This is why both theorems of this section will also have an example in which the structure looks symmetric and the response is not.

Imagine a T-shaped bracket welded to a wall. In the middle of the stem, where the bracket is narrowest, we place a flat mirror, perpendicular to the wall and to the plane of the page, so that we see it from the side as a line. The plane of the mirror is called the plane of reflection (ravnina zrcaljenja) and we denote it by \(\Pi\), the Greek capital pi. In the mirror we see the whole bracket: the right half appears as the left one and the reverse. Each point \(\vek x\) on the shoulder has its image \(Z\vek x\) on the left shoulder, which is as far behind the mirror as \(\vek x\) is in front of it distance. The point and its image lie on the same perpendicular to the mirror, that is on a line with the normal \(\vek m\) of the plane, which we take to be a unit vector. Let us write this with a matrix. If we choose the origin of coordinates on the plane, the displacement from the point to its image is \(-2\,(\vek x\cdot\vek m)\,\vek m\), twice the orthogonal projection of the point on \(\vek m\) with the sign reversed, and we get \(Z\vek x = \vek x - 2\,(\vek m\cdot\vek x)\,\vek m\).

Definition 19.1 Reflection in a plane (zrcaljenje čez ravnino)

Let \(\Pi\) be a plane in the space \(\mathbb{R}^3\) through the origin of a rectangular Cartesian coordinate system and \(\vek m\) a unit vector perpendicular to it. The reflection in the plane \(\Pi\) (zrcaljenje čez ravnino \(\Pi\)) is the map \(\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3\), \(\vek x \mapsto \mat Z\vek x\), with the matrix of order \(3\)

\[\mat Z = \mat I - 2\,\vek m\,\vek m^\T , \tag{19.1}\]

that is \(\mat Z\vek x = \vek x - 2\,(\vek m\cdot\vek x)\,\vek m\). The point \(\mat Z\vek x\) is the mirror image (zrcalna slika) of the point \(\vek x\), the set \(\mat Z(V)\) the mirror image of the set \(V\) of points.

Source: COOK §2.11 (PDF p. 69) describes mirror symmetry as a property with respect to a plane that the reflection maps "onto itself". The matrix (19.1) is our notation for this map. We use the letter \(\mat Z\) because the letter \(S\) is already taken in the book: the surfaces \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) in chapter 11 and the geometric stiffness in chapter 12.

What does a reflection preserve? We shall need this in every proof of this chapter, so we prove it at once.

Lemma 19.2 Properties of reflection (lastnosti zrcaljenja)

For the reflection \(\mat Z\) in the plane \(\Pi\) with the normal \(\vek m\) (definition 19.1) the following holds:

  1. \(\mat Z^\T = \mat Z\) and \(\mat Z^2 = \mat I\), so \(\mat Z\) is an orthogonal matrix, \(\mat Z^\T\mat Z = \mat I\).
  2. \(\mat Z\vek x = \vek x\) for every point \(\vek x\) on the plane \(\Pi\) and \(\mat Z\vek m = -\vek m\).
  3. The distance between two points and the distance between their mirror images are equal: \(|\mat Z\vek x - \mat Z\vek y| = |\vek x - \vek y|\). The midpoint of the segment between \(\vek x\) and \(\mat Z\vek x\) lies on the plane \(\Pi\).
  4. In a coordinate system with the axis \(z\) along \(\vek m\) we have \(\mat Z = \mathrm{diag}(1, 1, -1)\) and \(\det\mat Z = -1\). This is the matrix \(\mat Q\) from the proof of lemma 3.21. In the original system, too, the determinant of the matrix (19.1) is \(-1\).
Proof

We must show that the properties follow from \(\vek m\cdot\vek m = 1\) and from the form (19.1).

  1. Transposition: \((\mat I - 2\,\vek m\vek m^\T)^\T = \mat I - 2\,\vek m\vek m^\T\), because \((\vek m\vek m^\T)^\T = \vek m\vek m^\T\). Square: \(\mat Z^2 = \mat I - 4\,\vek m\vek m^\T + 4\,\vek m\,(\vek m^\T\vek m)\,\vek m^\T = \mat I - 4\,\vek m\vek m^\T + 4\,\vek m\vek m^\T = \mat I\), since \(\vek m^\T\vek m = 1\). Hence \(\mat Z^\T\mat Z = \mat Z^2 = \mat I\).
  2. The point \(\vek x\) lies on \(\Pi\) if \(\vek m\cdot\vek x = 0\) (a plane through the origin, perpendicular to \(\vek m\)). Then \(\mat Z\vek x = \vek x\). For \(\vek m\) we have \(\mat Z\vek m = \vek m - 2\,(\vek m\cdot\vek m)\,\vek m = -\vek m\).
  3. By step 1, \(|\mat Z\vek w|^2 = \vek w^\T\mat Z^\T\mat Z\vek w = |\vek w|^2\) for every \(\vek w\). With \(\vek w = \vek x - \vek y\) and linearity, \(\mat Z\vek x - \mat Z\vek y = \mat Z\vek w\), we get the first claim. The midpoint of the segment is \(\tfrac12(\vek x + \mat Z\vek x) = \vek x - (\vek m\cdot\vek x)\,\vek m\), and its scalar product with \(\vek m\) is \(\vek m\cdot\vek x - \vek m\cdot\vek x = 0\).
  4. Let \(\vek e_1\) and \(\vek e_2\) be perpendicular unit vectors on the plane \(\Pi\), \(\vek e_3 = \vek m\). By step 2, \(\mat Z\vek e_1 = \vek e_1\), \(\mat Z\vek e_2 = \vek e_2\) and \(\mat Z\vek e_3 = -\vek e_3\). The columns of the matrix in this basis are thus \((1, 0, 0)\), \((0, 1, 0)\) and \((0, 0, -1)\), and the determinant of a diagonal matrix is the product of the diagonal, \(-1\). For the original system let \(\mat R\) be the rotation matrix (definition 2.37) with the rows \(\vek e_1\), \(\vek e_2\) and \(\vek m\). By lemma 2.38 a point \(\vek x\) has the components \(\mat R\vek x\) in the new axes, and from the new components we get the old ones with \(\mat R^\T\). So in the original system \(\mat Z = \mat R^\T\,\mathrm{diag}(1, 1, -1)\,\mat R\), and by theorem 2.52 \(\det\mat Z = \det\mat R^\T\cdot(-1)\cdot\det\mat R = -\det(\mat R^\T\mat R) = -\det\mat I = -1\).

Source: The lemma is ours. Every rotation matrix of definition 2.37 is orthogonal (lemma 2.40), and the definition includes mirrored axes. The determinant tells the two cases apart (section 2.10): \(+1\) for a rotation, \(-1\) for a reflection.

A reflection is thus like a rotation, except that it has determinant \(-1\): it preserves lengths and angles but not orientation. A right-handed system of axes turns into a left-handed one in the mirror. For a rotation, chapter 2 told us how the components of tensors change. For a reflection the same rule, with \(\mat Z\) in place of \(\mat Q\), does the same job.

Now we load the bracket. On both shoulders we put the same vertical force downward, one on each shoulder: the mirror shows on the left shoulder exactly the force that we see on the right shoulder in reality, so the image of the load is the load itself. What we see in the mirror is the same bracket with the same wall. We say that the load is symmetric. If, however, we turn the left force upward, so that it pulls the shoulder, the mirror image of the right force, that is a force downward on the left shoulder, is not the load that is there but its opposite. We say that the load is antisymmetric (protisimetrična obremenitev): the prefix anti- is Greek and means against, antisymmetric is what would become symmetric if we reversed its sign. The mirror image of the same bracket is again the same bracket, only the load is the opposite.

For a body that is not just a bracket we must say this for all data of the boundary value problem from chapter 11: for the body, for the part of the surface with a prescribed displacement, for the part with a prescribed force, for the material and for three kinds of load, body force, surface force and prescribed displacement.

Definition 19.3 Symmetric and antisymmetric problem (simetričen in protisimetričen problem)

Let a boundary value problem of elasticity be given (definition 11.1) with a body \(V\), a part of the surface \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) with a prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\), a part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) with a prescribed surface force \(\bar{\vek t}\), a body force \(\vek b\) and a homogeneous material (definition 3.5). Let \(\mat Z\) be the reflection in the plane \(\Pi\) (definition 19.1).

The structure (body, supports and material) is mirror symmetric with respect to the plane \(\Pi\) (zrcalno simetrična glede na ravnino \(\Pi\)) if:

  1. \(\mat Z(V) = V\), \(\mat Z(S_{\mathrm{u}}) = S_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(\mat Z(S_{\mathrm{t}}) = S_{\mathrm{t}}\),
  2. \(\Pi\) is a plane of symmetry of the material (definition 3.20).

The load is symmetric (simetrična obremenitev) if for every point \(\vek x\)

\[\mat Z\,\vek b(\mat Z\vek x) = \vek b(\vek x) , \qquad \mat Z\,\bar{\vek t}(\mat Z\vek x) = \bar{\vek t}(\vek x) \ \ (\vek x \in S_{\mathrm{t}}) , \qquad \mat Z\,\bar{\vek u}(\mat Z\vek x) = \bar{\vek u}(\vek x) \ \ (\vek x \in S_{\mathrm{u}}) , \tag{19.2}\]

and antisymmetric (antisymmetric load) if the same holds with a minus sign on the right side of all three equations. The boundary value problem is a symmetric (antisymmetric) problem if the structure is mirror symmetric and the load is symmetric (antisymmetric).

Source: COOK §2.11 (PDF p. 69): symmetry of geometry, supports and elastic properties with respect to a plane, an antisymmetric load is symmetric "except that the loads must be reversed". ONATE1 §9.6.1 (PDF p. 346): an antisymmetric load is a system of forces such that reflecting the structure with the load and reversing the sign of all forces gives a match. BARBER §5.2.3 (PDF p. 81): the load is split into a symmetric and an antisymmetric part. The notation with the matrix \(\mat Z\) is ours.

What does the second requirement for the structure mean? For an isotropic material every plane is a plane of symmetry. By theorem 3.11, Hooke's law (3.13) holds with the same \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) in every rectangular Cartesian system, so also in the system with the axis \(z\) along the normal of the plane. When we reverse this axis, only the components with one index \(z\) change sign (lemma 3.21), the trace \(\tr\ten\varepsilon\) stays the same, and in the equations \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 2\mu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) the sign changes on both sides at once. The law therefore has the same constants in both systems. For an orthotropic material (definition 3.23, section 3.4.4) there are three such planes, perpendicular to the axes of the material. A material with inclined fibres has no plane perpendicular to the axis \(y\).

Now we come to the question for which we wrote all this. What can we say about displacements if the problem is symmetric? Let us see what would happen if we read the solution \(\vek u\) off the mirror: at the point \(\vek x\) we take the displacement that the solution has at the point \(\mat Z\vek x\) and reflect it, \(\mat Z\vek u(\mat Z\vek x)\). The mirror changes nothing that matters for equilibrium: not distances, not the material, not the load, and a piece of a body in equilibrium under forces is, once reflected, in equilibrium under the reflected forces, since the laws of equilibrium are the same in a left-handed and a right-handed system of axes. So the reflected displacement should solve the same problem. The solution of a boundary value problem is unique by theorem 11.4, so the mirror image of the solution must be the solution itself. For an antisymmetric load the calculation is the same with a reversed sign. We now carry out this idea on components.

Theorem 19.4 Symmetry of the solution of the boundary value problem (simetrija rešitve robnega problema)

Let the boundary value problem of elasticity be symmetric or antisymmetric with respect to the plane \(\Pi\) with the reflection \(\mat Z\) (definition 19.3). Let the material be linearly elastic (definition 3.3) with a strain energy density that is positive for every small strain that is not zero, and let the only small rigid motion that vanishes on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) be the field \(\vek 0\). Let \(\vek u\) be the solution. Then:

  1. for a symmetric problem \(\vek u(\vek x) = \mat Z\,\vek u(\mat Z\vek x)\), for an antisymmetric one \(\vek u(\vek x) = -\mat Z\,\vek u(\mat Z\vek x)\), for every point \(\vek x\) of the body,
  2. strains and stresses have the same property: \(\ten\varepsilon(\vek x) = \pm\mat Z\,\ten\varepsilon(\mat Z\vek x)\,\mat Z\) and \(\ten\sigma(\vek x) = \pm\mat Z\,\ten\sigma(\mat Z\vek x)\,\mat Z\), with the plus sign for a symmetric and the minus sign for an antisymmetric problem,
  3. at a point \(\vek x\) of the plane \(\Pi\) we have \(\vek u(\vek x)\cdot\vek m = 0\) for a symmetric problem, and for an antisymmetric one \(\vek u(\vek x)\) is parallel to \(\vek m\).

Item 2 holds also without the hypothesis on rigid motions, that is also when some small rigid motion other than \(\vek 0\) vanishes on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\).

Proof

We must show that the field \(\tilde{\vek u}(\vek x) = \mat Z\,\vek u(\mat Z\vek x)\) solves the boundary value problem with the data \((\pm\vek b, \pm\bar{\vek t}, \pm\bar{\vek u})\), and use uniqueness.

  1. The field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is defined on \(V\), because \(\mat Z(V) = V\), and is continuously differentiable as a composition of \(\vek u\) with a linear map. By the chain rule \(\partial\tilde u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{a},\mathrm{c}} Z_{\mathrm{ia}}\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{a}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{c}})(\mat Z\vek x)\,Z_{\mathrm{cj}}\), which we write \(\nabla\tilde{\vek u}(\vek x) = \mat Z\,\nabla\vek u(\mat Z\vek x)\,\mat Z\).
  2. Since \(\mat Z^\T = \mat Z\) (lemma 19.2), \((\mat Z\,\mat G\,\mat Z)^\T = \mat Z\,\mat G^\T\mat Z\) for every matrix \(\mat G\). Hence the tensor of small strains, the symmetric part of the gradient, is \(\tilde{\ten\varepsilon}(\vek x) = \mat Z\,\ten\varepsilon(\mat Z\vek x)\,\mat Z\).
  3. We choose a coordinate system with the axis \(z\) along \(\vek m\), in which \(\mat Z = \mathrm{diag}(1, 1, -1)\) (lemma 19.2, item 4). By lemma 3.21 the components of strain and stress in the system with the axis \(z\) reversed are \(\mat Z\,\ten\varepsilon\,\mat Z\) and \(\mat Z\,\ten\sigma\,\mat Z\). By definition 3.20 the material has the same elastic constants in both systems. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) denote the map \(\ten\varepsilon \mapsto \ten\sigma\) of Hooke's law. The same constants mean: \(\ten\sigma = \mathcal{C}(\ten\varepsilon)\) implies \(\mat Z\,\ten\sigma\,\mat Z = \mathcal{C}(\mat Z\,\ten\varepsilon\,\mat Z)\). This is an equation between tensors, so it holds in every system, and at every point, because the material is homogeneous. The stresses of the field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) at the point \(\vek x\) are therefore \(\mathcal{C}(\tilde{\ten\varepsilon}(\vek x)) = \mathcal{C}(\mat Z\,\ten\varepsilon(\mat Z\vek x)\,\mat Z) = \mat Z\,\ten\sigma(\mat Z\vek x)\,\mat Z\).
  4. Equilibrium. The derivative of the stress \(\tilde\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(\vek x) = \sum_{\mathrm{a},\mathrm{b}} Z_{\mathrm{ia}}\,\sigma_{\mathrm{ab}}(\mat Z\vek x)\,Z_{\mathrm{jb}}\) with respect to \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) and the sum over \(j\) give \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial\tilde\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{a},\mathrm{b},\mathrm{c}} Z_{\mathrm{ia}}\,(\partial_{\mathrm{c}}\sigma_{\mathrm{ab}})(\mat Z\vek x)\,\sum_{\mathrm{j}} Z_{\mathrm{cj}}Z_{\mathrm{jb}} = \sum_{\mathrm{a},\mathrm{b}} Z_{\mathrm{ia}}\,(\partial_{\mathrm{b}}\sigma_{\mathrm{ab}})(\mat Z\vek x)\), since \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} Z_{\mathrm{cj}}Z_{\mathrm{jb}} = (\mat Z^2)_{\mathrm{cb}} = \delta_{\mathrm{cb}}\). Because \(\vek u\) satisfies the equations of equilibrium at the point \(\mat Z\vek x\), \(\sum_{\mathrm{b}}\partial_{\mathrm{b}}\sigma_{\mathrm{ab}}(\mat Z\vek x) = -b_{\mathrm{a}}(\mat Z\vek x)\), so \(\operatorname{div}\tilde{\ten\sigma}(\vek x) + \mat Z\,\vek b(\mat Z\vek x) = \vek 0\). The field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) has the body force \(\tilde{\vek b}(\vek x) = \mat Z\,\vek b(\mat Z\vek x)\).
  5. Surface force. A reflection is an isometry that maps the body onto the body, so it maps the outward normal at the point \(\vek x\) of the surface onto the outward normal at the point \(\mat Z\vek x\), \(\vek n(\mat Z\vek x) = \mat Z\,\vek n(\vek x)\) (the normal is perpendicular to the tangent plane and points out of the body, and an isometry preserves both). For \(\vek x\in S_{\mathrm{t}}\), by step 3 and by Cauchy's formula for \(\vek u\) at the point \(\mat Z\vek x\in S_{\mathrm{t}}\), the traction vector of the field \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is \(\tilde{\ten\sigma}(\vek x)\,\vek n(\vek x) = \mat Z\,\ten\sigma(\mat Z\vek x)\,\mat Z\,\vek n(\vek x) = \mat Z\,\ten\sigma(\mat Z\vek x)\,\vek n(\mat Z\vek x) = \mat Z\,\bar{\vek t}(\mat Z\vek x)\).
  6. Displacement. For \(\vek x\in S_{\mathrm{u}}\) we have \(\mat Z\vek x\in S_{\mathrm{u}}\), so \(\tilde{\vek u}(\vek x) = \mat Z\,\bar{\vek u}(\mat Z\vek x)\).
  7. By steps 4, 5 and 6, \(\tilde{\vek u}\) is the solution for the data \((\mat Z\vek b(\mat Z\,\cdot), \mat Z\bar{\vek t}(\mat Z\,\cdot), \mat Z\bar{\vek u}(\mat Z\,\cdot))\), that is by equation (19.2) for \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t}, \bar{\vek u})\) in the symmetric and for \((-\vek b, -\bar{\vek t}, -\bar{\vek u})\) in the antisymmetric problem. In the symmetric problem \(\tilde{\vek u}\) and \(\vek u\) are solutions of the same data, so by item 3 of theorem 11.4 \(\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u\). In the antisymmetric problem \(-\tilde{\vek u}\) is by corollary 11.3 with \(\alpha = -1\) the solution of the data \((\vek b, \bar{\vek t}, \bar{\vek u})\), so \(-\tilde{\vek u} = \vek u\). This is item 1.
  8. Item 2: from \(\vek u = \pm\tilde{\vek u}\) and steps 2 and 3 follow \(\ten\varepsilon(\vek x) = \pm\mat Z\,\ten\varepsilon(\mat Z\vek x)\,\mat Z\) and the same for stresses.
  9. Item 3: for \(\vek x\in\Pi\) we have \(\mat Z\vek x = \vek x\) (lemma 19.2, item 2), so \(\vek u = \pm\mat Z\vek u\). With the plus sign \(\vek u = \vek u - 2\,(\vek m\cdot\vek u)\,\vek m\), so \(\vek m\cdot\vek u = 0\). With the minus sign \(\vek u = -\vek u + 2\,(\vek m\cdot\vek u)\,\vek m\), so \(\vek u = (\vek m\cdot\vek u)\,\vek m\).
  10. Without the hypothesis on rigid motions, by step 7 \(\tilde{\vek u}\) and \(\vek u\) are still solutions for the same data in a symmetric problem, and \(-\tilde{\vek u}\) and \(\vek u\) in an antisymmetric one. Item 1 of theorem 11.4 does not need this hypothesis and gives both solutions the same strains and stresses. The strains of the field \(-\tilde{\vek u}\) are \(-\tilde{\ten\varepsilon}\) by corollary 11.3, so \(\ten\varepsilon = \pm\tilde{\ten\varepsilon}\), and the same for stresses. With steps 2 and 3 this is item 2.

Source: The theorem is ours, the proof follows the idea of lemma 7.38 (the mirror image of the solution solves the same problem, uniqueness). COOK §2.11 (PDF p. 69): a symmetric load on a symmetric structure gives symmetric results, without proof. Item 3 is the content of the rules S1 and A1 of COOK (PDF p. 69), which we prove in full in section 19.2.

The proof showed what the theorem needs: that the mirror maps onto itself everything that determines the problem, and that the solution is unique. Item 3 already says what happens on the plane: in symmetry the points of the plane do not leave the plane, and in antisymmetry they move only perpendicular to it. We treat this in detail in section 19.2.

What if one of the conditions is not met? Let us see that the second requirement is really needed. The composite strip that we pulled obliquely to the fibres in section 3.4.6 (figure 3.39) is a rectangle that we pull at both ends with the same stress \(\sigma = 10\) MPa, as described there: the stress is uniform along the strip, as it is further from the jaws (SADD §5.6, PDF pp. 114-115). The shape and the load are symmetric with respect to the plane that is perpendicular to the plane of the strip and runs along its middle, that is perpendicular to the axis \(\bar y\). The first requirement of the definition is met, the load is symmetric. The strip is not fixed anywhere, so it is a traction problem, \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is empty, and the hypothesis of the theorem on rigid motions does not hold: the strip can move as a whole. Item 2, however, holds by the theorem also without this hypothesis. The fibres are inclined (direction cosines \(c = 0{,}8\) and \(s = 0{,}6\)), so by section 3.4.6 the plane perpendicular to the axis \(\bar y\) is not a plane of symmetry of the material: the constant \(k = \bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}/\bar\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 5{,}362\cdot 10^{-5}\) MPa\(^{-1}\) has the opposite sign in the reflected system.

If the theorem held, the strain at a point of the middle plane would by item 2 be \(\ten\varepsilon = \mat Z\,\ten\varepsilon\,\mat Z\) with \(\mat Z = \mathrm{diag}(1, -1, 1)\) in the axes of the strip. The component \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) has one index \(y\), so by lemma 3.21, which holds for every axis, it changes sign, \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\). The solution of section 3.4.6, however, has everywhere \(\bar\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 5{,}362\cdot 10^{-4}\) at \(10\) MPa, so \(\bar\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 2{,}681\cdot 10^{-4} \ne 0\). The conclusion of item 2 does not hold, and since this item does not need the hypothesis on rigid motions, the only hypothesis that fails here is the one on the material. The mirror image of the strip has fibres inclined to the other side and a shear \(-5{,}362\cdot 10^{-4}\): the mirror image of the solution is the solution of another strip, not of the same one. A symmetric shape is therefore not enough for symmetry.

For a mesh model, instead of the field \(\vek u\) we get a column of unknowns \(\vek d\). We write the same idea for a column and test it on the frame of chapter 12. Take a portal frame of steel \(E = 196\) GPa with a section \(20 \times 40\) mm, where the height of the section in the plane of the frame is \(40\) mm, so \(A = 800\) mm\(^2\) and \(I = 106\,667\) mm\(^4\), \(EA = 1{,}568\cdot 10^{8}\) N and \(EI = 20\,907\) N m\(^2\). The columns \(AB\) and \(EC\) are \(1\) m high and clamped at \(A\) and \(E\), the beam \(BC\) is \(1\) m long. We divide the columns into four elements each (definition 12.17) and the beam into eight, four on each half \(BD\) and \(DC\), and the nodes include \(B\), \(C\) and the middle of the beam \(D\). In all there are \(17\) nodes and \(51\) unknowns, of which \(6\) are prescribed and \(45\) are free.

Each node has three unknowns as in chapter 12: the horizontal displacement \(u\), the vertical displacement \(v\) and the rotation \(\varphi\) counterclockwise. We place the mirror through the middle of the beam, vertically, and the node \(B\) goes into \(C\). Let the node \(B\) move by \(u_{\mathrm{B}}\) to the right, by \(v_{\mathrm{B}}\) upward and rotate by \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}\). Where does its mirror image, the node \(C\), move? We reflect the displacement as a point: the horizontal component reverses direction, the vertical one stays. We reflect the rotation as a turning: a wheel that turns counterclockwise in front of the mirror turns clockwise in the mirror, because the mirror reverses orientation. The image of the node \(B\) therefore has the displacement \((-u_{\mathrm{B}}, v_{\mathrm{B}})\) and the rotation \(-\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}\). Each node \(i\) has its mirror node \(\bar i\), a node on the plane has \(\bar i = i\), and there the same formula prescribes the mirror image of the displacement. We collect these rules in a matrix and state them precisely.

Definition 19.5 Mirror matrix of a frame model (zrcalna matrika modela okvirja)

Let a plane frame model (chapter 12) have nodes \(1, \dots, n\) with coordinates \((x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{i}})\), and let the plane \(\Pi\) be perpendicular to the axis \(x\), \(x = x_0\). For the node \(i\) let \(\bar i\) be the node with coordinates \((2x_0 - x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{i}})\), if it exists. The model is mirror symmetric with respect to \(\Pi\) (zrcalno simetričen glede na \(\Pi\)) if:

  1. every node has a mirror node, \(i \mapsto \bar i\),
  2. every element between the nodes \(i\) and \(j\) has a mirror element between \(\bar i\) and \(\bar j\) with the same length, \(EA\) and \(EI\), and no element crosses the plane (an element with the nodes \(i\) and \(\bar i\) is not allowed, a node must be placed on the plane),
  3. an unknown of the node \(i\) is prescribed exactly when the same unknown of the node \(\bar i\) is prescribed, and the prescribed values are zero.

The mirror matrix (zrcalna matrika) \(\mat P\) of order \(3n\) is the matrix whose \(3\times 3\) block in the row of the node \(i\) and the column of the node \(\bar i\) is \(\mathrm{diag}(-1, 1, -1)\), all other blocks are zero. For a column of unknowns \(\vek d\) we thus have \((\mat P\vek d)_{\mathrm{i}} = (-u_{\bar{i}},\ v_{\bar{i}},\ -\varphi_{\bar{i}})\). It is a permutation matrix (definition 7.45) with signs: every row and every column has exactly one nonzero value, \(\pm 1\).

Source: The definition is ours, a generalization of the matrix of reflection of a node from lemma 7.36. Chapter 7 denoted the matrix by the letter \(S\), which in chapter 12 is the geometric stiffness, so we write \(\mat P\) here. For a plane \(\Pi\) in another position the blocks are orthogonal instead of diagonal, and \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\) holds in the same way. The rule \(\varphi \mapsto -\varphi\) as the reflection of a rotation is COOK §2.11 (PDF p. 69), rule S2: the rotation vector has no component in the plane of symmetry.

The matrix \(\mat P\) is symmetric and \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\). For \(\mat P^\T\) the block \((i, \bar i)\) comes from the block \((\bar i, i)\), which is the same diagonal matrix, so \(\mat P^\T = \mat P\). For \(\mat P^2\) the block \((i, i)\) is \(\mathrm{diag}(-1, 1, -1)^2 = \mat I\) and all others are zero, because two reflections return a node to its place. Hence \(\mat P^\T = \mat P^{-1} = \mat P\), as for \(\mat Z\) in lemma 19.2.

In lemma 7.36 chapter 7 proved \(\mat S\,\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\mat S = \mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) for a cantilever of three bars by calculation and concluded the response from it. For an arbitrary mesh model we cannot check this by calculation for every case separately, so we first prove that \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) follows from the symmetry of the elements, and then the response.

Theorem 19.6 Symmetry of the solution of a frame model (simetrija rešitve mrežnega modela okvirja)

Let a plane frame model be mirror symmetric with respect to the plane \(\Pi\) (definition 19.5) and let theorem 12.20 have valid hypotheses, that is, let the reduced system have exactly one solution. Let \(\mat K\) be the matrix of the frame, \(\mat P\) the mirror matrix, and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) and \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\) the rows and columns of the free unknowns. Then:

  1. \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) and \(\mat P\mat K = \mat K\mat P\),
  2. \(\mat P\) maps free unknowns to free ones, \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is a permutation matrix with signs, \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}^2 = \mat I\) and \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\),
  3. if the column of loads of the free unknowns \(\vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\) is symmetric, \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek f_{\mathrm{f}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\), the solution \(\vek d_{\mathrm{f}}\) is symmetric, \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = \vek d_{\mathrm{f}}\). If the load is antisymmetric, \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek f_{\mathrm{f}} = -\vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\), the solution is antisymmetric, \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = -\vek d_{\mathrm{f}}\).
Proof

We must show that reflection does not change the energy of any element, hence \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\), and then use the uniqueness of the solution, as in the proof of lemma 7.36.

  1. Let the element \(e\) lie between the nodes \(i\) and \(j\), with the unit tangent \(\vek t\) and the normal \(\vek n_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat Q_{90}\,\vek t\), where \(\mat Q_{90}\) rotates by \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise (local axes from lemma 12.18). The mirror element \(\bar e\) between \(\bar i\) and \(\bar j\) has the tangent \(\mat Z_2\vek t\), where \(\mat Z_2 = \mathrm{diag}(-1, 1)\) is the reflection of the plane, and the normal \(\mat Q_{90}\mat Z_2\vek t = -\mat Z_2\,\mat Q_{90}\,\vek t = -\mat Z_2\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\), because the reflection reverses orientation.
  2. For the column \(\mat P\vek d\) the node \(i\) has the displacement \(\mat Z_2(u_{\bar{i}}, v_{\bar{i}})\) and the rotation \(-\varphi_{\bar{i}}\). The local components of the element \(e\) are then: along the tangent \(\vek t\cdot\mat Z_2\vek w = (\mat Z_2\vek t)\cdot\vek w\), so equal to the axial component of the element \(\bar e\) for \(\vek d\). Along the normal \(\vek n_{\mathrm{e}}\cdot\mat Z_2\vek w = (\mat Z_2\vek n_{\mathrm{e}})\cdot\vek w = -\vek n_{\bar{e}}\cdot\vek w\), so opposite to the transverse component of the element \(\bar e\). The rotation is the opposite rotation. The local column \(\bar{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) of the element \(e\) for \(\mat P\vek d\) is thus \(\mat Y\,\bar{\vek d}_{\bar{e}}\) with \(\mat Y = \mathrm{diag}(1, -1, -1, 1, -1, -1)\) and the local column \(\bar{\vek d}_{\bar{e}}\) of the element \(\bar e\) for \(\vek d\).
  3. The local stiffness matrix \(\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\) (lemma 12.18) is the same for \(e\) and \(\bar e\) (same length, \(EA\) and \(EI\)), and the axial part \(\{1, 4\}\) is not coupled to the bending part \(\{2, 3, 5, 6\}\). The matrix \(\mat Y\) reverses the sign of all bending components at once, so \(\mat Y\,\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Y = \bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\): a nonzero entry of the row \(a\) and column \(b\) gets the factor \(Y_{\mathrm{aa}}Y_{\mathrm{bb}}\), which is \(1\cdot 1\) in the axial part and \((-1)(-1)\) in the bending part, and there are no mixed entries.
  4. The energy of the element \(e\) for \(\mat P\vek d\) is \(\tfrac12\,\bar{\vek d}_{\bar{e}}^\T\,\mat Y\,\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Y\,\bar{\vek d}_{\bar{e}} = \tfrac12\,\bar{\vek d}_{\bar{e}}^\T\,\bar{\mat k}_{\bar{e}}\,\bar{\vek d}_{\bar{e}}\), which is the energy of the element \(\bar e\) for \(\vek d\). The map \(e \mapsto \bar e\) is a bijection of the elements, so \((\mat P\vek d)^\T\mat K\,(\mat P\vek d) = \vek d^\T\mat K\vek d\) by theorem 7.13 (the energy is the sum of the energies of the elements).
  5. The matrix \(\mat A = \mat P\mat K\mat P - \mat K\) is symmetric and \(\vek d^\T\mat A\vek d = 0\) for every \(\vek d\) by step 4 and \(\mat P^\T = \mat P\). For a column \(\vek d\) with a one at the place \(i\) and zeros elsewhere we get \(A_{\mathrm{ii}} = 0\), and for a column with ones at the places \(i\) and \(j\) we get \(A_{\mathrm{ii}} + 2A_{\mathrm{ij}} + A_{\mathrm{jj}} = 2A_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\), so \(\mat A = \mat 0\). From \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) and \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\) follows \(\mat P\mat K = \mat K\mat P\). This is item 1.
  6. By item 3 of the definition an unknown is prescribed exactly when its mirror unknown is prescribed, so \(\mat P\) maps free unknowns to free ones and prescribed to prescribed. Hence \(\mat P\) has no blocks between free and prescribed unknowns, the rows and columns of the free unknowns from \(\mat P\mat K = \mat K\mat P\) give \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\), from which \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}^2\), and from \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\) follows \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}^2 = \mat I\). The matrix \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is a permutation matrix with signs, because it maps the set of free unknowns into itself. This is item 2.
  7. Let \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek f_{\mathrm{f}} = \pm\vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\). Then \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{f}}) = \mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = \mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek f_{\mathrm{f}} = \pm\vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\), so \(\pm\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{f}}\) solves the same reduced system as \(\vek d_{\mathrm{f}}\). By theorem 12.20 the solution is unique, so \(\pm\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{f}} = \vek d_{\mathrm{f}}\). This is item 3.

Source: The theorem is ours. It generalizes lemma 7.36 and lemma 7.38 from one case to an arbitrary frame model. The energy argument of steps 4 and 5 is the same as in step 2 of lemma 7.38.

The proof showed where the symmetry of the elements enters: at every element and its image the axial and the bending stiffness are equal. If any element lacks this property, step 3 and with it the whole proof has a gap.

We test the theorem on the frame of chapter 12. We draw the portal frame with the clamps at \(A\) and \(E\), as before. Through the middle of the beam we draw the plane of reflection. At \(D\) on the plane we hang a weight, that is, we press on the frame with the force \(F = 500\) N downward. The force lies on the plane, so the load is symmetric by definition 19.3. The deformed shape is a mirror image. The section of both columns, under the feet seen along the column, is \(20 \times 40\) mm, the longer side in the plane of the frame. A calculation in NumPy for the \(45\) free unknowns confirms \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\), \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) (the largest difference of the entries is \(0\)) and \(\mat P\vek f = \vek f\). The solution: \(v_{\mathrm{D}} = -0{,}2508\) mm, \(u_{\mathrm{D}} = 0\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{D}} = 0\) up to the rounding error of the computer (of the order of \(10^{-15}\) mm), \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = +0{,}00020\) mm and \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = -0{,}00020\) mm, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}} = -0{,}000498\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{C}} = +0{,}000498\). The mirror nodes have opposite horizontal displacements and opposite rotations, as \(\mat P\vek d = \vek d\) demands: the new number of the node \(B\) is the old number \(C\) and \((-u_{\mathrm{C}}, v_{\mathrm{C}}, -\varphi_{\mathrm{C}}) = (u_{\mathrm{B}}, v_{\mathrm{B}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{B}})\). At \(D\) we have \(\bar i = i\), so \((-u_{\mathrm{D}}, v_{\mathrm{D}}, -\varphi_{\mathrm{D}}) = (u_{\mathrm{D}}, v_{\mathrm{D}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{D}})\) and \(u_{\mathrm{D}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{D}} = 0\). The largest difference between \(\mat P\vek d\) and \(\vek d\) is \(4{,}5\cdot 10^{-18}\) (in metres and radians), which is the error of the computer. The reaction at \(A\) has the horizontal component \(62{,}475\) N, the vertical \(250{,}00\) N and the moment \(-20{,}817\) N m, at \(E\) the horizontal component and the moment are opposite, \(-62{,}475\) N and \(+20{,}817\) N m, and the vertical one is the same: the mirror image of a force and a moment, as in the reflection of a displacement and a rotation.

Now we draw the same frame once more, on the right, with the same plane of reflection and the same force at \(D\). Let us turn the right column by a quarter turn about its axis, which is the same as if it had been installed sideways by mistake during manufacture. The outer shape of the frame is still mirror symmetric, only the section of the right column is now \(40 \times 20\) mm instead of \(20 \times 40\) mm. For \(40 \times 20\) mm the second moment of area in the plane of the frame is \(I = 40\cdot 20^3/12 = 26\,667\) mm\(^4\), which is four times less than before (\(106\,667/26\,667 = 4{,}0\)), and \(EI\) of the right column is \(5\,227\) N m\(^2\) instead of \(20\,907\) N m\(^2\). The mirror element of the column no longer has the same \(EI\): step 3 of the proof of the theorem does not hold, \(\mat P\mat K\mat P \ne \mat K\) (the entries \(12EI/h^3\) of the left and the right column differ by a factor \(4\)), and the solution is not symmetric. The deformed shape shows this: \(v_{\mathrm{D}} = -0{,}3227\) mm, \(1{,}29\) times more than before, and \(u_{\mathrm{D}} = +0{,}2134\) mm sideways, which is a distance of \(0{,}66\) of the deflection, not a small correction. The rotations of the beam are \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}} = -0{,}000741\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{C}} = +0{,}000831\), so no longer opposite. With the largest rotation \(0{,}00083\) and the largest displacement \(0{,}33\) mm on an element of length \(1\) m (ratio below \(4\cdot 10^{-4}\)) the calculation stays within the limits of the linear model, so the loss of symmetry is a property of the frame and not an error of the model.

Why does the frame move sideways? Let us look at the equilibrium of the beam as a body. Horizontally only the tops of the two columns act on it, since the force \(F\) is vertical, so the horizontal forces on the beam must add up to zero (Newton's law). By the law of action and reaction the beam acts on the top of a column with the opposite force, so the sum of the horizontal forces \(H\) that the beam exerts on the two tops is zero too, \(H_{\mathrm{L}} + H_{\mathrm{R}} = 0\). A column of length \(h = 1\) m is clamped at the bottom. By item 3 of theorem 12.20 the field in its four elements is the exact displacement of the frame. The column carries no load, neither along it nor at its interior nodes, so the shear force in it is constant over the whole height and the moment is linear, and the deflection, whose second derivative is by (5.24) the moment divided by \(EI\), is a single cubic polynomial over the whole height \(h\). The column therefore behaves as one element of length \(h\), and the force at its top for a displacement \(u\) and a rotation \(\varphi\) of the top is, by the matrix of lemma 12.18 (row 5, we look at the column from the clamp upward, the local transverse axis points in \(-x\)), \(H = 12EI\,u/h^3 + 6EI\,\varphi/h^2\). The beam is almost inextensible: \(EA\,h^2/EI = 7\,500\) and its shortening is below \(0{,}0004\) mm, so the tops of the columns have the same displacement, \(u_{\mathrm{B}} \approx u_{\mathrm{C}} = u\). From \(H_{\mathrm{L}} + H_{\mathrm{R}} = 0\) follows

\[u = -\frac{h}{2}\,\frac{EI_{\mathrm{L}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{B}} + EI_{\mathrm{R}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{C}}}{EI_{\mathrm{L}} + EI_{\mathrm{R}}} . \tag{19.3}\]

For equal columns and opposite rotations, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{C}} = -\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}\), we have \(u = 0\). For the turned right column \(u = -\tfrac12\,\big(20\,907\cdot(-0{,}000741) + 5\,227\cdot 0{,}000831\big)/26\,134\ \text{m} = 0{,}2133\) mm, which agrees with the calculation, \(0{,}2134\) mm. The softer right column holds the top of the beam back less, so \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{C}}| > |\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}|\), the sum \(EI_{\mathrm{L}}\varphi_{\mathrm{B}} + EI_{\mathrm{R}}\varphi_{\mathrm{C}}\) is no longer zero and the frame moves sideways. The displacement is therefore a consequence of the different stiffnesses of the columns, not of an error of the calculation.

Theorem 19.6 is thus usable only when the model is truly mirror symmetric in all three points of the definition, and it fails if the elements are not equal, as the frame with the turned column showed. In the following sections we use it for three things: the conditions on the plane (section 19.2), the split of an arbitrary load (section 19.3) and vibration, where the symmetry tells what the half model misses (section 19.4).

19.2 Conditions on the plane of symmetry and the half model

Section 19.1 showed that the solution of a symmetric problem cannot differ from its mirror image: for a symmetric load theorem 19.4 gives \(\vek u(\vek x) = \mat Z\,\vek u(\mat Z\vek x)\), for an antisymmetric load \(\vek u(\vek x) = -\mat Z\,\vek u(\mat Z\vek x)\), and for the frame model theorem 19.6 gives \(\vek d = \mat P\vek d\) or \(\vek d = -\mat P\vek d\). What does this save us in the computation? If the right half is the image of the left half, we need not compute the right one. But we cannot simply cut out the left half and leave it free, because at the cut, in the plane of symmetry (the plane of reflection \(\Pi\), with respect to which the structure is mirror symmetric), it was held by the right half. The question of this section is therefore: with what support at the cut do we replace the removed half, so that the left half receives the same displacements and forces as in the whole? And what happens to the load and the stiffness that lie on the plane itself?

We test the answer on the portal frame of section 19.1 (figure 19.2): columns \(AB\) and \(EC\) \(1\) m high, clamped at \(A\) and \(E\), beam \(BC\) \(1\) m long with node \(D\) in the middle, steel \(E = 196\) GPa, cross-section \(20 \times 40\) mm (height \(40\) mm in the plane of the frame), \(EA = 1{,}568 \cdot 10^8\) N and \(EI = 20\,907\) N m\(^2\), the columns each made of four frame elements, the beam of eight, four on each half \(BD\) and \(DC\), in all \(17\) nodes and \(45\) free unknowns. The model is the one of chapter 12: an Euler-Bernoulli frame with small displacements and neglected shear deformation. We check smallness on the solution below, for a horizontal force of \(500\) N at \(B\): the largest displacement is \(1{,}43\) mm over a length of \(1\) m, that is \(1{,}4 \cdot 10^{-3}\) of the length, and the largest rotation is \(1{,}9 \cdot 10^{-3}\) rad (in the columns). Equilibrium on the undeformed shape neglects that the deformation moves the points of application of the forces by the displacements and turns the directions of the elements by the rotations. The neglected terms are therefore of order \(2 \cdot 10^{-3}\) of the kept ones, and the computation is accurate to a few parts per thousand. For this frame we write \(\mat P\) for the mirror matrix (definition 19.5) and \(\mat Z\) for the reflection of points of space.

Let us draw the frame part by part. First the frame: columns \(AB\) and \(EC\) are clamped at \(A\) and \(E\), the beam joins \(B\) and \(C\), and its midpoint is \(D\). Through \(D\) we place the plane of symmetry \(\Pi\), vertical and perpendicular to the plane of the frame, so in the figure we see it as a line. We call it so because we can set it up as a mirror: the frame in the mirror is the same frame. The mirror arrow shows where the mirror sends the nodes: \(B\) to \(C\), \(A\) to \(E\), and \(D\) to \(D\), since it lies on the plane. Finally the force \(H\) at \(B\), directed towards \(C\). In the middle and right figures it is the same frame (middle, right) with the same plane and with the deformation that the computation gives for the load of the right figure. The midpoint \(D\) of the beam lies in the plane before the deformation and moves horizontally, perpendicular to the plane, as the frame deforms.

The load \(H\) is neither symmetric nor antisymmetric. The mirror would send the force at \(B\) to a force at \(C\) in the opposite direction, which is neither the same load nor its opposite. How to split such a load into two parts, each symmetric or antisymmetric by itself, is the subject of the next section. Here we only add: a pair of forces that mirror each other, \(\tfrac12 H = 250\) N at \(B\) to the right and \(250\) N at \(C\) to the left, is mapped by the mirror into itself, a pair of forces in the same direction, \(250\) N at \(B\) and \(250\) N at \(C\) to the right, is mapped by the mirror into its opposite, since the mirror image would point at \(C\) and \(B\) to the left. The sum at \(B\) is \(250 + 250 = 500\) N, at \(C\) it is \(-250 + 250 = 0\), so this is the original load \(H\).

What does the computation of the whole frame show on the plane? We build the mirror matrix \(\mat P\) by the rule: node \(i\) goes to the mirror node \(\bar i\), the horizontal displacement changes sign because the mirror reverses the direction of the \(x\) axis, the vertical one stays, and the rotation changes sign because a counterclockwise rotation is seen in the mirror as a clockwise one (a wheel turning left turns right in the mirror). So \((\mat P\vek d)_{\bar{i}} = (-u_{\mathrm{i}},\ v_{\mathrm{i}},\ -\varphi_{\mathrm{i}})\), the block \(\mathrm{diag}(-1, 1, -1)\) at each node. A NumPy computation confirms \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) and \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\). For the two parts of the load the computed solutions at \(D\) are:

part of the load \(u_{\mathrm{D}}\) \(v_{\mathrm{D}}\) \(\varphi_{\mathrm{D}}\)
symmetric \(< 10^{-19}\) m \(-0{,}00020\) mm \(< 10^{-19}\)
antisymmetric \(1{,}4247\) mm \(< 10^{-16}\) m \(0{,}000424\)

For the symmetric load \(u_{\mathrm{D}}\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{D}}\) are zero but \(v_{\mathrm{D}}\) is not. For the antisymmetric load it is exactly the opposite, \(v_{\mathrm{D}}\) is zero. Is this an accident of this frame? No: why, the theorem shows, first for a body, then for a frame.

For the body we ask what the mirror image and Newton's third law said about a point on the plane. A point \(\vek x\) on the plane is its own mirror image. If the load is symmetric, then under reflection everything that is displaced coincides with its image, so the point cannot move perpendicular to the plane: a displacement to one side would have its image on the other side, but both would be the displacement of the same point. It can slide along the plane. The same holds for the force with which the right half acts on the left. The force of the left half on the right is, by Newton's third law, its opposite, and its mirror image must be that force, since the state is symmetric. A force that is the opposite of its mirror image is perpendicular to the plane, since reflection leaves the tangential component and reverses the perpendicular one. The tangential (shear) component of the force on the plane is therefore zero. For an antisymmetric load the mirror image of the state is the opposite state, so everything is reversed: the point slides only perpendicular to the plane and the force has no component perpendicular to it. We carry out the proof without pictures, from theorem 19.4.

Theorem 19.7 Conditions on the plane of symmetry (pogoji na ravnini simetrije)

Let the boundary value problem be symmetric or antisymmetric with respect to the plane \(\Pi\) with unit normal \(\vek m\) and reflection \(\mat Z\) (definition 19.3), and let it satisfy the hypotheses of theorem 19.4. Let \(\vek u\) be the solution with stress \(\ten\sigma\), continuous up to the plane, \(\vek x\) a point on \(\Pi\) and \(\vek t = \ten\sigma(\vek x)\,\vek m\) the traction vector on a surface with normal \(\vek m\). Then:

  1. for a symmetric load \(\vek m\cdot\vek u(\vek x) = 0\) (the displacement has no perpendicular component) and \(\vek t = (\vek m\cdot\vek t)\,\vek m\) (the shear component of the traction vector is zero),
  2. for an antisymmetric load \(\vek u(\vek x) = (\vek m\cdot\vek u)\,\vek m\) (the displacement has no component in the plane) and \(\vek m\cdot\vek t = 0\) (the perpendicular component of the traction vector is zero).
Proof

We must show that the equality of stresses from theorem 19.4 at a point on the plane contradicts itself unless the stated components vanish. The sign \(\pm\) means \(+\) for a symmetric and \(-\) for an antisymmetric load.

  1. Displacement. For \(\vek x\in\Pi\) we have \(\mat Z\vek x = \vek x\) (lemma 19.2, item 2), so by item 1 of theorem 19.4 \(\vek u(\vek x) = \pm\,\mat Z\,\vek u(\vek x)\). By definition (19.1) \(\mat Z\vek u = \vek u - 2\vek m(\vek m\cdot\vek u)\). For the sign \(+\) it follows that \(\vek m\cdot\vek u = 0\), for the sign \(-\) that \(\vek u = -\vek u + 2\vek m(\vek m\cdot\vek u)\), so \(\vek u = \vek m(\vek m\cdot\vek u)\). This is item 3 of theorem 19.4, which is here the first part of the claim.
  2. Stress. By item 2 of theorem 19.4 \(\ten\sigma(\vek x) = \pm\,\mat Z\,\ten\sigma(\mat Z\vek x)\,\mat Z\). For \(\vek x\in\Pi\) this is \(\ten\sigma = \pm\,\mat Z\ten\sigma\mat Z\).
  3. Multiply by \(\vek m\) and use \(\mat Z\vek m = \vek m - 2\vek m = -\vek m\) (lemma 19.2): \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\vek m = \pm\,\mat Z\ten\sigma\mat Z\vek m = \mp\,\mat Z\,\ten\sigma\vek m = \mp\,\mat Z\,\vek t\).
  4. For the sign \(+\) we have \(\vek t = -\mat Z\vek t = -\vek t + 2\vek m(\vek m\cdot\vek t)\), so \(\vek t = \vek m(\vek m\cdot\vek t)\). For the sign \(-\) we have \(\vek t = \mat Z\vek t = \vek t - 2\vek m(\vek m\cdot\vek t)\), so \(\vek m\cdot\vek t = 0\). This is the second part of the claim.

Source: COOK §2.11 (PDF p. 69): the rules S1 "Translational motion has no component normal to a plane of symmetry" and A1 "Translational motion has no component in a plane of antisymmetry", ONATE1 §9.6.1 (PDF p. 347) the same rules. The conditions for the traction vector and the proof are not from the source.

The theorem says what the half we keep must have at the cut. The symmetric case: the removed half is replaced by a smooth wall. Its wall with rollers allows sliding along the plane, so the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{t}}\) along the plane is free and the displacement perpendicular to it is zero (first part of the theorem), and the rollers can push only perpendicular to the wall, with a force \(t_{\mathrm{n}}\), so the shear component of the force is zero. The antisymmetric case is the twin: the removed half is replaced by a rod in a sleeve, which allows only a displacement perpendicular \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) and the sleeve pushes it only along the plane, with a force \(t_{\mathrm{t}}\). The first support acts as a roller, the second as a rod in a sleeve, and each allows what the other forbids. The plane \(\Pi\) is dashed in both figures, since it is absent after the cut.

The conditions hold only if the stiffness is symmetric as well. The frame with a rotated right column from section 19.1 has symmetric geometry, supports and load, but the stiffness is not (\(\mat P\mat K\mat P \ne \mat K\)), and under a vertical force of \(500\) N at \(D\) the point \(D\) moves horizontally by \(u_{\mathrm{D}} = 0{,}2134\) mm. The condition \(u_{\mathrm{D}} = 0\), which the table showed for equal columns and a symmetric load, therefore fails: theorem 19.6 requires \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\), so the solution is not symmetric and the condition \(u_{\mathrm{D}} = 0\) has no basis. A half model that enforced \(u_{\mathrm{D}} = 0\) would miss all of the horizontal motion of the point \(D\), that is \(0{,}2134\) mm.

In a frame the unknowns are not a displacement field but \(u\), \(v\) and \(\varphi\) of the nodes, so we prove the theorem for a frame directly with the matrix \(\mat P\). The rotation in the plane of the frame is a rotation vector along the \(z\) axis, which lies in \(\Pi\), so the rule S2 of COOK ("rotation vectors have no components in a plane of symmetry") forbids a rotation in the symmetric case. Let us prove it.

Corollary 19.8 Conditions at a frame node on the plane of symmetry (pogoji v vozlišču okvirja na ravnini simetrije)

Let a plane frame (definition 5.90), divided into frame elements (definition 12.17) with no loads on the elements, be symmetric with respect to a vertical plane \(\Pi\) perpendicular to the plane of the frame, and let \(\vek d\) be the solution of theorem 12.20 for a symmetric (\(\mat P\vek f = \vek f\)) or antisymmetric (\(\mat P\vek f = -\vek f\)) load. Let \(J\) be a node on \(\Pi\) with no external force, in which exactly two elements meet, \(e_1\) left of \(\Pi\) and its mirror image \(e_2\). Let \(\vek F_{\mathrm{i}} = (X_{\mathrm{i}}, Y_{\mathrm{i}}, M_{\mathrm{i}})^\T\) be the column of the components of force and moment with which the element \(e_{\mathrm{i}}\) acts on the node \(J\) (global axes, item 3 of theorem 12.20). Then:

  1. for a symmetric load \(u_{\mathrm{J}} = 0\), \(\varphi_{\mathrm{J}} = 0\) and \(\vek F_2 = (-X_1, Y_1, -M_1)^\T\) and \(Y_1 = 0\),
  2. for an antisymmetric load \(v_{\mathrm{J}} = 0\) and \(\vek F_2 = (X_1, -Y_1, M_1)^\T\) and \(X_1 = 0\) and \(M_1 = 0\).

If the member \(e_1e_2\) is horizontal, as in example A, then \(X\) is the axial force, \(Y\) the shear force and \(M\) the bending moment of the member at \(J\) (up to sign).

Proof

We must show that the mirror image of the solution at the node \(J\) gives an equality that requires the stated components to vanish, and that the equilibrium of the node requires the stated forces to vanish.

  1. By theorem 19.6 \(\vek d = \pm\,\mat P\vek d\) (\(+\) for a symmetric load). The node \(J\) is its own mirror node, so \((u_{\mathrm{J}}, v_{\mathrm{J}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{J}}) = \pm(-u_{\mathrm{J}},\ v_{\mathrm{J}},\ -\varphi_{\mathrm{J}})\).
  2. For the sign \(+\) we have \(u_{\mathrm{J}} = -u_{\mathrm{J}}\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{J}} = -\varphi_{\mathrm{J}}\), so \(u_{\mathrm{J}} = 0\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{J}} = 0\). For the sign \(-\) we have \(v_{\mathrm{J}} = -v_{\mathrm{J}}\), so \(v_{\mathrm{J}} = 0\).
  3. The element \(e_2\) is the mirror image of the element \(e_1\): the same length, cross-section and material. We number the two nodes of \(e_2\) in the same order as their mirror images in \(e_1\). By steps 1 to 4 of the proof of theorem 19.6 the energy of the element \(e_2\) at the column \(\vek d_2\) equals the energy of the element \(e_1\) at the column \(\vek d_1 = \mat P_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_2\), where \(\mat P_{\mathrm{e}} = \mathrm{diag}(\mat D, \mat D)\) and \(\mat D = \mathrm{diag}(-1, 1, -1)\). The matrix \(\mat k_2\) is therefore the matrix of the quadratic form \(\vek d_2 \mapsto \vek d_1^\T\mat k_1\vek d_1\), so \(\mat k_2 = \mat P_{\mathrm{e}}\mat k_1\mat P_{\mathrm{e}}\) (two symmetric matrices with the same quadratic form are equal, step 5 of the proof of theorem 19.6).
  4. By step 1 the displacements of the element \(e_2\) are the mirrored displacements of \(e_1\): \(\vek d_2 = \pm\,\mat P_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_1\). Hence \(\vek F_2^{\text{el}} = \mat k_2\vek d_2 = \mat P_{\mathrm{e}}\mat k_1\mat P_{\mathrm{e}}(\pm\mat P_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_1) = \pm\,\mat P_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat k_1\vek d_1 = \pm\,\mat P_{\mathrm{e}}\vek F_1^{\text{el}}\). The components of these six numbers at the node \(J\) are \(\vek F_2 = \pm\,\mat D\,\vek F_1\), which is \((-X_1, Y_1, -M_1)\) for the sign \(+\) and \((X_1, -Y_1, M_1)\) for the sign \(-\).
  5. The node \(J\) has no external force, so by item 1 of theorem 12.20 \(\vek F_1 + \vek F_2 = \vek 0\). For the sign \(+\) this is \((0,\ 2Y_1,\ 0) = \vek 0\), so \(Y_1 = 0\). For the sign \(-\) it is \((2X_1,\ 0,\ 2M_1) = \vek 0\), so \(X_1 = 0\) and \(M_1 = 0\).

Source: COOK §2.11 (PDF p. 69): the rules S2 "Rotation vectors have no components in a plane of symmetry" and A2 "Rotation vectors have no components normal to a plane of antisymmetry", ONATE1 §9.6.1 (PDF p. 347). The proof and the forces in the member are not from the source.

On example A: for the symmetric part the shear force of the beam at \(D\) is zero, the axial force is \(-249{,}90\) N (the beam is compressed by almost exactly \(\tfrac12 H = 250\) N, the difference of \(0{,}10\) N is the shear force of the column, which resists the motion of \(B\) towards the middle) and the moment is \(0{,}033\) N m, and neither is zero. For the antisymmetric part the axial force and the moment are zero, the shear force is \(214{,}19\) N. The computation on the whole frame gives the same: the left and the right element act on \(D\) with opposite forces and opposite moments, and the sum is zero in both cases, as step 5 requires.

Now we have the conditions the half needs. But what about the load and the stiffness that lie on the plane itself? Chapter 7 already saw this with the bridge: the bar \(b_3t_3\) on the axis of symmetry had half the cross-section in the half model, and the load at \(b_3\) was halved (lemma 7.39). Why a half? Take a node \(J\) on the plane. Its row in the system \(\mat K\vek d = \vek f\) contains the contributions of all the elements that meet at \(J\): the elements on the left, their mirror images on the right, and the elements that lie in the plane. The left and right groups contribute equally, so twice as much as the left one alone. If the half model keeps only the left group, the row must stay the same, so the load must be halved and the contribution of the elements in the plane must be halved, and this is exactly the rule of the bridge. We prove it for every mirror symmetric frame model and both types of load.

Lemma 19.9 Half model of a symmetric frame (polovični model simetričnega okvirja)

Let a plane frame model be mirror symmetric with respect to the plane \(\Pi\) (definition 19.5), with the matrix \(\mat K\), the displacement column \(\vek d\) and the mirror matrix \(\mat P\), so that \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) (theorem 19.6). Let the elements be left (\(L\), both nodes left of \(\Pi\) or on it, at least one left), their mirror images right (\(R\)), or lie on \(\Pi\) (\(\Pi\)-elements, both nodes on \(\Pi\), the mirror image is the element itself). Let the load be \(\vek f\) with \(\mat P\vek f = \pm\vek f\) (\(+\) symmetric, \(-\) antisymmetric). By item 3 of the definition the prescribed unknowns have zero values and map into themselves. Let the reduced matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) of the whole structure be positive definite (theorem 7.18). The half model \(H\) (polovični model), so called because it has only half of the structure, has the nodes from the left and from the plane, the elements \(L\) with stiffnesses \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\), the elements \(\Pi\) with stiffnesses \(\tfrac12\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\), the load \(\vek f_{\mathrm{i}}\) at the left nodes and \(\tfrac12\vek f_{\mathrm{J}}\) at the nodes \(J\) on \(\Pi\), the prescribed unknowns of the left half and, on the plane, those unknowns that \(\mat P\) multiplies by \(\mp 1\), that is \(u = \varphi = 0\) for the sign \(+\) and \(v = 0\) for the sign \(-\) (corollary 19.8). Then:

  1. the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}^H\) of the model \(H\) is positive definite and its solution \(\vek d_{\mathrm{H}}\) is unique,
  2. \(\vek d_{\mathrm{H}}\) is the restriction of the solution \(\vek d\) of the whole structure to the left and plane nodes, and on the right \(\vek d = \pm\,\mat P\vek d\),
  3. if only elements \(L\) and \(R\) meet at a node \(J\) on the plane, the reaction of the model \(H\) in the unknown \(c\) that the plane forbids is equal to \(-\Sigma_{\mathrm{L}}\), so up to sign the force with which the left elements act on \(J\) (notation in step 2 of the proof). The support in \(H\) replaces the removed half.
Proof

We must show that \(\vek d\) solves the rows of the model \(H\), and use uniqueness, which we prove by energy.

  1. Let \(i\) be a left node and \(a\) its free unknown. In the row \(a\) of the system \(\mat K\vek d = \vek f + \vek r\) only the elements that meet at \(i\) appear, these are elements \(L\) (elements \(R\) and \(\Pi\) have no left nodes). The row is therefore equal to the row of the model \(H\) with the same column \(\vek d\) and the same right-hand side \(f_{\mathrm{a}}\).
  2. Let \(J\) be a node on \(\Pi\) and \(c\) its unknown that is not prescribed in \(H\) (\(v\) for the sign \(+\), \(u\) and \(\varphi\) for the sign \(-\)). The row \(c\) of the system contains the contribution of the elements \(L\), the elements \(R\) and the elements \(\Pi\) at \(J\): \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{L}} + \Sigma_{\mathrm{R}} + \Sigma_\Pi = f_{\mathrm{Jc}}\). As in step 4 of the proof of corollary 19.8, which requires only that the element \(R\) is the mirror image of the element \(L\), the force of the element \(R\) on \(J\) is \(\pm\,\mat D\) times the force of its mirror element \(L\). For the sign \(+\) the component \(c = v\) is multiplied by \(+1\), for the sign \(-\) the components \(c = u, \varphi\) are multiplied by \((-1)(-1) = +1\), so \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{R}} = \Sigma_{\mathrm{L}}\). The row is \(2\Sigma_{\mathrm{L}} + \Sigma_\Pi = f_{\mathrm{Jc}}\), that is \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{L}} + \tfrac12\Sigma_\Pi = \tfrac12 f_{\mathrm{Jc}}\), the row of the model \(H\).
  3. The prescribed unknowns of the model \(H\) are held by \(\vek d\) by step 2 of the proof of corollary 19.8, which needs only \(\vek d = \pm\,\mat P\vek d\) (the plane), and by assumption (the supports on the left). The rows of all free unknowns of the model \(H\) are satisfied by steps 1 and 2, so \(\vek d_{\mathrm{H}} = \vek d|_{\mathrm{H}}\) solves \(H\).
  4. Positive definiteness. Let \(\vek w \ne \vek 0\) be a column of unknowns of the model \(H\) with zero prescribed values. We extend it to the right half with \(\mat P\): \(\hat{\vek w} = \vek w\) at the left and plane nodes, \(\hat{\vek w} = \pm\,\mat P\vek w\) at the right ones. This is well defined, because on the plane \(\vek w = \pm\,\mat P\vek w\) holds: the components that would change sign under reflection are prescribed and zero. \(\hat{\vek w} \ne \vek 0\) satisfies the prescribed conditions of the whole structure (the supports map into themselves with zero values).
  5. Energy: \(\hat{\vek w}^\T\mat K\hat{\vek w} = \sum_{\mathrm{L}}\vek w_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek w_{\mathrm{e}} + \sum_{\mathrm{R}}(\dots) + \sum_{\Pi}\vek w_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek w_{\mathrm{e}}\) (item 2 of theorem 7.13). The elements \(R\) contribute the same as their images \(L\) (step 3 of the proof of corollary 19.8), so the sum is \(2\sum_{\mathrm{L}} + \sum_\Pi = 2\big(\sum_{\mathrm{L}} + \tfrac12\sum_\Pi\big) = 2\,\vek w^\T\mat K^H\vek w\). The left side is positive by the assumption on \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\), so also \(\vek w^\T\mat K^H_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek w > 0\). By theorem 6.29 \(H\) has exactly one solution, so \(\vek d_{\mathrm{H}} = \vek d|_{\mathrm{H}}\). These are items 1 and 2 (the right side by step 1 of the corollary).
  6. Let \(c\) be the unknown of the node \(J\) that the plane forbids and \(r_{\mathrm{c}}\) the reaction of the model \(H\). Its row \(c\) is \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{L}} + r_{\mathrm{c}} = \tfrac12 f_{\mathrm{Jc}}\). The component \(f_{\mathrm{Jc}}\) is zero, because \(\mat P\vek f = \pm\vek f\) at this component (which changes sign) gives \(f_{\mathrm{Jc}} = -f_{\mathrm{Jc}}\). So \(r_{\mathrm{c}} = -\Sigma_{\mathrm{L}}\). This is item 3.

Source: COOK §2.11 (PDF p. 69): "if a stiffening beam under a floor slab is longitudinally bisected by a plane of symmetry, only half its stiffness is retained in the portion analyzed", "Load on this octant is Px/2, because the original load Px is bisected by the symmetry plane". ONATE1 §9.6.1 (PDF p. 346-347). The proof is not from the source.

What have we shown? A half with the right supports at the cut does not merely approximate but exactly reproduces the solution of the whole, provided the load and the stiffness on the plane are halved. Chapter 7 proved this for the bridge with the bar \(b_3t_3\) on the axis of symmetry and symmetric vertical loads. Now it holds for every mirror symmetric frame model with supports that the mirror maps into themselves, and for both types of load. The bridge of chapter 7 is a truss with nonsymmetric supports, fixed at \(b_0\) and movable at \(b_6\), so it also needs the rigid shift from the proof of lemma 7.38.

We check it on example A. We keep the left half, that is the column \(AB\) and half of the beam \(BD\): \(9\) nodes and \(27\) unknowns. The symmetric model has a clamp at \(A\) and at \(D\) a guide where \(u = 0\) and \(\varphi = 0\) and \(v\) is free, so \(27 - 3 - 2 = 22\) unknowns. The antisymmetric model has at \(D\) a roller that allows \(u\) and \(\varphi\) and forbids \(v\), so \(27 - 3 - 1 = 23\) unknowns. The sum \(22 + 23 = 45\) is the number of free unknowns of the whole, and this is no accident: every column \(\vek d\) splits in exactly one way into \(\tfrac12(\vek d + \mat P\vek d)\) and \(\tfrac12(\vek d - \mat P\vek d)\), the first symmetric, the second antisymmetric. Both halves carry the load \(\tfrac12 H\) at \(B\).

The solutions of the models agree with the whole. Symmetric model: \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 0{,}0008\) mm, \(v_{\mathrm{D}} = -0{,}00020\) mm, the reaction at \(D\) is an axial force \(249{,}90\) N and a moment \(0{,}033\) N m, which is the force of the removed half (item 3 of the lemma). Antisymmetric model: \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 1{,}4247\) mm, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{D}} = 0{,}000424\) and the reaction at \(D\) is a shear force \(214{,}19\) N. The sum \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 0{,}0008 + 1{,}4247 = 1{,}4255\) mm is the horizontal displacement of \(B\) in the whole frame with \(H = 500\) N. Two computations with \(22\) and \(23\) unknowns replace one with \(45\).

What if we do not halve the stiffness of an element on the plane? Let us add to the frame a short column \(DG\) in the plane of symmetry: \(1\) m long, the same cross-section, clamped at \(G\), four elements, in all \(21\) nodes. In the whole the load \(F = 500\) N acts downwards at \(D\) on the plane. The column lies in the plane and \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) still holds (NumPy). The displacement is \(v_{\mathrm{D}} = -0{,}00315\) mm: the column takes \(493{,}72\) N, each part of the beam \(3{,}14\) N of shear force (\(493{,}72 + 2 \cdot 3{,}14 = 500{,}00\) N). So little, because the column is very stiff axially, \(EA/L = 1{,}568 \cdot 10^8\) N/m, and by itself it would give \(500/(1{,}568 \cdot 10^8) = 3{,}19 \cdot 10^{-6}\) m.

Let us compare three computations. The correct half model has the left half of the frame, the column with halved stiffness, a guide at \(D\) and a force of \(250\) N, and gives \(v_{\mathrm{D}} = -0{,}00315\) mm, as the whole. The wrong model has the same half of the frame and the same force, but the column with full stiffness, and gives \(v_{\mathrm{D}} = -0{,}00158\) mm, half of the true displacement (ratio \(0{,}503\)). Why almost exactly half? The column carries almost the entire load, so the displacement is about the load divided by the stiffness of the column. The wrong model has half the load and full stiffness, hence half the displacement.

The same happens for the antisymmetric part of \(H\), where \(v = 0\) on the plane and the column acts in bending. The whole frame has \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 0{,}8049\) mm and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{D}} = -0{,}000096\), the model with halved stiffness the same, and the model with full stiffness \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 0{,}6148\) mm (\(24\) % too small) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{D}} = -0{,}000233\). Without the column \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 1{,}4247\) mm: the column, clamped at \(G\), holds back the midpoint of the beam.

Is the halved matrix really the stiffness of half of the column? If we cut the column lengthwise by the plane \(\Pi\), each strip has cross-section \(A/2\), so the axial stiffness \(EA/2\) is exactly halved. In bending about the axis through the centroid of the whole cross-section the strip has, by Steiner's theorem (theorem 5.28), \(20\cdot 20^3/12 + 400\cdot 10^2 = 13\,333 + 40\,000 = 53\,333\) mm\(^4 = I/2\), since its centroid is \(10\) mm from the axis and its area is \(400\) mm\(^2\). The halving is therefore also in bending the stiffness of a strip that remains connected to the axis of the whole column. If we took the strip as an independent beam with its own axis, we would get only \(I/8\) (\(13\,333\) mm\(^4\)) and an error.

The error is not caught by the sum of reactions, since the model with the wrong stiffness is again a correctly solved system, as with the wrong support of the bridge (chapter 7). It is caught by the comparison with the whole and by the rule of the lemma: an element on the plane gets half of the stiffness, just as it gets half of the load.

The conditions on the plane hold for each part of the load separately. The next section therefore answers the question that example A only hinted at: how to split an arbitrary load into a symmetric and an antisymmetric part and how to add the solutions.

19.3 Splitting a load into symmetric and antisymmetric parts

Mirror symmetry saved us half the work in sections 19.1 and 19.2, but only for a load that the mirror maps onto itself or onto its negative (definition 19.3). Such loads are not common. A typical case is a horizontal force on a frame (figure 19.8, left). Take a steel portal frame: two columns of length \(1\) m clamped at \(A\) and \(E\) and a beam of length \(1\) m between the nodes \(B\) and \(C\), all of a \(20 \times 40\) mm section (height \(40\) mm in the plane of the frame) with \(E = 196\) GPa. A force \(H = 500\) N acts on the node \(B\) to the right. The mirror that maps the frame onto itself maps this force to a force at the node \(C\) pointing left, a load the frame does not have. Does this make the symmetry useless?

It does not, because a law we know from every statics problem holds: if the model is linear (small displacements, Hooke's law, corollary 11.3), the response to a sum of loads is the sum of the responses. In our frame the displacements are below \(1{,}5\) mm in \(1\) m, which is less than \(0{,}15\) %, and the steel is far below yield. We can therefore write the load \(H\) as a sum of two loads, each symmetric or antisymmetric, solve each on a half of the frame and add the results. Instead of one problem with the whole frame we solve two with half frames. This is how COOK (section 2.11, PDF p. 70) solves a frame in which symmetry is not visible at first sight, and BARBER (section 5.2.3, PDF p. 81) a beam that is symmetric while its load is not symmetric about its axis. Figure 19.8 shows such a split.

Let us do this on the board. First we draw the frame, carried by the columns with clamps at \(A\) and \(E\), and the beam between the rigid corners \(B\) and \(C\). We mark the middle of the beam with the node \(D\), because it lies on the mirror plane that divides the frame into a left and a right half. Then we add the force \(H\) at \(B\). To the right of the equals sign we draw the same frame twice, each with a part of the force. In the first, the force \(H/2\) at \(B\) points right and the force \(H/2\) at \(C\) points left, a mirror pair that the mirror maps onto itself. In the second, both forces \(H/2\) point right, an antisymmetric pair, because the mirror maps the first force onto the second but with the opposite sign. The sum at \(B\) is \(H/2 + H/2 = H\) and at \(C\) it is \(-H/2 + H/2 = 0\), exactly our load. Next we cut the beam at \(D\) and draw what the halves exchange. In the symmetric part the forces \(H/2\) press the beam from both ends towards each other, so the right half acts on the left half with an axial force \(N\) pointing left, and the left half on the right half likewise. In the antisymmetric part both forces point right, the frame tilts, and the cut beam carries a shear force \(V\) that pulls the left half up and the right half down. Why choose exactly the halves? Because this is the only choice for which each part is symmetric or antisymmetric. The next lemma proves it for every load column and every mirror matrix.

Lemma 19.10 Split of a load into symmetric and antisymmetric parts (razcep bremena na simetrični in protisimetrični del)

Let \(\mat P\) be a matrix of size \(n \times n\) with \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\) (for instance a mirror matrix of definition 19.5), and \(\vek f \in \mathbb{R}^n\) a column of loads. Then:

  1. The columns
    \[\vek f_{\mathrm{s}} = \tfrac12\,(\vek f + \mat P\vek f) , \qquad \vek f_{\mathrm{a}} = \tfrac12\,(\vek f - \mat P\vek f) \tag{19.4}\]
    satisfy \(\vek f = \vek f_{\mathrm{s}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\), \(\mat P\vek f_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\mat P\vek f_{\mathrm{a}} = -\vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\). The column \(\vek f_{\mathrm{s}}\) is a symmetric load, \(\vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\) an antisymmetric one.
  2. If \(\vek f = \vek g_{\mathrm{s}} + \vek g_{\mathrm{a}}\) with \(\mat P\vek g_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek g_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\mat P\vek g_{\mathrm{a}} = -\vek g_{\mathrm{a}}\), then \(\vek g_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\vek g_{\mathrm{a}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\).
Proof

We must show that the split exists (item 1) and that it is the only one (item 2). Existence is checked by computation, uniqueness comes from a trick we shall use several times: apply the matrix \(\mat P\) to the equation and add or subtract.

  1. Sum: \(\vek f_{\mathrm{s}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{a}} = \tfrac12(\vek f + \mat P\vek f) + \tfrac12(\vek f - \mat P\vek f) = \vek f\).
  2. Since \(\mat P\) is linear and \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\), \(\mat P\vek f_{\mathrm{s}} = \tfrac12(\mat P\vek f + \mat P^2\vek f) = \tfrac12(\mat P\vek f + \vek f) = \vek f_{\mathrm{s}}\).
  3. Likewise \(\mat P\vek f_{\mathrm{a}} = \tfrac12(\mat P\vek f - \mat P^2\vek f) = \tfrac12(\mat P\vek f - \vek f) = -\vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\).
  4. Let \(\vek f = \vek g_{\mathrm{s}} + \vek g_{\mathrm{a}}\) be another split. The equation multiplied by \(\mat P\) gives \(\mat P\vek f = \vek g_{\mathrm{s}} - \vek g_{\mathrm{a}}\), because \(\mat P\vek g_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek g_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\mat P\vek g_{\mathrm{a}} = -\vek g_{\mathrm{a}}\).
  5. Adding the equations of step 4 and the original equation gives \(\vek f + \mat P\vek f = 2\vek g_{\mathrm{s}}\), so \(\vek g_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{s}}\). Subtracting gives \(\vek f - \mat P\vek f = 2\vek g_{\mathrm{a}}\), so \(\vek g_{\mathrm{a}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\).

Source: COOK section 2.11 (PDF p. 70): the load is the "sum of symmetric and antisymmetric parts". BARBER section 5.2.3 (PDF p. 81): the same split for a continuous body. The formulas and the proof are not from the sources.

The lemma says what the split is, but not whether we may use it to compute displacements. The theorem says so, and it asks for the same as section 19.1: the structure is symmetric, that is \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) (theorem 19.6), and the supports are symmetric, so the mirror maps clamped unknowns onto clamped unknowns. Chapter 7 marked the free unknowns with the index \(f\), and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is the stiffness matrix after clamping. Here \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\) denotes the rows and columns of \(\mat P\) that belong to the free unknowns.

Theorem 19.11 Two half models instead of one (dva polovična modela namesto enega)

Let \(\mat K\) be the stiffness matrix of a discrete structure with clamped unknowns that are zero, and \(\mat P\) a signed permutation (a permutation matrix with signs, like the mirror matrix of definition 19.5) with \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\) and \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) that maps the set of clamped unknowns onto itself. Let \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) be positive definite and \(\vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\) the load on the free unknowns. Then items 1 to 3 hold, and for a frame model with the mirror matrix \(\mat P\) also item 4:

  1. \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is a signed permutation (a permutation matrix with signs, definition 19.5) of the free unknowns, \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}^2 = \mat I\) and \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\).
  2. The systems \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{a}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\) with the split (19.4) (for \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\)) have one solution each, and \(\vek d = \vek d_{\mathrm{s}} + \vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\) is the solution of the system \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\,\vek d = \vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\).
  3. \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek d_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{a}} = -\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\): the displacements of the symmetric load are symmetric, those of the antisymmetric load antisymmetric.
  4. The restriction of the column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{s}}\) to the left half and the plane is the solution of the half model with symmetric conditions on the mirror plane, the restriction of the column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\) the solution of the half model with antisymmetric conditions (corollary 19.8, lemma 19.9), both with the load of the left half and half the load on the plane.
Proof

We must show four things. The first comes from splitting the unknowns into free and clamped, the second from linearity and uniqueness, the third from the same trick as in lemma 19.10, the fourth is lemma 19.9 applied to each part separately.

  1. The matrix \(\mat P\) is a signed permutation and maps clamped unknowns onto clamped ones, so it also maps free onto free. If we order the unknowns free first and clamped second, \(\mat P = \operatorname{diag}(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}, \mat P_{\mathrm{cc}})\) with signed permutations \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\) and \(\mat P_{\mathrm{cc}}\) (\(c\) for clamped, constrained). The free-free block of \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\) is \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}^2 = \mat I\), and that of \(\mat P\mat K\mat P\) is \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\), since \(\mat P\) is block diagonal. By hypothesis this block equals \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\).
  2. By lemma 19.10 (for \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\)) \(\vek f_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\) exist. The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is positive definite, so each system has exactly one solution by theorem 6.29.
  3. Linearity: \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}(\vek d_{\mathrm{s}} + \vek d_{\mathrm{a}}) = \vek f_{\mathrm{s}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{a}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\). The solution of \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d = \vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\) is unique (step 2), so \(\vek d = \vek d_{\mathrm{s}} + \vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\).
  4. Step 1 gives \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}} = \mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}^2\,\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}} = \mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\,(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}) = \mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\).
  5. Hence \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{s}}) = \mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{s}} = \mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek f_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{s}}\) by lemma 19.10. The column \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{s}}\) solves the same system as \(\vek d_{\mathrm{s}}\), so by the uniqueness of step 2 it equals \(\vek d_{\mathrm{s}}\).
