  6. Similarly \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}(-\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}) = -\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek f_{\mathrm{a}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\), so \(-\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_{\mathrm{a}} = \vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\).
  7. The load \(\vek f_{\mathrm{s}}\) satisfies \(\mat P\vek f_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{s}}\) (lemma 19.10), so by lemma 19.9 with the sign \(+\) the restriction of the column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{s}}\) solves the half model with the conditions \(u = \varphi = 0\) at the nodes on the plane (corollary 19.8). The load \(\vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\) satisfies \(\mat P\vek f_{\mathrm{a}} = -\vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\), so the same holds for \(\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\) with the sign \(-\) and the condition \(v = 0\).

Source: COOK section 2.11 (PDF p. 70): the solution of the original problem is the "superposition of solutions" of the symmetric and antisymmetric case, one analysis of the whole structure is exchanged for two analyses of half of it. The proof is not from the source.

The theorem says that the split loses nothing: the sum of the solutions of two half models is the exact solution, not an approximation. It asks for two things that the example tests on both sides: that both halves are used, and that the structure is really symmetric.

Example 19.12 Splitting the force \(H\) on the portal frame (razcep sile \(H\) na portalnem okviru)

The model is the frame of figure 19.8: every element has \(EA = 1{,}568 \cdot 10^{8}\) N and \(EI = 20\,907\) N m², the columns have four elements each and the beam eight, four on each half \(BD\) and \(DC\), clamps at \(A\) and \(E\), \(H = 500\) N at \(B\). The mirror \(x \mapsto 1 - x\) maps the node \((x, y)\) to \((1 - x, y)\) and changes the sign of the components \(u\) and \(\varphi\) while \(v\) stays. A NumPy computation confirms \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\) and \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\).

The split (19.4) gives \(\vek f_{\mathrm{s}}\) with forces of \(250\) N at \(B\) to the right and at \(C\) to the left, and \(\vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\) with forces of \(250\) N at \(B\) and \(C\) to the right, as the middle and right frame of figure 19.8 show. For the whole frame the displacement of the node \(B\) to the right is \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 1{,}4255\) mm.

  1. Symmetric part. The half model with the conditions \(u = 0\) and \(\varphi = 0\) at \(D\) (corollary 19.8) gives \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 0{,}0008\) mm and at \(D\) an axial force \(N = -249{,}90\) N, a moment of \(0{,}033\) N m and a shear force of zero (middle frame of figure 19.9, on this scale the blue line cannot be told from the grey one). The displacement is so small because the beam holds the nodes: a free column would under \(250\) N move \(250\ \text{N} \cdot (1\ \text{m})^3/(3 \cdot 20\,907\ \text{N m}^2) = 3{,}986\) mm, while the beam as a strut shortens by \(250\ \text{N} \cdot 0{,}5\ \text{m}/(1{,}568 \cdot 10^{8}\ \text{N}) = 0{,}0008\) mm. The force \(250\) N goes through the beam because the axial path is about \(5000\) times stiffer than the bending path (ratio \(3{,}986/0{,}0008 \approx 5000\)). A free-body diagram of the left part (force \(250\) N at \(B\) to the right, force of the right part \(-249{,}90\) N at \(D\) along the horizontal and the reaction at \(A\)) confirms it: \(\sum F_{\mathrm{x}} = 250 - 249{,}90 + R_{\mathrm{Ax}} = 0\) gives the horizontal reaction \(R_{\mathrm{Ax}} = -0{,}10\) N, and the moment about \(A\), \(M_{\mathrm{A}} - 1\ \text{m} \cdot 250\ \text{N} + 1\ \text{m} \cdot 249{,}90\ \text{N} + 0{,}033\ \text{N m} = 0\), gives \(M_{\mathrm{A}} = 0{,}067\) N m. The column carries only \(0{,}10\) N and so it does not bend.
  2. Antisymmetric part. The half model (right frame of figure 19.8) with the condition \(v = 0\) at \(D\) gives \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 1{,}4247\) mm, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{D}} = 0{,}000424\), at \(D\) a moment of zero, an axial force of zero and a shear force \(V = 214{,}19\) N. Free-body diagram of the left part: \(\sum F_{\mathrm{x}} = 250\ \text{N} + R_{\mathrm{Ax}} = 0\), so \(R_{\mathrm{Ax}} = -250\) N. \(\sum F_{\mathrm{y}} = V + R_{\mathrm{Ay}} = 0\), so \(R_{\mathrm{Ay}} = -214{,}19\) N. Moment about \(A\): \(M_{\mathrm{A}} - 1\ \text{m} \cdot 250\ \text{N} + 0{,}5\ \text{m} \cdot 214{,}19\ \text{N} = 0\), so \(M_{\mathrm{A}} = 142{,}91\) N m. The equilibrium of the whole frame confirms it: the clamps carry \(2 \cdot 142{,}91 = 285{,}81\) N m together and the pair of vertical reactions \(\mp 214{,}19\) N on the arm \(1\) m carries \(214{,}19\) N m, the sum is \(500\) N m, which is \(H \cdot 1\ \text{m}\).
  3. Sum (left frame of figure 19.9). At \(B\) it is \(0{,}0008 + 1{,}4247 = 1{,}4255\) mm and at \(C\) it is \(-0{,}0008 + 1{,}4247 = 1{,}4239\) mm, the displacements of the whole frame from the first computation. The symmetric part contributes \(0{,}056\) % of the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{B}}\). A horizontal force on a portal frame with an axially stiff beam is almost purely antisymmetric.

In the figure the grey frame is the undeformed frame and the blue line the frame after loading. For the whole frame and for the antisymmetric part both columns lean to the right and the beam takes the shape of an S, for the symmetric part nothing can be seen. The displacement \(\vek d\) is therefore almost equal to \(\vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\).

We proved the theorem under the assumption \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\), so let us test a case in which it does not hold.

Example 19.13 Splitting with a turned column (razcep ob obrnjenem stebru)

The same frame as in figure 19.8, but the right column turned by a right angle, so that it bends about its weak axis (\(I = 26\,667\) mm\(^4\) instead of \(106\,667\) mm\(^4\), the frame of section 19.1). The shape, supports and load are still symmetric, the stiffness is not: \(\mat P\mat K\mat P \ne \mat K\) (NumPy). We load the frame with a force of \(500\) N downward on the beam, at a quarter of its length from \(B\). The split (19.4) still holds, since lemma 19.10 does not depend on stiffness: \(\vek f_{\mathrm{s}}\) has \(250\) N downward at both quarter points, \(\vek f_{\mathrm{a}}\) has \(250\) N downward and \(250\) N upward. Also \(\vek d = \vek d_{\mathrm{s}} + \vek d_{\mathrm{a}}\) still holds, since it is only linearity (step 3 of the proof of theorem 19.11).

Steps 4 and 5 of the proof fail: \(\mat K\mat P \ne \mat P\mat K\) and \(\mat P\vek d_{\mathrm{s}}\) does not solve the same system as \(\vek d_{\mathrm{s}}\). For the good frame (middle frame of figure 19.9) the symmetric part really is symmetric: \(u_{\mathrm{D}} = 0\), \(\varphi_{\mathrm{D}} = 0\) and the deflection of the quarter point is \(0{,}1106\) mm, as the half model with the conditions \(u = \varphi = 0\) at \(D\) gives. For the turned column \(u_{\mathrm{D}} = 0{,}1601\) mm, the nodes \(B\) and \(C\) rotate through different angles, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}} = -0{,}00056\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{C}} = 0{,}00062\), and the frame as a whole moves sideways, \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 0{,}1602\) mm and \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = 0{,}1600\) mm. With equal columns the moment of the beam would move the top of the left column in one direction and the top of the right column in the opposite direction, but the beam is axially stiff and holds them at the same distance, so the displacements cancel. With columns whose bending stiffnesses differ by a factor of four they do not cancel. The deflection of the quarter point is \(0{,}1480\) mm, while the half model still gives \(0{,}1106\) mm and is wrong by \(25\) %. The half model with symmetric conditions is wrong for such a frame although the load is symmetric.

What if the structure has two mirror planes, for instance a rectangle with the axes \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\)? The mirror matrices \(\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\mat P_{\mathrm{y}}\) are then signed permutations that commute. We apply lemma 19.10 twice, first for \(\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}\) and then to both parts for \(\mat P_{\mathrm{y}}\). We get four parts, each with a sign with respect to each plane. The corollary that follows proves only this split of the load. That each part is solved exactly by a quarter of the structure we do not prove here. The way to it is lemma 19.9 applied twice, first for \(\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}\) and then on the half model for \(\mat P_{\mathrm{y}}\). The elements and the load on the second plane are halved again, and the load at the node where the planes meet is reduced to a quarter.

Corollary 19.14 Split of a load with respect to two planes (razcep bremena glede na dve ravnini)

Let \(\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\mat P_{\mathrm{y}}\) be mirror matrices with \(\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = \mat P_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = \mat I\) and \(\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}\mat P_{\mathrm{y}} = \mat P_{\mathrm{y}}\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}\). For \(\sigma, \tau \in \{1, -1\}\) put

\[\vek f_{\sigma\tau} = \tfrac14\,(\mat I + \sigma\mat P_{\mathrm{x}})(\mat I + \tau\mat P_{\mathrm{y}})\,\vek f . \tag{19.5}\]

Then \(\vek f = \sum_{\sigma,\tau}\vek f_{\sigma\tau}\), \(\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}\vek f_{\sigma\tau} = \sigma\vek f_{\sigma\tau}\) and \(\mat P_{\mathrm{y}}\vek f_{\sigma\tau} = \tau\vek f_{\sigma\tau}\).

Proof

We must show the sum and the sign for both matrices. The sum comes from adding over \(\sigma\) and over \(\tau\) separately, the sign from \(\sigma^2 = 1\).

  1. Adding over \(\sigma = \pm 1\) gives \(\sum_\sigma(\mat I + \sigma\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}) = 2\mat I\), and likewise over \(\tau\). So \(\sum_{\sigma,\tau}\vek f_{\sigma\tau} = \tfrac14\cdot 2\mat I \cdot 2\mat I\,\vek f = \vek f\).
  2. Since \(\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = \mat I\) and \(\sigma^2 = 1\), \(\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}(\mat I + \sigma\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}) = \mat P_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma\mat I = \sigma(\mat I + \sigma\mat P_{\mathrm{x}})\).
  3. The matrix \(\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}\) commutes with \(\mat P_{\mathrm{y}}\), so \(\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}\vek f_{\sigma\tau} = \tfrac14\,\mat P_{\mathrm{x}}(\mat I + \sigma\mat P_{\mathrm{x}})(\mat I + \tau\mat P_{\mathrm{y}})\vek f = \sigma\vek f_{\sigma\tau}\) by step 2. For \(\mat P_{\mathrm{y}}\) the same holds with the roles exchanged.

Source: COOK section 2.11 (PDF p. 69): a structure with the mirror planes \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\) (figure 2.11-1a), the force on the plane is halved, for equal forces one eighth is enough. The split into four parts is not from the source. The proof is not from the source, a NumPy computation confirms it on a random column.

If the two forces in COOK's figure 2.11-1a are equal (the book calls them \(P_{\mathrm{x}} = P_{\mathrm{y}}\)), the planes \(x = y\) and \(x = -y\) are also mirror planes and one eighth of the structure is enough (COOK, PDF p. 69). The force on a plane is halved in the half model, as for the bar on the mirror plane of the bridge in lemma 7.39. We have proved nothing new here, so we do not state the eighth as a theorem.

So far we always used the mirror. For a frame that has no mirror symmetry but is mapped onto itself by a rotation through half a turn, the mirror does not help, but the split still does. COOK calls this "skew" or "inversion" symmetry (PDF p. 70). We call it half-turn symmetry, because the name says what happens: we turn the structure through half a turn about an axis through the centre perpendicular to the plane, and it is the same as before. Two successive reflections, in the plane \(x = 0\) and in the plane \(y = 0\), give the same result as this rotation (COOK, PDF p. 70). Take the steel Z frame of \(20 \times 40\) mm shown in the first frame of figure 19.10: columns \(AB\) and \(CE\) of length \(1\) m and a slanted beam \(BC\) through the centre \(O\), clamped at \(A\) and \(E\). Two arcs around \(O\) show the half-turn that maps \(A\) onto \(E\) and \(B\) onto \(C\). The mirror \(x \mapsto 1 - x\) does not map the frame onto itself, \(\mat P\mat K\mat P \ne \mat K\) (NumPy), while the half-turn does.

In a half-turn (figure 19.10) the components \(u\) and \(v\) reverse, as every vector in the plane does, and the rotation \(\varphi\) does not change, because turning the body is only a motion together with its picture. The new matrix \(\mat R\) is thus a signed permutation that exchanges the node \((x, y)\) with \((2x_{\mathrm{O}} - x, 2y_{\mathrm{O}} - y)\), multiplies the components \(u\) and \(v\) by \(-1\) and \(\varphi\) by \(+1\). Since a half-turn done twice is the identity, \(\mat R^2 = \mat I\). Let \(\mat R\mat K\mat R = \mat K\) (the half-turn maps every element onto an element with the same \(EA\), \(EI\) and length, as the mirror does in section 19.1).

Corollary 19.15 Half-turn symmetry (simetrija pri polovičnem zasuku)

Let \(\mat R\) be the signed permutation of the half-turn about the centre \(O\) with \(\mat R^2 = \mat I\) and \(\mat R\mat K\mat R = \mat K\), let it map clamped unknowns onto clamped ones and let \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) be positive definite. Then for every load \(\vek f_{\mathrm{f}}\):

  1. \(\vek f_{\mathrm{f}} = \vek f_+ + \vek f_-\) with \(\vek f_\pm = \tfrac12(\vek f_{\mathrm{f}} \pm \mat R\vek f_{\mathrm{f}})\), \(\mat R\vek f_\pm = \pm\vek f_\pm\), and this split is unique.
  2. The solutions \(\vek d_\pm\) of the systems \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\vek d_\pm = \vek f_\pm\) satisfy \(\mat R\vek d_\pm = \pm\vek d_\pm\) and \(\vek d = \vek d_+ + \vek d_-\).
  3. At the centre \(O\) (if it is a node), \(u_{\mathrm{O}} = v_{\mathrm{O}} = 0\) for \(\vek d_+\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{O}} = 0\) for \(\vek d_-\).
  4. Let \(O\) be a node of the frame and let the frame split into two halves that meet only at \(O\) and that the half-turn maps onto each other. Then the restriction of the column \(\vek d_\pm\) to one half is the solution of that half with the conditions of item 3 at \(O\) and half the load at \(O\).
Proof

We must show that the proof of theorem 19.11 does not change when \(\mat P\) is replaced by \(\mat R\), that item 3 follows from the signs of the matrix \(\mat R\), and that the proof of lemma 19.9 gives item 4 when \(\mat P\) is replaced by \(\mat R\).

  1. In steps 1 to 6 of the proof of theorem 19.11 we needed only four properties of \(\mat P\): a signed permutation, \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\), \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) and mapping clamped unknowns onto clamped ones. \(\mat R\) has all four by hypothesis, so items 1 and 2 hold (lemma 19.10 and steps 1 to 6).
  2. The node \(O\) stays in place under the rotation, so \(\mat R\) acts on its unknowns only by signs: \(u_{\mathrm{O}} \mapsto -u_{\mathrm{O}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{O}} \mapsto -v_{\mathrm{O}}\), \(\varphi_{\mathrm{O}} \mapsto \varphi_{\mathrm{O}}\).
  3. For \(\mat R\vek d_+ = \vek d_+\) we have \(u_{\mathrm{O}} = -u_{\mathrm{O}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{O}} = -v_{\mathrm{O}}\), so \(u_{\mathrm{O}} = v_{\mathrm{O}} = 0\). For \(\mat R\vek d_- = -\vek d_-\) we have \(\varphi_{\mathrm{O}} = -\varphi_{\mathrm{O}}\), so \(\varphi_{\mathrm{O}} = 0\).
  4. Item 4 is lemma 19.9 with \(\mat R\) in place of \(\mat P\) and the node \(O\) in place of the plane. Of a pair of elements its proof needs only the relation between their matrices. The half-turn maps the element \(e_1\) with the nodes \(i\) and \(j\) to the element \(e_2\) with the nodes that \(i\) and \(j\) are mapped to, with the same length, \(EA\) and \(EI\) and with the opposite direction. In the matrix (12.11) \(c\) and \(s\) therefore change sign, the matrix that turns global displacements into local ones in (12.13) is multiplied from the right by \(\mat T = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -1, 1, -1, -1, 1)\), and \(\mat k_2 = \mat T\mat k_1\mat T\).
  5. From \(\vek d_\pm = \pm\mat R\vek d_\pm\) the element columns satisfy \(\vek d_2 = \pm\mat T\vek d_1\), so \(\mat k_2\vek d_2 = \pm\mat T\mat k_1\vek d_1\): the force of the element \(e_2\) on \(O\) is \(\pm\operatorname{diag}(-1, -1, 1)\) times the force of the element \(e_1\) on \(O\). The free unknowns at \(O\) are \(\varphi\) for \(+\) and \(u\) and \(v\) for \(-\), exactly those that \(\pm\operatorname{diag}(-1, -1, 1)\) multiplies by \(+1\). In step 2 of the proof of the lemma therefore again \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{R}} = \Sigma_{\mathrm{L}}\), and the row of the half is \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{L}} = \tfrac12 f_{\mathrm{Oc}}\). In step 5 \(e_2\) contributes the same energy as \(e_1\), since \(\vek d_2^\T\mat k_2\vek d_2 = \vek d_1^\T\mat T\mat T\mat k_1\mat T\mat T\vek d_1 = \vek d_1^\T\mat k_1\vek d_1\). The other steps of the lemma stay as they are.

Source: COOK section 2.11 (PDF p. 70-71): a half-turn (or two successive reflections) maps the structure onto itself, and with reversed loads, onto the other type. Half of the structure is enough, the conditions are in reference [2.22] of the book. The proof is not from the source.

In the figure the force \(H\) is drawn at the top left, its symmetric part in the middle and its antisymmetric part on the right. In the bottom row is the half \(ABO\), in which the centre for the symmetric part stays at rest, \(u_{\mathrm{O}} = v_{\mathrm{O}} = 0\), and for the antisymmetric one does not rotate, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{O}} = 0\).

Example 19.16 The force \(H\) on the Z frame (sila \(H\) na Z-okviru)

The Z frame has columns \(AB\) and \(CE\) of length \(1\) m and a beam \(BC\) of length \(\sqrt2\) m (\(4\) elements per member), clamped at \(A\) and \(E\), force \(H = 500\) N at \(B\) to the right. \(\mat R^2 = \mat I\) and \(\mat R\mat K\mat R = \mat K\) (NumPy). The split gives \(\vek f_+\) with forces of \(250\) N at \(B\) to the right and at \(C\) to the left (middle frame of figure 19.10) and \(\vek f_-\) with forces of \(250\) N at \(B\) and \(C\) to the right (right frame).

  1. The displacement \(u_{\mathrm{B}}\) (figure 19.10) of the whole frame is \(2{,}2386\) mm, that of the symmetric part \(\vek d_+\) only \(0{,}0038\) mm and that of the antisymmetric part \(\vek d_-\) is \(2{,}2348\) mm. The sum \(0{,}0038 + 2{,}2348 = 2{,}2386\) mm. The symmetric part presses the beam from \(B\) and \(C\), so it is carried by the axial stiffness of the beam, as in example 19.12.
  2. At the centre (figure 19.10), for \(\vek d_+\) \(u_{\mathrm{O}} = v_{\mathrm{O}} = 0\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{O}} = -5{,}4 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and for \(\vek d_-\) \(\varphi_{\mathrm{O}} = 0\) and \(u_{\mathrm{O}} = 1{,}6156\) mm, \(v_{\mathrm{O}} = -0{,}6191\) mm (item 3 of the corollary).
  3. The two half models are the part \(ABO\) with a condition at \(O\) (item 4 of the corollary, bottom frames of figure 19.10): at \(O\) in the first \(u_{\mathrm{O}} = v_{\mathrm{O}} = 0\), in the second \(\varphi_{\mathrm{O}} = 0\). The first gives \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 0{,}0038\) mm and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{O}} = -5{,}4 \cdot 10^{-6}\), the second \(u_{\mathrm{B}} = 2{,}2348\) mm and \(u_{\mathrm{O}} = 1{,}6156\) mm. Both agree with the whole frame.

The mirror (figure 19.10) would not help here: \(\mat P\mat K\mat P \ne \mat K\), because the Z frame has no mirror symmetry. Without the half-turn we would have to solve the whole frame (13 nodes, \(33\) unknowns after clamping), with it two parts with \(7\) nodes.

The section has three results. We split a load \(\vek f\) into a symmetric and an antisymmetric part (lemma 19.10) and solve each on a half (theorem 19.11), and with two mirror planes we split it into four parts (corollary 19.14). The same split works for half-turn symmetry (corollary 19.15). The example with the turned column showed what happens when the stiffness is not symmetric: the split stays exact, but the half models do not. The split works as long as the structure is symmetric. In vibration and buckling a new difficulty appears, because we must solve both half models, not only one. This is the subject of the next section 19.4.

19.4 Symmetry in vibration and buckling

In sections 19.1 to 19.3 symmetry saved us half the work: a symmetrically loaded frame was computed on one half, an antisymmetrically loaded one on the same half with other conditions on the plane, and the two results were added. Now we want the same trick for questions where there is no load at all: at which frequency does the frame vibrate, and at which force does it buckle? There is no load to split into a symmetric and an antisymmetric part, so the trap is bigger. COOK warns (COOK PDF p. 71 and 448) to use symmetry in vibration and buckling sparingly and with care, because a half model catches only part of the modes. This section proves which part, and shows what happens when we forget it.

19.4.1 The frame and its modes

Take the portal frame of sections 19.1 to 19.3, shown at rest in figure 19.11. The frame is plane, made of steel with a \(20 \times 40\) mm section that bends about the axis with second moment of area \(I = 106\,667\) mm\(^4\), with Young's modulus \(E = 196\) GPa and density \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m\(^3\). The columns \(AB\) and \(EC\) are \(1\) m high and clamped at \(A\) and \(E\), the beam \(BC\) is \(1\) m long, and its midpoint is the node \(D\). The columns are divided into four frame elements each (definition 12.17), the beam into eight, four on each half \(BD\) and \(DC\). There are \(16\) elements, \(17\) nodes and \(3 \cdot 17 - 6 = 45\) free unknowns. The mass matrix is consistent (lemma 12.47). The free vibrations of such a frame are the solutions of the eigenvalue problem \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi = \lambda\,\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi\) (definition 10.7), where \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) are the stiffness and mass matrices of the free unknowns. In this section the letter \(\mat P\) always means the mirror matrix (definition 19.5) restricted to the free unknowns, that is \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\) of point 2 of theorem 19.6, never a force, and \(\mat M\) the mass matrix, never a moment.

The lowest modes of the frame are in figure 19.11. We draw them as the modes in chapter 10: the frame at rest and above it the mode, strongly magnified.

First we draw the frame at rest: the columns joined by the nodes \(B\) and \(C\) and the beam between them, all grey dashed so that we know where it moves from. The clamps at \(A\) and \(E\) are hatched, because there the frame can neither move nor turn. Through the middle of the beam, the node \(D\), we draw the mirror plane known from section 19.1, in the figure a dash-dot line. Right of it the frame, the clamps and the mass are the mirror image of the left. Now we draw a mode on the frame. The first mode, \(f_1 = 29{,}511\) Hz, is a sway of the whole frame sideways: the columns bend to the same side, the beam only turns and moves. The second, \(f_2 = 116{,}201\) Hz, bends the columns mirror-wise and bends the beam like an arch, the third and the fourth have more bends in the columns and the beam.

Each of them in figure 19.11 is either the mirror image of itself or the mirror image with the sign reversed. In the first and third modes the tops of both columns move in the same direction. The mirror image of the left column's displacement would be a displacement of the right one in the opposite direction, so the true displacement of the right one is its reversed image: the mode is antisymmetric. In the second and fourth modes the tops move in opposite directions, so the right column is the mirror image of the left: the mode is symmetric. If we write the eigenvector with the unknowns \((u, v, \varphi)\) of every node (horizontal displacement, vertical displacement and rotation), the mirror \(x \mapsto 1 - x\) maps a node to its mirror node and the components \((u, v, \varphi)\) to \((-u, v, -\varphi)\), since the horizontal direction turns round, the vertical does not, and a rotation changes its sense, as the hands of a clock do in a mirror. This is the mirror matrix \(\mat P\). With NumPy we checked for the first eight modes that \(\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi\) equals \(\boldsymbol\varphi\) or \(-\boldsymbol\varphi\) to six places, namely \(\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi = \boldsymbol\varphi\) for the modes \(2, 4, 6, 8\) with frequencies \(116{,}201\), \(205{,}094\), \(509{,}015\) and \(858{,}916\) Hz, and \(\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi = -\boldsymbol\varphi\) for the modes \(1, 3, 5, 7\) with frequencies \(29{,}511\), \(190{,}141\), \(411{,}964\) and \(584{,}994\) Hz. Is this an accident?

It is not. Look at the vibrating frame in a mirror. The frame, the supports and the mass are mirror symmetric, so the mirror image of the vibration obeys the law of motion of the same structure: the forces at the mirror node are the mirror images of the forces at the original (the law of action and reaction and Newton's law hold in a mirror in the same way, section 19.1). If the mode is \(\boldsymbol\varphi\cos\omega t\), the mirror image \(\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi\cos\omega t\) is again a vibration with the same frequency. If the frequency is simple, this is the only mode at it up to a factor, and so \(\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi = c\,\boldsymbol\varphi\). The mirror applied twice leaves everything where it was, so \(c^2 = 1\) (figure 19.11).

Definition 19.17 Symmetric and antisymmetric mode (simetričen in protisimetričen način)

Let \(\mat P\) be a matrix of order \(n\) that has exactly one nonzero entry, \(1\) or \(-1\), in each row and each column and satisfies \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\), for example the mirror matrix of the free unknowns \(\mat P_{\mathrm{ff}}\) of point 2 of theorem 19.6. Let \(\boldsymbol\varphi\) be an eigenvector of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) with \(n\) entries (definition 10.7). The column \(\boldsymbol\varphi\) is a symmetric mode (simetričen način) if \(\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi = \boldsymbol\varphi\), and an antisymmetric mode (protisimetričen način) if \(\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi = -\boldsymbol\varphi\). The sign is a property of the mode, not of a displacement: the symmetric load and the symmetric solution of sections 19.1 and 19.3 are described by the same condition \(\mat P\vek d = \vek d\), the antisymmetric ones by \(\mat P\vek d = -\vek d\).

Source: The naming follows COOK PDF p. 71 ("symmetric modes", "antisymmetric modes" of a simply supported beam). The definition with the mirror matrix is ours.

Each name has its reason. Symmetric (Greek syn, together, and metron, measure) means "of the same measure": the left and the right half have the same measures. Anti means "opposite": the mirror image of the mode has the opposite sign. The name is the same as for the antisymmetric load (definition 19.3), because the condition is the same.

19.4.2 The theorem on the modes of a symmetric system

Now a theorem that turns the observation above into a proof. The condition that the mirror image of the frame is the frame itself in every detail is, for matrices, \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) (stiffness, section 19.1) and \(\mat P\mat M\mat P = \mat M\) (mass). For our frame both equalities hold, also with the supports, if the mirror maps a free unknown to a free unknown: the clamps \(A\) and \(E\) are mirror images of each other. With NumPy, \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) and \(\mat P\mat M\mat P = \mat M\) hold for the frame (num-04.py).

Theorem 19.18 Modes of a symmetric system (načini simetričnega sistema)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric matrix and \(\mat M\) a symmetric, positive definite matrix of order \(n\), and let \(\mat P\) be a matrix of order \(n\) as in definition 19.17 (a single nonzero entry \(\pm 1\) in each row and each column, \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\)) with \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) and \(\mat P\mat M\mat P = \mat M\). Let \(V_{\mathrm{s}}\) be the set of columns with \(\mat P\vek v = \vek v\) and \(V_{\mathrm{a}}\) the set of columns with \(\mat P\vek v = -\vek v\). Then:

  1. If \((\lambda, \boldsymbol\varphi)\) is an eigenpair of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\), then \((\lambda, \mat P\boldsymbol\varphi)\) is an eigenpair too.
  2. If an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) has only one linearly independent eigenvector, this is a symmetric or an antisymmetric mode (definition 19.17).
  3. There is an \(\mat M\)-orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) (definition 10.10) in which every column lies in \(V_{\mathrm{s}}\) or in \(V_{\mathrm{a}}\).
  4. Let \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\mat B_{\mathrm{a}}\) be matrices whose columns are a basis of \(V_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{a}}\), and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{s}} = \mat B_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat K\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\), \(\mat M_{\mathrm{s}} = \mat B_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{a}} = \mat B_{\mathrm{a}}^\T\mat K\mat B_{\mathrm{a}}\), \(\mat M_{\mathrm{a}} = \mat B_{\mathrm{a}}^\T\mat M\mat B_{\mathrm{a}}\). The eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\), counted with multiplicity, are exactly the eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K_{\mathrm{s}}, \mat M_{\mathrm{s}})\) together with the eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K_{\mathrm{a}}, \mat M_{\mathrm{a}})\).
Proof

We must show that the mirror keeps eigenpairs (points 1 and 2), and that the space of columns splits into \(V_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{a}}\) so that \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) map each of them into itself, so we find the eigenpairs in each separately and put them together (points 3 and 4).

  1. Each column of \(\mat P\) has a single nonzero entry \(\pm 1\), and different columns have it in different rows, because each row has only one. The columns are therefore unit columns perpendicular to each other, \(\mat P^\T\mat P = \mat I\). With \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\) we get \(\mat P^\T = \mat P^{-1} = \mat P\). If we multiply the equality \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) by \(\mat P\) from the right, we get \(\mat P\mat K = \mat K\mat P\), and likewise \(\mat P\mat M = \mat M\mat P\).
  2. (Point 1.) From \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi = \lambda\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi\), multiplying by \(\mat P\) and using step 1, we get \(\mat K\,\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi = \lambda\mat M\,\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi\). The column \(\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi\) is not zero, because \(\mat P\) is invertible.
  3. (Point 2.) By step 2, \(\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi\) is an eigenvector of the same value \(\lambda\), so \(\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi = c\,\boldsymbol\varphi\) with some constant \(c\). From \(\mat P^2 = \mat I\) we get \(\boldsymbol\varphi = c^2\boldsymbol\varphi\), so \(c = 1\) or \(c = -1\).
  4. Every column \(\vek v\) is the sum \(\vek v_{\mathrm{s}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{a}}\) with \(\vek v_{\mathrm{s}} = \tfrac12(\vek v + \mat P\vek v)\) and \(\vek v_{\mathrm{a}} = \tfrac12(\vek v - \mat P\vek v)\), and \(\mat P\vek v_{\mathrm{s}} = \tfrac12(\mat P\vek v + \vek v) = \vek v_{\mathrm{s}}\), \(\mat P\vek v_{\mathrm{a}} = -\vek v_{\mathrm{a}}\). A column in both sets satisfies \(\vek v = \mat P\vek v = -\vek v\), so it is zero. Hence \(V_{\mathrm{s}} \oplus V_{\mathrm{a}}\) is the whole space of columns, and if \(n_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{a}}\) are the dimensions, \(n_{\mathrm{s}} + n_{\mathrm{a}} = n\).
  5. If \(\vek v \in V_{\mathrm{s}}\), then by step 1 \(\mat P\mat K\vek v = \mat K\mat P\vek v = \mat K\vek v\), so \(\mat K\vek v \in V_{\mathrm{s}}\), and likewise \(\mat M\vek v \in V_{\mathrm{s}}\). The same holds for \(V_{\mathrm{a}}\) with the sign reversed.
  6. The columns \(\vek u \in V_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\vek w \in V_{\mathrm{a}}\) are \(\mat M\)-orthogonal: \(\vek u^\T\mat M\vek w = (\mat P\vek u)^\T\mat M(-\mat P\vek w) = -\vek u^\T\mat P\mat M\mat P\vek w = -\vek u^\T\mat M\vek w\), so \(\vek u^\T\mat M\vek w = 0\).
  7. The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{s}}\) is symmetric and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{s}}\) is symmetric and positive definite, because \(\vek x^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x = (\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x)^\T\mat M(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x) > 0\) for \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\) (the columns of \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\) are independent, \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x \ne \vek 0\)). By the spectral theorem 10.13 there are \(\mat M_{\mathrm{s}}\)-orthonormal \(\vek x_1, \dots, \vek x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{s}}\) with \(\mat K_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\mat M_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{r}}\). Let \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{r}} \in V_{\mathrm{s}}\). The column \(\vek w = \mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) lies in \(V_{\mathrm{s}}\) by step 5, so \(\vek w = \mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek c\), and \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\vek w = \mat K_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\mat M_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek 0\). Hence \(\vek c^\T\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek c = |\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek c|^2 = 0\) and \(\vek w = \vek 0\). The column \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is an eigenvector with value \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{q}} = \vek x_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{q}}\), so the \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) are \(\mat M\)-orthonormal.
  8. In the same way for \(V_{\mathrm{a}}\) we get \(n_{\mathrm{a}}\) eigenvectors in \(V_{\mathrm{a}}\). Together there are \(n_{\mathrm{s}} + n_{\mathrm{a}} = n\) (step 4) columns that are \(\mat M\)-orthonormal within each group (step 7) and between the groups (step 6). Columns with \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}^\T\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are linearly independent (from \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek 0\) and multiplication by \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}^\T\mat M\) we get \(c_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\)), so they form a basis. This is point 3.
  9. (Point 4.) Let \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1, \dots, \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) be the columns of step 8 with values \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\), that is the values of the pairs \((\mat K_{\mathrm{s}}, \mat M_{\mathrm{s}})\) and \((\mat K_{\mathrm{a}}, \mat M_{\mathrm{a}})\) together. Let \((\lambda, \boldsymbol\varphi)\) be any eigenpair and \(\boldsymbol\varphi = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\). From \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi - \lambda\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} - \lambda)\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek 0\) and multiplication by \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}^\T\) we get \(c_{\mathrm{i}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{i}} - \lambda) = 0\). So \(\boldsymbol\varphi\) is a combination of the columns with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} = \lambda\), and \(\lambda\) is among the numbers \(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}}\). The eigenspace of the value \(\lambda\) therefore has dimension equal to the number of \(j\) with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} = \lambda\), and the values \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) are indeed all the eigenvalues with multiplicities.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. COOK PDF p. 71 and 448 warns that a half model catches only the symmetric or only the antisymmetric modes, without proving it.

The theorem says two things. First, points 2: in a symmetric system every eigenvector with a simple frequency is either symmetric or antisymmetric, which is why we found only two classes above. Second, point 4: all the eigenvalues of the whole system are obtained by solving two smaller eigenvalue problems, one on \(V_{\mathrm{s}}\) and one on \(V_{\mathrm{a}}\), and putting the results together. We must not drop a class, because there are frequencies in only one of them. Point 3 was proved with half spaces, which we now recognize as the half models of section 19.2.

Corollary 19.19 Each half model gives the modes of one class (polovični model in načini)

Let the system of theorem 19.18 have a mesh of elements in which the mirror plane passes only through nodes (no element crosses it), in which every element has a mirror element with the mirror image of the same stiffness and mass matrix, and let \(\mat P\) be the mirror matrix of this mesh, restricted to the free unknowns. Let \(\mat K_{\mathrm{h}}^{s}, \mat M_{\mathrm{h}}^{s}\) be the matrices of the left half model, which has the nodes left of the plane and on it, the elements left of the plane with their full stiffness and mass matrices and the elements lying in the plane with half of both, as in lemma 19.9, and \(u = 0\) and \(\varphi = 0\) at the nodes of the plane (symmetric conditions), and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{h}}^{a}, \mat M_{\mathrm{h}}^{a}\) the matrices of the same half model with \(v = 0\) on the plane (antisymmetric conditions). Then \(\mat K_{\mathrm{s}} = 2\mat K_{\mathrm{h}}^{s}\), \(\mat M_{\mathrm{s}} = 2\mat M_{\mathrm{h}}^{s}\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{a}} = 2\mat K_{\mathrm{h}}^{a}\), \(\mat M_{\mathrm{a}} = 2\mat M_{\mathrm{h}}^{a}\). The eigenvalues of the half model with symmetric conditions are therefore exactly the eigenvalues of the symmetric modes of the whole system, and the eigenvalues of the half model with antisymmetric conditions exactly the eigenvalues of the antisymmetric modes.

Proof

We must show that the columns of \(V_{\mathrm{s}}\) correspond exactly to the unknowns of the half model with symmetric conditions, and that the energy of a column of \(V_{\mathrm{s}}\) is twice the energy of the half.

  1. The mirror maps a node of the plane to itself with the components \((u, v, \varphi) \mapsto (-u, v, -\varphi)\) (section 19.2, theorem 19.7). So \(\mat P\vek v = \vek v\) gives on the plane \(u = -u\) and \(\varphi = -\varphi\), that is \(u = \varphi = 0\), and \(v\) is free. \(\mat P\vek v = -\vek v\) gives \(v = -v\), that is \(v = 0\), and \(u\) and \(\varphi\) are free. The unknowns left of the plane are free, and those on the right are by \(\mat P\vek v = \pm\vek v\) the mirror images of the left ones.
  2. So \(V_{\mathrm{s}}\) is the set of columns \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x\), where \(\vek x\) runs over the unknowns of the half model with symmetric conditions and \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\) copies the left part from \(\vek x\) and mirrors it into the right part. The columns of \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\) are independent, because the left half determines the right. The same holds for \(V_{\mathrm{a}}\) and the antisymmetric conditions.
  3. The energy is a sum over elements, \(\vek v^\T\mat K\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) (theorem 7.13). For \(\vek v = \mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x\) the nodal vector of a mirror element is the mirror image of the nodal vector of the original and the matrix of the mirror element the mirror image of the matrix, so the contribution of the mirror element equals that of the original.
  4. An element lying in the plane is its own mirror image and counts only once. If \(\sum_{\mathrm{L}}\) is the sum of the contributions of the elements left of the plane and \(\sum_\Pi\) the sum of those of the elements in it, the sum over all elements is \(2\sum_{\mathrm{L}} + \sum_\Pi = 2\big(\sum_{\mathrm{L}} + \tfrac12\sum_\Pi\big)\), and the bracket is the energy of the half model: \(\vek x^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x = 2\,\vek x^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{h}}^{s}\vek x\) for every \(\vek x\). Likewise \(\vek x^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x = 2\,\vek x^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{h}}^{s}\vek x\) from the kinetic energy.
  5. If \(\mat C\) is a symmetric matrix with \(\vek x^\T\mat C\vek x = 0\) for every \(\vek x\), then \(\mat C = \mat 0\): for \(\vek x = \vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) we get \(C_{\mathrm{ii}} = 0\) and for \(\vek x = \vek e_{\mathrm{i}} + \vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) we get \(2C_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\). So step 4 gives \(\mat K_{\mathrm{s}} = 2\mat K_{\mathrm{h}}^{s}\) and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{s}} = 2\mat M_{\mathrm{h}}^{s}\). The factor \(2\) in the eigenvalue problem \(\mat K_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x = \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x\) cancels, and the claim follows from point 4 of theorem 19.18. For the antisymmetric class the proof is the same.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. COOK PDF p. 71 (figures 2.11-1b and 2.11-1c, symmetry and antisymmetry conditions) and PDF p. 448 (the same caution for a simply supported beam).

The factor \(2\) belongs to the computation only. In the eigenvalue problem it cancels in both matrices, in a static load it appears as the halving of load and stiffness on the plane (section 19.2).

19.4.3 Example: the portal frame

Example 19.20 Modes of the portal frame and its half models (načini portalnega okvirja in polovična modela)

The frame of section 19.4.1 has, by NumPy, the lowest eight modes and the classes by the mirror matrix \(\mat P\): \(f_1 = 29{,}511\) Hz antisymmetric, \(f_2 = 116{,}201\) Hz symmetric, \(f_3 = 190{,}141\) Hz antisymmetric, \(f_4 = 205{,}094\) Hz symmetric, \(f_5 = 411{,}964\) Hz antisymmetric, \(f_6 = 509{,}015\) Hz symmetric, \(f_7 = 584{,}994\) Hz antisymmetric and \(f_8 = 858{,}916\) Hz symmetric. The smallest gap between consecutive frequencies is \(7{,}9\) % (between \(f_3\) and \(f_4\)), all are simple, so by point 2 of theorem 19.18 none is a mixture (figure 19.11).

Figure 19.12 shows the left halves. With symmetric conditions the half is guided vertically at \(D\), because \(u = 0\) and \(\varphi = 0\) and the displacement \(v\) is free. With antisymmetric conditions the half rests at \(D\) on a horizontally moving roller, because \(v = 0\) and \(u\) and \(\varphi\) are free. The model has \(22\) free unknowns with symmetric and \(23\) with antisymmetric conditions, \(45\) together (step 4 of the proof of theorem 19.18).

We draw the half as the frame at rest from the clamp at \(A\) to \(B\) and \(D\). At \(D\) we put a guide for the symmetric modes and a roller for the antisymmetric ones, each time on the mirror plane, where the middle of the beam is. The half with the guide has the lowest symmetric mode at \(f = 116{,}20\) Hz, the half with the roller the antisymmetric one at \(f = 29{,}51\) Hz. The half model with symmetric conditions gives the frequencies \(116{,}201\), \(205{,}094\), \(509{,}015\) and \(858{,}916\) Hz, the one with antisymmetric conditions \(29{,}511\), \(190{,}141\), \(411{,}964\) and \(584{,}994\) Hz, equal to the whole frame by class in every place (NumPy). The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{s}}\) of the theorem is indeed exactly twice the matrix of the half model: the ratio of the largest entries is \(2{,}000\).

What if we relied on one half model only, as COOK warns? If we computed the frame with symmetric conditions at \(D\) only, we would get \(116{,}20\) Hz for the lowest frequency instead of \(29{,}51\) Hz, \(3{,}94\) times too much, and we would miss the sway of the whole frame, which is the lowest mode and usually the one we want most. With antisymmetric conditions we would lose \(f_2 = 116{,}20\) Hz and all the other symmetric ones. Both half models are needed, and only together they give all the modes (point 4 of theorem 19.18) (figure 19.12).

Here we have a first case that satisfies the theorem, and now one that does not. The theorem requires \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\). Turn the right column by a quarter turn so that it bends about the weak axis, with \(I = 26\,667\) mm\(^4\) instead of \(106\,667\) mm\(^4\), and leave everything else. The shape, the supports and the mass stay mirror symmetric, the stiffness does not. NumPy gives \(\mat P\mat K\mat P \ne \mat K\) and the frequencies \(22{,}951\), \(90{,}880\), \(126{,}741\) and \(195{,}562\) Hz. The distance to the nearest class, the smaller of the numbers \(|\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi - \boldsymbol\varphi|/|\boldsymbol\varphi|\) and \(|\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi + \boldsymbol\varphi|/|\boldsymbol\varphi|\), is \(0{,}39\), \(0{,}89\), \(1{,}08\) and \(1{,}39\) for the first four modes, and for a symmetric or antisymmetric mode it would be zero. No mode is symmetric or antisymmetric any more. The left half model has the unturned column and stayed the same, so with the symmetric and antisymmetric conditions together it gives the old frequencies \(29{,}51\), \(116{,}20\), \(190{,}14\) and \(205{,}09\) Hz, and none of them is among the new ones (figure 19.11).

The hypothesis of the theorem holds for the supports too, as a beam shows. Take a simply supported beam of length \(1\) m with the same section, divided into \(8\) elements: a pin at the left end, a roller at the right (figure 19.13).

Example 19.21 Simply supported beam (enostavno podprt nosilec)

For a simply supported beam of length \(L\) the modes are by theorem 13.35 \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) with frequencies in the ratio \(1 : 4 : 9 : 16\) (chapter 13). The mirror \(x \mapsto L - x\) maps \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) to \(\sin(n\pi - n\pi x/L) = (-1)^{n+1}\sin(n\pi x/L)\), because \(\sin n\pi = 0\) and \(\cos n\pi = (-1)^n\). Odd \(n\) are therefore symmetric and even \(n\) antisymmetric (figure 19.13). This is the example given by COOK (PDF p. 71): a half model with the conditions of figure 2.11-1b gives only the odd modes, with those of figure 2.11-1c only the even ones.

The beam stands on its supports, a pin on the left and a roller on the right. Through the middle we draw the mirror plane. Above each grey line at rest there is one mode. The first, \(n = 1\), is one arch, the middle has its largest displacement, so it is symmetric. The second is at zero in the middle (open circle), the left half goes up, the right half down, so it is antisymmetric. The third again has its largest displacement in the middle, the fourth is at zero.

A model of eight beam elements gives by NumPy the frequencies \(90{,}924\), \(363{,}783\), \(819{,}353\) and \(1460{,}497\) Hz for \(n = 1, 2, 3, 4\), in the classes symmetric, antisymmetric, symmetric and antisymmetric. The exact values from theorem 13.35 are \(90{,}922\), \(363{,}689\), \(818{,}300\) and \(1454{,}755\) Hz. The ratios to the first are \(1 : 4{,}001 : 9{,}011 : 16{,}063\), and the classes agree with theorem 19.18 (figure 19.13).

Among them there is one more frequency, \(1255{,}2\) Hz, which is in neither class. It is an axial vibration: the left end is fixed in the axis and the right end is free, so the supports in the axial direction are not mirror images of each other (the hypothesis of theorem 19.18 fails for the axial unknowns). The frequency corresponds to the lowest frequency of a bar fixed at one end and free at the other, \(c/(4L) = 1253{,}2\) Hz with \(c = 5012{,}80\) m/s (theorem 13.18 (b)). So the beam is mirror symmetric as a bending model, because for a straight beam the axial motion does not couple with bending (figure 19.13).

The theorem speaks of eigenvalues, which may also be multiple. Then point 2 does not hold, as the smallest example shows (figure 19.14).

Example 19.22 A double eigenvalue without a class (dvojna lastna vrednost brez razreda)

A point mass \(m\) moves in the plane \((x, y)\) and is held on each side by a spring of stiffness \(\kappa\), so \(\mat K = 2\kappa\,\mat I\) and \(\mat M = m\,\mat I\) (figure 19.14). The mirror \(x \mapsto -x\) has \(\mat P = \mathrm{diag}(-1, 1)\), since the displacement \(x\) changes sign and \(y\) does not, and \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\), \(\mat P\mat M\mat P = \mat M\). The eigenvalue \(\lambda = 2\kappa/m\) is double, its eigenspace is the whole plane.

The mass in the middle of four springs and the mirror plane through it are in the figure. The motion along \(x\) is reversed by the mirror, so \(\mat P(1, 0)^\T = -(1, 0)^\T\) makes it antisymmetric, the motion along \(y\) is left as it is, so it is symmetric. The motion along the diagonal, \((1, 1)^\T\), is also a mode with the same frequency, but its mirror image is \((-1, 1)^\T\), a different column, so it is neither symmetric nor antisymmetric. The theorem holds here too (point 3 gives the basis \((1, 0)^\T\), \((0, 1)^\T\)), but only for a chosen basis, not for every eigenvector.

This is why point 2 of the theorem requires a simple eigenvalue. Double values often appear when a system has another symmetry besides the mirror, here a quarter turn. For a wheel with circular symmetry, which comes later in the chapter, they will be the rule (figure 19.14).

19.4.4 Buckling

In buckling the same question arises. The linear buckling analysis of definition 12.51 looks for the numbers \(\mu > 0\) at which the equation \((\mat K + \mu\,\mat G)\,\vek d = \vek 0\) has a solution \(\vek d \ne \vek 0\). The matrix \(\mat G\) is the geometric matrix of the reference load (lemma 12.50) and is not positive definite, so the spectral theorem 10.13 cannot be used and theorem 19.18 cannot be copied. The proof works, however, because it needs only that \(\mat P\) commutes with the matrices.

The reference load is a force of \(1\) N downward at \(B\) and at \(C\). The state in which the columns are only compressed with the axial force \(N = -1\) N and the beam has neither axial force nor bending satisfies the equilibrium of all nodes (the force passes down the column to the ground at the node \(B\)) and compatibility (the nodes \(B\) and \(C\) both go down by the same amount, the beam moves as a rigid body, without strain) (figure 19.15). By theorem 12.20 (point 2) the solution of the linear computation is unique, so this is it. With NumPy the axial force in a column is \(-1{,}000000\) N, in the beam at most \(5 \cdot 10^{-16}\) N, which is round-off. The geometric matrix \(\mat G\) is therefore a sum over the columns, in each element with \(N = -1\) N. The mirror image of a column is a column with the same axial force, so \(\mat P\mat G\mat P = \mat G\).

Lemma 19.23 Buckling modes of a symmetric system (uklonske oblike simetričnega sistema)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat G\) be symmetric matrices of order \(n\) and \(\mat P\) a matrix of order \(n\) as in definition 19.17 with \(\mat P\mat K\mat P = \mat K\) and \(\mat P\mat G\mat P = \mat G\). Let \(V_{\mathrm{s}}\), \(V_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\), \(\mat B_{\mathrm{a}}\) be as in theorem 19.18. Then:

  1. If \((\mat K + \mu\mat G)\vek d = \vek 0\) and \(\vek d \ne \vek 0\), then also \((\mat K + \mu\mat G)\,\mat P\vek d = \vek 0\), and the columns \(\vek d_{\mathrm{s}} = \tfrac12(\vek d + \mat P\vek d)\) and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{a}} = \tfrac12(\vek d - \mat P\vek d)\) are each zero or a buckling mode with the same \(\mu\). A solution is therefore the sum of a symmetric and an antisymmetric one.
  2. If the solution for \(\mu\) is unique up to a factor, it is symmetric or antisymmetric.
  3. The number \(\mu\) is a buckling factor if and only if the equation \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}^\T(\mat K + \mu\mat G)\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\,\vek x = \vek 0\) or the equation \(\mat B_{\mathrm{a}}^\T(\mat K + \mu\mat G)\mat B_{\mathrm{a}}\,\vek x = \vek 0\) has a solution \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\).
Proof

We must show that the kernel of \(\mat K + \mu\mat G\) is mapped into itself by the mirror and that the kernel is the sum of its symmetric and antisymmetric parts, which are solutions of the half models.

  1. By step 1 of the proof of theorem 19.18, \(\mat P(\mat K + \mu\mat G) = (\mat K + \mu\mat G)\mat P\). So \((\mat K + \mu\mat G)\mat P\vek d = \mat P(\mat K + \mu\mat G)\vek d = \vek 0\). The kernel is therefore closed under \(\mat P\) and under the sums \(\tfrac12(\vek d \pm \mat P\vek d)\), and each of these two is in the kernel.
  2. A single solution: \(\mat P\vek d\) is a solution, so \(\mat P\vek d = c\,\vek d\) and \(c^2 = 1\) as in step 3 of the mentioned proof.
  3. If \(\vek d = \mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x\) with \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\) and \((\mat K + \mu\mat G)\vek d = \vek 0\), multiplication by \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\) gives the first equation of point 3. Conversely, if \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}^\T(\mat K + \mu\mat G)\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x = \vek 0\), the column \(\vek w = (\mat K + \mu\mat G)\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x\) lies in \(V_{\mathrm{s}}\) (step 5 of the proof of theorem 19.18, because \(\mat P\) commutes with both matrices) and so \(\vek w = \mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek c\) with \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\vek w = \vek 0\). Hence \(|\vek w|^2 = \vek c^\T\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\vek w = 0\) and \(\vek w = \vek 0\). For \(V_{\mathrm{a}}\) the proof is the same. By step 1 every buckling factor belongs to at least one class.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. COOK PDF p. 71 warns that symmetry in vibration and buckling needs care, but does not prove which buckling modes are lost.

Point 3 is the same claim as corollary 19.19, for buckling: the half model with symmetric conditions gives the symmetric buckling modes, the half model with antisymmetric conditions the antisymmetric ones. The proof of the corollary holds for \(\mat G\) too, because the geometric matrix is also a sum over elements (the energy of the axial forces, lemma 12.50), so \(\mat G_{\mathrm{s}} = 2\mat G_{\mathrm{h}}^{s}\), where \(\mat G_{\mathrm{h}}^{s}\) too has an element in the plane with half its matrix, and the factor \(2\) cancels again in \(\mu\).

Example 19.24 Buckling of the portal frame (uklon portalnega okvirja)

There are two idealizations: the model is linearly elastic and the axial forces do not change until buckling (definition 12.51), and the elements are beams with a small slope (lemma 12.50). Let \(\pi^2 EI/h^2 = 206\,340{,}5\) N with \(h = 1\) m. Since the reference force is \(1\) N, the buckling factors are simply the critical forces in newtons. By NumPy the first three are (figure 19.15):

\[\mu_1 = 154\,186{,}8\ \text{N} = 0{,}7472\,\frac{\pi^2 EI}{h^2}, \quad \mu_2 = 527\,820{,}7\ \text{N} = 2{,}558\,\frac{\pi^2 EI}{h^2}, \quad \mu_3 = 643\,206{,}0\ \text{N} = 3{,}117\,\frac{\pi^2 EI}{h^2} .\]

The first and the third are antisymmetric, the second symmetric (figure 19.15).

We draw the frame at rest with the clamps and the two forces \(F\) that compress the columns. The arrows end at the nodes \(B\) and \(C\), because the force pushes the node. The first shape is the sway: the beam stays almost straight and moves, the columns bend into an S, because the beam holds them against turning only partly, and it is the lowest. The second is symmetric: the tops do not move sideways, because the beam holds them axially, the beam bends like an arch and turns the nodes in opposite directions, and the columns bend into an S mirror-wise (figure 19.15).

We check the result with the limits that the stiffness of the beam gives. If the beam is \(10^{-6}\) times softer, the tops of the columns are free to move sideways and turn, and the sway gives \(0{,}2500\,\pi^2EI/h^2\), which is the cantilever column with \(\pi^2EI/(4h^2)\) (theorem 8.131). The symmetric shape gives \(2{,}0497\) for this beam, the top does not move sideways because the beam holds it axially, but turns freely. If the beam is \(10^{6}\) times stiffer, it does not bend, but it still turns as a rigid body, because the columns stretch and shorten axially: in the sway the top of one column rises a little and the top of the other goes down. The tops of the columns turn with the beam, by \(0{,}0026\) radian per metre of sway, and the sway gives \(0{,}9994\). If we also make the axial stiffness of the columns \(10^6\) times larger, the tops turn only by about \(10^{-6}\) radian per metre of sway and the sway gives \(1{,}0005\). Such a column is clamped at the bottom and moves sideways at the top without turning, so its slope \(v'\) is zero at both ends. Point 1 (a) of lemma 12.52 with \(\eta = v'\) and \(\ell = h\) gives for it \(EI\int_0^h v''^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ge (\pi^2EI/h^2)\int_0^h v'^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), with equality for \(v' = \sin(\pi x/h)\). The smallest quotient, which is the buckling factor (point 1 of theorem 12.53), is therefore \(\pi^2EI/h^2\), in our units \(1\), and the mesh gives a little more. The symmetric shape gives \(4{,}0301\) for the stiff beam, which is close to the \(4\,\pi^2EI/h^2\) of the column clamped at both ends (theorem 8.135, the mesh gives by theorem 12.53 a value not below the true one). Our frame with \(0{,}7472\) and \(2{,}558\) lies between \(0{,}25\) and \(0{,}9994\) and between \(2{,}0497\) and \(4{,}0301\) (figure 19.15).

It must, because the buckling factor of the sway and of the symmetric shape does not fall with the stiffness of the beam. The equation of point 3 of lemma 19.23 for the symmetric class, \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}^\T(\mat K + \mu\mat G)\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x = \vek 0\), is \(-\mat G_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x = (1/\mu)\,\mat K_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x\) with \(\mat K_{\mathrm{s}} = \mat B_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat K\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\mat G_{\mathrm{s}} = \mat B_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat G\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\). The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{s}}\) is positive definite, because \(\mat K\) is positive definite (proof of point 2 of theorem 12.20) and the columns of \(\mat B_{\mathrm{s}}\) are independent, so by theorem 10.26 for the pair \((-\mat G_{\mathrm{s}}, \mat K_{\mathrm{s}})\) the smallest positive \(\mu\) is the reciprocal of the largest quotient \(-\vek x^\T\mat G_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x/\vek x^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x\). The matrix \(\mat G\) comes from the columns and does not change with the beam. The energy \(\vek x^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x\), however, grows or stays the same for every \(\vek x\) when the beam gets stiffer. The largest quotient therefore does not grow and the smallest \(\mu\) does not fall. For the antisymmetric class it is the same. Intermediate stiffnesses of the beam show this too: with the stiffness multiplied by \(10^{-2}\) and \(10^{2}\) the sway is \(0{,}2620\) and \(0{,}9961\), the symmetric shape \(2{,}0560\) and \(3{,}9892\) (NumPy).

A mesh with two, four, eight and sixteen elements per column (and twice as many on the beam) gives for the sway \(0{,}7494\), \(0{,}7472\), \(0{,}7471\), \(0{,}7471\) and for the symmetric shape \(2{,}6112\), \(2{,}5580\), \(2{,}5518\), \(2{,}5514\). Four elements per column give the first value to three places and the second to \(0{,}25\) % (figure 19.15).

The first buckling is therefore the sway. Whoever computed the frame only with the half model with symmetric conditions at \(D\) (because the frame is symmetric, as for statics) would get \(527{,}82\) kN instead of \(154{,}19\) kN, that is \(3{,}42\) times too much. The error is in the dangerous direction: the model says the frame carries more than it does. At the force \(154{,}19\) kN the stress in a column is \(N/A = 192{,}7\) MPa, which is \(88\) % of the yield strength \(220\) MPa of chapter 8. The linearly elastic model is therefore nearly at the edge of its validity at this force, and the ratio \(3{,}42\) says something about the shape of the frame, not about the true load capacity. At the force \(527{,}82\) kN the stress would be \(659{,}8\) MPa, far above the yield strength, so for a steel frame the symmetric shape is only a computation, not an event. For the sway shape the largest slope of a section is \(1{,}389\) per metre of largest horizontal displacement, so the slope \(0{,}1\) is reached at the displacement \(72{,}0\) mm (seven percent of the height). Up to this displacement the bound \(v_{\mathrm{h}}'^2 \le 10^{-2}\) of lemma 12.50 holds, which is the basis of the geometric matrix (figure 19.15).

The case with the column turned by a quarter turn (example 19.20) gives a counterexample to the lemma in buckling too: the critical forces are \(92{,}27\), \(182{,}13\) and \(408{,}35\) kN, and the distances to the nearest class are \(0{,}44\), \(1{,}33\) and \(1{,}33\). Since \(\mat P\mat K\mat P \ne \mat K\), no shape is symmetric or antisymmetric. The left half model with the unturned column gives with the symmetric and antisymmetric conditions together the old forces \(154{,}19\), \(527{,}82\) and \(643{,}21\) kN, none of the new ones (figure 19.15).

19.4.5 What we proved and what not

Theorem 19.18 and lemma 19.23 turn COOK's warning (PDF p. 71 and 448) into a proof. In a symmetric system every mode with a simple frequency is symmetric or antisymmetric, and the two half models with conditions on the plane together give exactly all the frequencies of the whole system, each its own class. The warning is therefore about the half model, not about symmetry: whoever leaves the computation at one half model misses the other class, for the portal frame the lowest mode, and the buckling force is too high by the factor \(3{,}42\).

The examples showed three edges of the theorem. First, everything that enters the equations must be mirror symmetric: the stiffness (the turned column), the supports (the axial vibration of the beam) and the reference load. Second, for a multiple eigenvalue the class is not a property of every mode, only of a basis (the mass on springs). Third, the theorem holds only for the linear eigenvalue problem. COOK (PDF p. 71) adds that in nonlinear problems a symmetry that is present when loading begins may disappear later, because the geometry changes. We do not treat this here. Shells of revolution have, according to COOK (PDF p. 71 and 448), often unsymmetric modes in vibration and buckling, because waves run around the circumference. There the mirror is only one of the symmetries, so the theorem is not enough, and we shall generalize it later in the chapter with a rotation instead of a reflection.

19.5 Elimination of constraints and the inclined support

In chapter 12 we supported the L-frame at \(C\) on a surface inclined at \(30°\) and imposed the constraint \(-\sin 30°\,u_{\mathrm{C}} + \cos 30°\,v_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\) in two ways (section 12.6). Multipliers (theorem 12.26) add an unknown to the system, and its matrix is no longer positive definite. The penalty (theorem 12.28) keeps the size of the system, but it is approximate and the matrix becomes worse conditioned. We only opened a third way (figure 19.17): in steps 1 and 2 of the proof of theorem 12.26 we expressed the dependent unknowns by the free ones. Here we follow it to the end and ask how much choice we have in doing so, whether every choice gives the same answer, when a choice fails and what it costs. We call the way elimination (izločanje), because the constraint removes a dependent unknown from the system, as the equation \(y = 2x\) removes \(y\) from a calculation. The letter \(\mat T\) means here what it meant in that proof, the matrix that expands the free numbers into all the unknowns. It is neither the sign matrix \(\mat T\) of lemma 12.22 nor the kinetic energy \(T\).

First we draw the support once more, now as something that chooses two axes.

We draw the frame: the column clamped at \(A\) and the beam with nodes \(B\) and \(D\), ending at \(C\). At \(D\) the force \(F = 500\) N acts downward. At \(C\) the frame rests on a roller support on a surface that makes the angle \(\beta = 30°\) with the horizontal (definition 5.5). The roller of this support carries only a force perpendicular to the surface. If the surface acted on the roller also with a force along itself, this force at the radius of the roller would make a moment about the roller's centre, the pin at the centre carries no moment, and the sum of moments on a roller that does not spin up must be zero. Along the surface the support therefore holds nothing, the roller rolls. So we choose the axis \(\vek t = (\cos\beta, \sin\beta)\) along the surface and the axis \(\vek n = (-\sin\beta, \cos\beta)\) perpendicular to it, both of unit length. The force of the support on the frame is \(\lambda\,\vek n\) with an unknown \(\lambda\), as in figure 12.18. The support is idealized: with a real roller, friction in the bearing would add a small force along the surface that the model does not know.

We split the displacement of the point \(C\) in figure 19.16 into two numbers: \(u_{\mathrm{t}} = \vek t\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) along the surface and \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek n\cdot\vek u_{\mathrm{C}}\) perpendicular to it. The surface is hard, so \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\). This is the same constraint as before, only written in the axes that the surface chose, and in these axes the constraint is a prescribed unknown. A prescribed unknown we know how to eliminate (theorem 7.18). Is this a peculiarity of a surface, or can we generalize it to every constraint?

Let us look at the unknowns \(u\) and \(v\) of the node \(C\) as a point in a plane.

We draw the axes \(u\) and \(v\): \(u\) is the displacement of the node \(C\) in the \(x\) direction, \(v\) the displacement in the \(y\) direction. The constraint \(-\sin\beta\,u + \cos\beta\,v = 0\) lets through only the points on a line through the origin, along the surface. Take an allowed point \(P\). To fix it we do not need both numbers, one is enough, in three ways. With the vertical dashed line we read off \(u\) and compute \(v = \tan\beta\,u\) from it, so \(v\) is dependent and \(u\) is master. With the horizontal dashed line we read off \(v\) and compute \(u = \cot\beta\,v\). With the length \(u_{\mathrm{t}}\) along the line we take a new number that is none of the original unknowns. Each of the three numbers can be the master unknown, because it determines all the rest. It is called master (glavna, "chief") because its value fixes the values of the others. These are dependent (odvisne), because the constraint determines them from the masters. We write the general form for all constraints at once.

Definition 19.25 Transformation of unknowns (transformacija neznank)

Let \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g\) be linear constraints (definition 12.25, figure 19.17) for a column \(\vek d\) of \(n\) unknowns, \(\mat C\) a matrix with \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns. A transformation of unknowns (transformacija neznank) is a representation

\[\vek d = \mat T\,\vek d_{\mathrm{m}} + \vek d_0 , \tag{19.6}\]

where \(\mat T\) is a real matrix with \(n\) rows and \(n - m\) columns that has linearly independent columns (\(\mat T\vek w = \vek 0\) implies \(\vek w = \vek 0\)) and satisfies \(\mat C\,\mat T = \mat 0\), and \(\vek d_0\) is a column of \(n\) elements with \(\mat C\,\vek d_0 = \vek g\). The column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{m}}\) of \(n - m\) numbers holds the master unknowns (glavne neznanke). When the master unknowns are some of the original unknowns (a partition, as in step 1 of the proof of theorem 12.26), the remaining original unknowns are dependent (odvisne).

Source: COOK §8.3, equation (8.3-3) and the text below it (PDF p. 290): the matrix \([T]\) "must be known but need have no special form", and §13.1, equations (13.1-1) to (13.1-3) (PDF pp. 503-504), where the master unknowns are "retained" and the dependent ones "eliminated" or "condensed out". The general form with any matrix \(\mat T\) with the conditions \(\mat C\,\mat T = \mat 0\) and independent columns is ours. ONATE1 §9.4.1 (PDF pp. 337-338) writes the same with a partition.

In figure 19.17 we have \(n = 2\), \(m = 1\) and \(\mat T\) is a column: \((1, \tan\beta)^\T\) for the master \(u\), \((\cot\beta, 1)^\T\) for the master \(v\) and \(\vek t = (\cos\beta, \sin\beta)^\T\) for the master \(u_{\mathrm{t}}\). Each of them lies along the line, so \(\mat C\,\mat T = (-\sin\beta, \cos\beta)\,\mat T = 0\), because \(\vek n\cdot\vek t = 0\). In all three \(\vek d_0 = \vek 0\), because \(g = 0\). For \(g \ne 0\) (\(\vek d_0\) is then one point of the line, for instance a support that has settled) the line moves parallel to itself. In the L-frame we have nine unknowns altogether, \(m = 1\) and \(\mat T\) is a matrix with 9 rows and 8 columns that leaves the unknowns \(u_{\mathrm{B}}\) to \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{D}}\) to \(\varphi_{\mathrm{D}}\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{C}}\) unchanged and in the column for \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) inserts one of the three above. Step 1 of the proof of theorem 12.26 knew only the form in which the unknowns split into free and dependent ones, that is \(\mat T\) with the column \((1, \tan\beta)^\T\) or \((\cot\beta, 1)^\T\). The definition allows every \(\mat T\). Let us see what this brings and what breaks. The letter \(\mat M\) in the theorem is, as in the proof of theorem 12.26, the matrix \(\mat T^\T\mat K\,\mat T\) and not the mass matrix of section 19.4.

Theorem 19.26 Elimination of constraints (izločanje vezi)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\vek f\), \(\mat C\), \(\vek g\) be as in theorem 12.26 (figure 19.17, \(\mat K\) symmetric positive semidefinite of order \(n\), \(\mat C\) with \(m\) pivots and \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d > 0\) for every \(\vek d \ne \vek 0\) with \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek 0\)), \(\vek d^*\) and \(\vek\lambda\) its solution and multipliers, and \(\vek d = \mat T\,\vek d_{\mathrm{m}} + \vek d_0\) any transformation of unknowns (definition 19.25). Then:

  1. Every column \(\vek d\) with \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g\) has the form (19.6) with exactly one \(\vek d_{\mathrm{m}}\).
  2. The matrix \(\mat M = \mat T^\T\mat K\,\mat T\) of order \(n - m\) is symmetric and positive definite, the system
    \[\mat M\,\vek d_{\mathrm{m}} = \mat T^\T(\vek f - \mat K\,\vek d_0) \tag{19.7}\]
    has exactly one solution \(\vek d_{\mathrm{m}}^*\) and \(\mat T\,\vek d_{\mathrm{m}}^* + \vek d_0 = \vek d^*\), for every choice of the transformation.
  3. The column \(\vek r = \mat K\,\vek d^* - \vek f\) equals \(\mat C^\T\vek\lambda\) and
    \[\vek\lambda = (\mat C\,\mat C^\T)^{-1}\,\mat C\,\vek r . \tag{19.8}\]
    If the dependent unknowns are last, \(\vek d = (\vek y, \vek z)\), \(\mat C = [\mat C_{\mathrm{y}}\ \mat C_{\mathrm{z}}]\) and \(\mat T = \begin{pmatrix} \mat I \\ -\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^{-1}\mat C_{\mathrm{y}} \end{pmatrix}\), then \(\vek\lambda = \mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^{-\mathsf T}\vek r_{\mathrm{z}}\), where \(\vek r_{\mathrm{z}}\) is the last \(m\) elements of the column \(\vek r\).
  4. The matrix \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}\) of \(m\) chosen columns of \(\mat C\) is invertible exactly when the chosen unknowns are determined by the others: if \(\vek d\) and \(\vek d'\) are solutions of \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g\) with the same free unknown \(\vek y\), then \(\vek d = \vek d'\). For one constraint, \(m = 1\), with the row \(\vek c^\T\), the unknown \(d_{\mathrm{k}}\) can be dependent exactly when \(c_{\mathrm{k}} \ne 0\).
  5. If \(\mat T\) has orthonormal columns (\(\mat T^\T\mat T = \mat I\)) and \(\mat K\) is positive definite, then \(\kappa(\mat M) \le \kappa(\mat K)\) (definition 6.31).
Idea

The constraint defines a flat line (plane) of allowed columns, as in figure 19.17. Every matrix \(\mat T\) is a coordinate system on it, and the energy in these coordinates is a quadratic function with a positive definite matrix. Its minimum is the same, because the line is the same, and the multipliers come from the equilibrium off the line.

Proof

We must show (figure 19.17) that the columns of \(\mat T\) cover all allowed columns (item 1), that the energy in these coordinates is strictly convex and that its minimum is \(\vek d^*\) (item 2), then connect the multipliers with the residuals (item 3), check when the partition works (item 4) and bound the conditioning (item 5).

  1. We number the unknowns so that the chosen pivot columns of \(\mat C\) are last, as in step 1 of the proof of theorem 12.26, \(\vek d = (\vek y, \vek z)\). The matrix \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}\) is invertible (lemma 8.21) and every \(\vek w\) with \(\mat C\,\vek w = \vek 0\) has the form \(\vek w = \mat T_0\vek w_{\mathrm{y}}\) with \(\mat T_0 = \begin{pmatrix} \mat I \\ -\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^{-1}\mat C_{\mathrm{y}} \end{pmatrix}\), because \(\mat C_{\mathrm{y}}\vek w_{\mathrm{y}} + \mat C_{\mathrm{z}}\vek w_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek 0\) and \(\vek w_{\mathrm{z}} = -\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^{-1}\mat C_{\mathrm{y}}\vek w_{\mathrm{y}}\).
  2. The columns of \(\mat T\) satisfy \(\mat C\,\mat T = \mat 0\), so \(\mat T = \mat T_0\,\mat B\), where \(\mat B\) is the top \(n - m\) rows of \(\mat T\). If \(\mat B\,\vek w = \vek 0\), then \(\mat T\vek w = \mat T_0\mat B\,\vek w = \vek 0\) and by the independence of the columns \(\vek w = \vek 0\). The square matrix \(\mat B\) is therefore invertible (lemma 8.21).
  3. For every \(\vek d\) with \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g\) we have \(\mat C(\vek d - \vek d_0) = \vek 0\), so by step 1 \(\vek d - \vek d_0 = \mat T_0(\vek y - \vek y_0) = \mat T\,\mat B^{-1}(\vek y - \vek y_0)\), where \(\vek y_0\) is the upper part of the column \(\vek d_0\), and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{m}} = \mat B^{-1}(\vek y - \vek y_0)\). Another \(\vek d_{\mathrm{m}}'\) with the same \(\vek d\) would give \(\mat T(\vek d_{\mathrm{m}} - \vek d_{\mathrm{m}}') = \vek 0\) and by the independence of the columns it would be equal.
  4. The matrix \(\mat M\) is symmetric, because \(\mat K\) is symmetric. For \(\vek w \ne \vek 0\) we have \(\mat T\vek w \ne \vek 0\) (independent columns) and \(\mat C\,\mat T\vek w = \vek 0\), so \(\vek w^\T\mat M\vek w = (\mat T\vek w)^\T\mat K(\mat T\vek w) > 0\) by the hypothesis of theorem 12.26. The matrix \(\mat M\) is positive definite and the system (19.7) has exactly one solution (theorem 6.29).
  5. The expansion from step 2 of the proof of theorem 12.26 gives \(\Pi(\mat T\vek d_{\mathrm{m}} + \vek d_0) = \tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{m}}^\T\mat M\,\vek d_{\mathrm{m}} - \vek h^\T\vek d_{\mathrm{m}} + \Pi(\vek d_0)\) with \(\vek h = \mat T^\T(\vek f - \mat K\vek d_0)\), which has its minimum exactly at the solution of the system (19.7) (lemma 6.30). By item 1 every allowed point belongs to one \(\vek d_{\mathrm{m}}\), so \(\mat T\,\vek d_{\mathrm{m}}^* + \vek d_0\) is the point of least energy on the set of constraints, and by item 1 of theorem 12.26 this is \(\vek d^*\).
  6. By item 2 of theorem 12.26 \(\vek r = \mat C^\T\vek\lambda\). For \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\) we have \(\mat C^\T\vek x \ne \vek 0\) (step 3 of the proof of theorem 12.26) and \(\vek x^\T\mat C\,\mat C^\T\vek x = |\mat C^\T\vek x|^2 > 0\). The matrix \(\mat C\,\mat C^\T\) is symmetric and positive definite, so invertible (theorem 6.29). Multiplying the equation \(\vek r = \mat C^\T\vek\lambda\) by \(\mat C\) from the left gives (19.8). For the partition the last \(m\) rows of \(\mat C^\T\) are \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^\T\), so \(\vek r_{\mathrm{z}} = \mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^\T\vek\lambda\), and \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^\T\) is invertible (lemma 8.21).
  7. Let \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}\) be invertible. From \(\mat C\,\vek d = \mat C\,\vek d' = \vek g\) and \(\vek y = \vek y'\) it follows that \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}(\vek z - \vek z') = \vek 0\), so \(\vek z = \vek z'\). Let \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}\) be not invertible. By lemma 8.21 there is \(\vek w \ne \vek 0\) with \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}\vek w = \vek 0\). Then \(\mat C\,(\vek 0, \vek w) = \vek 0\) and \(\vek d' = \vek d + (\vek 0, \vek w)\) is another solution with the same \(\vek y\). For \(m = 1\) we have \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}} = (c_{\mathrm{k}})\), a square matrix of order 1, invertible exactly when \(c_{\mathrm{k}} \ne 0\).
  8. For \(\vek w \ne \vek 0\) we have \(|\mat T\vek w|^2 = \vek w^\T\mat T^\T\mat T\vek w = |\vek w|^2\), so the Rayleigh quotient of \(\mat M\) at \(\vek w\) is the quotient of \(\mat K\) at \(\mat T\vek w\). By theorem 10.26 with \(\mat M = \mat I\) it lies between \(\lambda_{\min}(\mat K)\) and \(\lambda_{\max}(\mat K)\). This holds for every \(\vek w\), also for the eigencolumns of \(\mat M\), so \(\lambda_{\max}(\mat M) \le \lambda_{\max}(\mat K)\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\mat M) \ge \lambda_{\min}(\mat K)\), and the ratio is smaller.

Source: COOK §13.1, equations (13.1-3) and (13.1-4) (PDF p. 504): \([T]^\T[K][T]\{D_{\mathrm{r}}\} = [T]^\T\{R\}\) for a partition, and "For multipoint constraints, the choice of which d.o.f. to place in {D_c} is not unique, but different choices should lead to the same final results". ONATE1 §9.4.1 (PDF p. 338): "The selection of \(a_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{e}}\) is not unique". The proof gives this claim, items 3 to 5 are not from the sources.

The proof showed (figure 19.17) that any matrix \(\mat T\) with independent columns and \(\mat C\,\mat T = \mat 0\) gives the same solution \(\vek d^*\), the same as the multipliers, and that we get the multipliers from the residual \(\mat K\,\vek d^* - \vek f\), as in equilibrium. The partition of chapter 12 is only one of the choices. We return to both: what the choice of \(\mat T\) does in numbers and what happens when the partition fails.

We eliminate the constraint \(u_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\) in the L-frame in three ways, with a \(\mat T\) that leaves \(u_{\mathrm{B}}\) to \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{D}}\) to \(\varphi_{\mathrm{D}}\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{C}}\) unchanged. The eight master unknowns in each are these seven and one of the three from figure 19.17. The frame has the same \(E = 196\) GPa, \(A = 800\) mm² and \(I = 106\,667\) mm⁴ as in chapter 12, \(F = 500\) N and \(h = 0{,}5\) m for the elements \(BD\) and \(DC\). The multipliers of theorem 12.26 give \(\lambda = 213{,}765\) N, \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = -0{,}1533\) mm, \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = -0{,}0885\) mm, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{C}} = 0{,}000891\).

\(u_{\mathrm{t}}\) (local axes) \((\cos 30°, \sin 30°)^\T\) \(2{,}91 \cdot 10^4\) \(9 \cdot 10^{-18}\) m \(213{,}765\) N

All three choices (figure 19.17, left) give the same displacement up to rounding (differences up to \(10^{-17}\) m for displacements of size \(10^{-4}\) m), as item 2 claims. The master \(u_{\mathrm{t}}\) gives \(u_{\mathrm{t}} = -0{,}1770\) mm, which is \(\cos 30°\cdot(-0{,}1533) + \sin 30°\cdot(-0{,}0885)\) mm. The multiplier comes from the residual \(\vek r = \mat K\,\vek d^* - \vek f\) by item 3. At \(C\) we have \(\vek r_{\mathrm{C}} = (-106{,}88,\ 185{,}13)\) N, which is \(\lambda\,\vek n\) of chapter 12, and with local axes \(\lambda = \vek n\cdot\vek r_{\mathrm{C}} = 213{,}765\) N. For the dependent \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) we have \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}} = \cos 30° = 0{,}866\) and \(\lambda = r_{\mathrm{v}_\mathrm{C}}/0{,}866 = 185{,}13/0{,}866\), for the dependent \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\) we have \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}} = -\sin 30°\) and \(\lambda = -106{,}88/(-0{,}5)\). The third choice gives a somewhat worse conditioned matrix, \(4{,}03 \cdot 10^4\) against \(2{,}91 \cdot 10^4\), which we look at below. The matrix \(\mat K\) of the nine free unknowns has \(\kappa = 2{,}76 \cdot 10^5\), so the constraint improved the matrix, because it stiffened the softest mode in which \(C\) moves (as for the penalty in chapter 12).

Now let us see what breaks when the partition is impossible. Item 4 of the theorem says that \(d_{\mathrm{k}}\) can be dependent only if \(c_{\mathrm{k}} \ne 0\). Take the horizontal surface of section 12.4.5. The constraint is \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\) with the row \(\vek c^\T = \vek e_{\mathrm{v}_\mathrm{C}}^\T\), at the place of \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\) we have \(c = 0\). If we choose \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\) as dependent, we would have to compute \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\) from \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\), but the constraint says nothing about \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\). In the right half of figure 19.17 the points \(P\) and \(Q\) on the horizontal line of the constraint have the same \(v\) and different \(u\), as the dashed lines on both axes show. The matrix \(\mat T_0\) does not exist, because we would have to divide by \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}} = c_{\mathrm{u}} = 0\). The master unknown must be \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\), the dependent one \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\), and this is the prescribed unknown that chapter 7 eliminated.

The failure is not only at exactly zero (figure 19.17, right). Tilt the surface back toward the horizontal and still take \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\) as dependent, so \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = \cot\beta\,v_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}} = -\sin\beta\). The table shows what happens to the matrix \(\mat M\) as \(\beta\) goes to zero, and what happens with the local axes.

\(\beta\) \(\vert\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}\vert = \sin\beta\) \(\cot\beta\) \(\kappa(\mat M)\), \(u_{\mathrm{C}}\) dependent \(\kappa(\mat M)\), local axes
\(30°\) \(0{,}5\) \(1{,}73\) \(4{,}03 \cdot 10^4\) \(2{,}91 \cdot 10^4\)
\(10°\) \(0{,}174\) \(5{,}67\) \(2{,}76 \cdot 10^5\) \(2{,}88 \cdot 10^4\)
\(1°\) \(0{,}0175\) \(57{,}3\) \(2{,}73 \cdot 10^7\) \(2{,}97 \cdot 10^4\)
\(0{,}1°\) \(0{,}00175\) \(573\) \(2{,}74 \cdot 10^9\) \(2{,}99 \cdot 10^4\)
