The growth has a reason (figure 19.17, left: for small \(\beta\) the horizontal dashed line along which we read \(v\) is very long, a small change of \(v\) is a large move of \(u\)). Take the master unknown \(v_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(\vek w\) with a one at that place. The column \(\mat T\vek w\) has \(v_{\mathrm{C}} = 1\) and \(u_{\mathrm{C}} = \cot\beta\), zero elsewhere. The quotient \((\mat T\vek w)^\T\mat K\,(\mat T\vek w)\) is \(\cot^2\beta\,K_{\mathrm{u}_\mathrm{Cu}_\mathrm{C}} + K_{\mathrm{v}_\mathrm{Cv}_\mathrm{C}}\), since \(K_{\mathrm{u}_\mathrm{Cv}_\mathrm{C}} = 0\) (axial and bending stiffness of the element \(DC\) do not mix). With \(K_{\mathrm{u}_\mathrm{Cu}_\mathrm{C}} = EA/h = 3{,}136 \cdot 10^8\) N/m this is at least \(3{,}136 \cdot 10^8\cot^2\beta\), and by theorem 10.26 (with \(\mat M = \mat I\)) \(\lambda_{\max}(\mat M)\) is at least that large. The smallest eigenvalue stays at \(3{,}76 \cdot 10^4\), so \(\kappa \approx 8{,}3 \cdot 10^3\cot^2\beta\), which the table confirms (\(8{,}6 \cdot 10^3\), \(8{,}3 \cdot 10^3\) and \(8{,}3 \cdot 10^3\) at \(10°\), \(1°\) and \(0{,}1°\)). A small angle is not zero, yet already at \(\beta = 1°\) the loss of conditioning is a factor of \(10^3\). The local axes have \(\mat T^\T\mat T = \mat I\) and by item 5 do not exceed \(\kappa(\mat K) = 2{,}76 \cdot 10^5\), and in the table they stay at \(2{,}9 \cdot 10^4\) to \(3{,}0 \cdot 10^4\) for all angles. The partition on the contrary has \(\mat T_0^\T\mat T_0 = \mat I + \mat C_{\mathrm{y}}^\T(\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}\mat C_{\mathrm{z}}^\T)^{-1}\mat C_{\mathrm{y}}\), which is larger than \(\mat I\), and there is no protection in that.

We used the local axes (figure 19.16) at \(C\) without proving that such a \(\mat T\) is a transformation in the sense of the definition. We write it in general.

Lemma 19.27 Inclined support by local axes (nagnjena podpora z lokalnimi osmi)

Let \(\mat K\) be a positive definite matrix of order \(n\), \(\vek f\) a column of \(n\) elements and let the node \(C\) (figure 19.16) have the unknowns \(u\) and \(v\) at the places \(i\) and \(j\). The support does not allow the node to move in the direction \(\vek n = (-\sin\beta, \cos\beta)\), the constraint is \(\vek c^\T\vek d = 0\) with \(c_{\mathrm{i}} = -\sin\beta\), \(c_{\mathrm{j}} = \cos\beta\) and \(0\) elsewhere. Let \(\mat R\) be the matrix of order \(n\) that is the identity except in the block at the places \(i\) and \(j\), where it is \(\mat Q = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\beta & \sin\beta \\ -\sin\beta & \cos\beta \end{pmatrix}\), the new unknowns \(\vek d' = \mat R\,\vek d\) (among them \(u_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{n}}\) at the places \(i\) and \(j\)), \(\mat K' = \mat R\,\mat K\,\mat R^\T\) and \(\vek f' = \mat R\,\vek f\). Then:

  1. The matrix \(\mat R\) is orthogonal (definition 2.39), \(\mat K'\) is positive definite, \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f\) is equivalent to \(\mat K'\vek d' = \vek f'\) and the constraint is \(d'_{\mathrm{j}} = u_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\).
  2. We eliminate the constraint by deleting row and column \(j\) of \(\mat K'\) and \(\vek f'\) (theorem 7.18). What remains is a system of order \(n - 1\) with the matrix \(\mat M\), which is the elimination of theorem 19.26 with \(\mat T = \mat R^\T\) without the column \(j\).
  3. The column \(\mat K'\vek d' - \vek f'\) has its only nonzero element at the place \(j\) and it is the multiplier \(\lambda\). The support acts on the frame with the force \(\lambda\,\vek n\) and none along \(\vek t\).
  4. \(\kappa(\mat M) \le \kappa(\mat K)\).
Idea

We put the axis \(\vek n\) (figure 19.16) on a coordinate axis of the new unknowns. The constraint is then one of them, and a rotation of the coordinates, which does not change lengths, does not change the eigenvalues.

Proof

We must show (figure 19.16) that the rotation of the node's coordinates keeps the system and the constraint, that the constraint is a prescribed unknown and that the residual in row \(j\) carries the multiplier.

  1. The block \(\mat Q\) is orthogonal, \(\mat Q^\T\mat Q = \mat I\) (\(\cos^2\beta + \sin^2\beta = 1\) and the mixed terms cancel), so \(\mat R\) is orthogonal too and \(\mat R^\T\mat R = \mat I\). For \(\vek w \ne \vek 0\) we have \(\vek w^\T\mat K'\vek w = (\mat R^\T\vek w)^\T\mat K(\mat R^\T\vek w) > 0\), because \(\mat R^\T\vek w \ne \vek 0\). Multiplying the equation \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f\) by \(\mat R\) from the left and using \(\vek d = \mat R^\T\vek d'\) gives \(\mat K'\vek d' = \vek f'\), and back with \(\mat R^\T\). The second row of the block \(\mat Q\) gives \(d'_{\mathrm{j}} = -\sin\beta\,u + \cos\beta\,v = \vek c^\T\vek d\).
  2. The constraint \(d'_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) is a prescribed unknown, and by theorem 7.18 the solution of the other unknowns is the solution of the system with row and column \(j\) deleted. The columns of \(\mat R^\T\) except the column \(j\) are \(\mat T\) with \(\mat C\,\mat T = \vek c^\T\mat R^\T = \vek e_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat R\mat R^\T\) without the column \(j\), so zero, \(\mat C\,\mat T = \mat 0\).
  3. By item 3 of theorem 19.26 \(\mat K\,\vek d - \vek f = \vek c\,\lambda\), because \(\mat C = \vek c^\T\). Multiplying by \(\mat R\) gives \(\mat K'\vek d' - \vek f' = \mat R\,\vek c\,\lambda\) and \(\mat R\,\vek c = \vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), because \(\vek c = \mat R^\T\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  4. The matrix \(\mat K'\) is orthogonally similar to \(\mat K\) and has the same eigenvalues (if \(\mat K\vek v = \lambda\vek v\), then \(\mat K'\mat R\vek v = \lambda\mat R\vek v\)). The matrix \(\mat M\) is \(\mat K'\) without row and column \(j\), that is \(\mat T^\T\mat K\,\mat T\), where \(\mat T\) (the columns of \(\mat R^\T\) without column \(j\)) has orthonormal columns. So by item 5 of theorem 19.26 \(\kappa(\mat M) \le \kappa(\mat K) = \kappa(\mat K')\).

Source: COOK §8.4, equation (8.4-4) (PDF pp. 290-291): \([T]^\T[K'][T]\) with \([T_3]\) for node 3 and "It is preferable to transform individual element matrices before assembly". ONATE1 §9.2, equations (9.1) to (9.4) (PDF pp. 332-333): local direction \(x'\), \(y'\) at the support, "The reactions at the inclined boundary nodes are directly computed in the local boundary system". The proof, the bound on the condition number and the form of \(\mat K'\vek d' - \vek f'\) are not from the sources.

Item 3 of the lemma is the same conclusion as the argument about the roller. In the L-frame the residual at \(C\) along \(\vek t\) is \(-2 \cdot 10^{-12}\) N (rounding), along \(\vek n\) it is \(213{,}765\) N, as the multiplier. The support really carries nothing along the surface (figure 19.16). The penalty with \(\alpha s = 10^4\) on the other hand satisfies the constraint only approximately, \(\vek c^\T\vek d = -1{,}6 \cdot 10^{-6}\) m instead of zero.

We put the three ways side by side, on the same frame and with the same constraint.

multipliers \(10\) \(9\) positive and \(1\) negative eigenvalue exact more unknowns

The rows on multipliers and penalty are from chapter 12 (figure 12.18), the row on elimination is new. COOK (PDF p. 503) says the same in words: multipliers "add to the number of equations but require less manipulation", the penalty leaves the number of unknowns and "may produce an ill-conditioned set of equations", and elimination requires "considerable bookkeeping in software and rearrangement of coefficients, especially for multipoint constraints". This last point holds for the general partition. For a single support with local axes there is little rearranging, because only the \(2 \times 2\) block of the node changes, as COOK states on PDF p. 291 (element matrices before assembly). For constraints between several nodes, which section 19.6 needs, the partition \(\mat T_0\) changes rows and columns of several nodes at once.

The section showed three things (figures 19.16 and 19.17). Elimination gives for every transformation the same solution as the multipliers (item 2), with no extra unknown and with a positive definite matrix. The choice of dependent unknowns is not indifferent: the partition is possible only for \(c_{\mathrm{k}} \ne 0\) and for a small \(\sin\beta\) it already loses conditioning, the local axes do not. The inclined support is therefore elimination, which chapter 7 already knew for a horizontal surface, with a rotation of the axes at the node. A matrix \(\mat T\) that is not orthogonal comes into its own with rigid links, where a constraint ties the displacements of several nodes.

19.6 Rigid links and constraints between several nodes

Take two steel bars with a 20 mm × 40 mm section and lay one on the other, like two planks. Fix one end into a wall and hang a force \(F = 100\) N on the free end. If the bars slide over each other, each bends on its own, and together they are only as stiff as two sections. If we glue them, they can no longer slide and behave as one bar with a 20 mm × 80 mm section. Chapter 5 already says how much the two cases differ: by Steiner's theorem (5.28) the second moment of the glued section is \(I_{\mathrm{c}} = 2\,(I + A\,e^2)\) with \(I = 106\,667\) mm⁴, \(A = 800\) mm² and the distance \(e = 20\) mm between the axis of each bar and the contact surface, so \(853\,333\) mm⁴, eight times the \(I\) of one bar. With free sliding it is only \(2I = 213\,333\) mm⁴.

In the finite element model of chapter 12 each bar is a line with nodes on its own axis, the axes are \(2e = 40\) mm apart and the nodes do not touch. How do we say that the bars are glued? We need a constraint that connects nodes of different bars. Such a constraint is called a constraint between several nodes, and the simplest one is the rigid link: a stick that neither bends nor lengthens.

Let us first look at it for one pair of nodes. Chapter 12 described a frame node by three numbers: the displacement \(u\) in the \(x\) direction, the displacement \(v\) in the \(y\) direction and the rotation of the section \(\varphi\), counterclockwise (definition 12.17). Every node thus has three unknowns, and a link will tie exactly these.

We draw two horizontal lines, the lower on the contact surface of the bars and the upper on the axis of the upper bar. On the lower one lies the master node \(M\), on the upper one the dependent node \(Z\) right above it. Between them is the rigid link, a stick of length \(e\) that neither bends nor lengthens. Why rigid: that is the name of a body that does not deform, and the link is a piece of such a body fixed to both sections. Why master and dependent: the unknowns of the master node stay in the system, those of the dependent node are already determined by them, they depend on them.

Now we load the structure. The master node moves by \(u_{\mathrm{M}}\) to \(M'\) and the section turns by \(\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\). The link is fixed to the section, so it turns with it, and the point \(Z\) goes to \(Z'\), which is displaced horizontally by \(e\sin\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\) to the left of \(M'\). For a small rotation this is \(e\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\) and the displacement of the point \(Z\) along \(x\) is \(u_{\mathrm{M}} - e\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\), while the vertical one does not change. That is the whole content of the link: the three numbers of the dependent node are expressed by the three of the master. We state it in general.

Definition 19.28 Rigid link (toga povezava)

Let \(M\) and \(Z\) be nodes of a plane frame (definition 5.90) with unknowns \((u_{\mathrm{M}}, v_{\mathrm{M}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{M}})\) and \((u_{\mathrm{Z}}, v_{\mathrm{Z}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{Z}})\) in the sense of definition 12.17, lying at distinct points, \(\overrightarrow{MZ} = (a, b) \ne (0, 0)\) before loading. A rigid link (toga povezava) between them is the model in which the two points and the sections at them belong to the same rigid body, which moves by lemma 4.72 on a small rigid displacement with the unknowns of node \(M\) as \(\delta\vek a = (u_{\mathrm{M}}, v_{\mathrm{M}})\) and \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi = \varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). Node \(M\) is the master (glavno vozlišče), node \(Z\) the dependent node (odvisno vozlišče).

Source: COOK §8.5 (PDF p. 294-295): "imaginary rigid links", the unknowns of one element become "slave" to those of another, "rotations are small". The notation with the small rigid displacement of chapter 4 is ours.

Does the link really determine the dependent unknowns by the master ones, and how? We show it with three equations and with the matrix that we shall need for elimination.

Lemma 19.29 Unknowns of the dependent node (neznanke odvisnega vozlišča)

For a rigid link with master node \(M\), dependent node \(Z\) (definition 19.28) and offset \(\overrightarrow{MZ} = (a, b)\):

  1. \(u_{\mathrm{Z}} = u_{\mathrm{M}} - b\,\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\), \(\quad v_{\mathrm{Z}} = v_{\mathrm{M}} + a\,\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\), \(\quad \varphi_{\mathrm{Z}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\).
  2. In the columns \(\vek d_{\mathrm{M}} = (u_{\mathrm{M}}, v_{\mathrm{M}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{M}})^\T\) and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{Z}} = (u_{\mathrm{Z}}, v_{\mathrm{Z}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{Z}})^\T\) this reads
    \[\vek d_{\mathrm{Z}} = \mat T_0\,\vek d_{\mathrm{M}} , \qquad \mat T_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & -b \\ 0 & 1 & a \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . \tag{19.9}\]
  3. The three equations of item 1 are linear constraints (definition 12.25), \(\vek d_{\mathrm{Z}} - \mat T_0\,\vek d_{\mathrm{M}} = \vek 0\), with the constraint matrix \([\mat I\ \ -\mat T_0]\) on the columns \((\vek d_{\mathrm{Z}}, \vek d_{\mathrm{M}})\) and three pivots in the columns of the dependent node.
  4. The distance between the points \(M\) and \(Z\) grows after the displacement of item 1 by at most the factor \(1 + \tfrac12\,\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}^2\) (lemma 4.72).
Proof

We must show that the displacement of the point \(Z\) is the displacement of a rigid body with origin at \(M\) and that the rotation of the section is the same everywhere. We write the vector product in components.

  1. By definition 19.28 the displacement of the point \(Z\) is \(\delta\vek u(Z) = \delta\vek a + \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\overrightarrow{MZ}\) with \(\delta\vek a = (u_{\mathrm{M}}, v_{\mathrm{M}}, 0)\), \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi = (0, 0, \varphi_{\mathrm{M}})\) and \(\overrightarrow{MZ} = (a, b, 0)\).
  2. By the definition of the vector product (definition 2.30), \((0, 0, \varphi_{\mathrm{M}})\times(a, b, 0) = (0\cdot 0 - \varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\,b,\ \varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\,a - 0\cdot 0,\ 0) = (-b\,\varphi_{\mathrm{M}},\ a\,\varphi_{\mathrm{M}},\ 0)\). Hence \(u_{\mathrm{Z}} = u_{\mathrm{M}} - b\,\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{Z}} = v_{\mathrm{M}} + a\,\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\).
  3. The field \(\delta\vek u(P) = \delta\vek a + \varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times\overrightarrow{MP}\) has in the plane the form \((u_{\mathrm{M}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\,y, v_{\mathrm{M}} + \varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\,x)\) in the coordinates \(x\), \(y\) of the point \(P\) relative to \(M\). Its small rotation tensor has the only nonzero component \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\), whatever the point (definition 1.116, as in step 4 of the proof of lemma 12.18). The section at \(Z\) therefore turns by \(\varphi_{\mathrm{Z}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{M}}\).
  4. Item 2 is steps 2 and 3 in matrix form, item 3 is a rewriting of the equations in the form \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek 0\) with the row block on the columns \(\vek d_{\mathrm{Z}}\) equal to \(\mat I\), which has three pivots.
  5. Item 4 is the statement of lemma 4.72 for the points \(M\) and \(Z\) and the angle \(|\delta\boldsymbol\varphi| = |\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}|\).

Source: COOK §8.5 (PDF p. 294, "rotations are small", equation 8.5-4, and PDF p. 295-296, equation 8.5-6) for the form \(\vek d_{\mathrm{Z}} = \mat T_0\,\vek d_{\mathrm{M}}\). The proof is not from the source, it follows from lemma 4.72.

The link is linear and therefore approximate. In figure 19.18 we get the true new position \(Z'\) (the orange dot) by turning the link about \(M'\). It differs from the place where the lemma puts it (the open circle) vertically by \(e\,(1 - \cos\varphi_{\mathrm{M}})\), which is of order \(\tfrac12 e\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}^2\), and the lemma leaves this term out. Why this does no harm: with the constraint we only have to put the node \(Z\) in the right place to first order, since the equations of the elements themselves (lemma 12.18) hold only for small displacements. The bound is item 4 of the lemma: the link lengthens by at most the factor \(1 + \tfrac12\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}^2\). In the cantilever that we compute below the rotation at the free end is \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}| = 2{,}99\cdot 10^{-4}\) (glued pair, force 100 N), so the lengthening of a link of length \(e = 20\) mm is at most \(20\cdot 0{,}5\cdot(2{,}99\cdot 10^{-4})^2 \approx 0{,}9\) nm. For \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{M}}| \le 10^{-2}\) it is at most \(5\cdot 10^{-5}\,e\). For a rotation of \(0{,}5\) rad as in the figure the lemma would allow up to \(12{,}5\,\%\), which is why the figure is enlarged and not a true picture.

The constraints \(\vek d_{\mathrm{Z}} - \mat T_0\,\vek d_{\mathrm{M}} = \vek 0\) of the lemma are a special kind of constraint, to which chapter 12 gave no name.

Definition 19.30 Constraint between several nodes (multipoint constraint, vez med več vozlišči)

Let \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g\) be a system of linear constraints (definition 12.25) in a finite element model with the unknowns of several nodes. A constraint whose row of \(\mat C\) has nonzero numbers at the unknowns of one node only is a single-point constraint (enotočkovna vez), for instance a prescribed displacement of a node or a support from section 19.5. A constraint with nonzero numbers at the unknowns of at least two nodes, such as a rigid link, is a multipoint constraint (vez med več vozlišči).

Source: COOK §13.1 (PDF p. 504): for single-point constraints "[C_r] null and [C_c] a unit matrix", for several points the choice of the dependent unknowns is not unique, and §8.5 (PDF p. 295): "a multipoint constraint". FELIPPA §9.1.2 (PDF p. 127): \(u_{\mathrm{x}2} - 2u_{\mathrm{x}4} + u_{\mathrm{x}6} = 0{,}25\) is a constraint among three nodes, linear and nonhomogeneous.

Each of the three equations of lemma 19.29 contains the unknowns of two nodes, so it is a multipoint constraint. The constraint that equates only the deflection, \(v_{\text{up}} - v_{\text{low}} = 0\) between the nodes of the upper and the lower bar, is also a multipoint constraint and will be enough for free sliding. With a rigid link the dependent unknowns offer themselves, the unknowns of the dependent node: the constraint rows have the unit matrix on its columns, square and invertible, as COOK says they must be (PDF p. 504, "square and nonsingular"). This choice is not the only one. COOK (PDF p. 504) says that for multipoint constraints the choice of dependent unknowns is not unique and that different choices give the same result. The matrix \(\mat T_0\) has determinant \(1\) and is invertible, so we could also take the unknowns of node \(M\) as dependent. In elimination by theorem 19.26 we choose the unknowns of node \(M\) as master unknowns and get \(\vek d = \mat T\,\vek d_{\mathrm{m}}\) with \(\mat T\) built from blocks \(\mat I\) and \(\mat T_0\). COOK (PDF p. 296) warns that for a rigid triangle a badly chosen triple of unknowns would lead to a division by zero. Here there is no such danger, since the block at the dependent node is the unit matrix.

19.6.1 The glued and the free pair of bars

Now we test the link on the pair of bars from the beginning of the section. The model is a cantilever of length \(L = 1\) m made of two equal steel bars with a 20 mm × 40 mm section (width 20 mm, height 40 mm), \(E = 196\) GPa, \(EA = 1{,}568\cdot 10^{8}\) N, \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\) N m². The bars lie one on the other, the axes are at \(y = \pm e\) with \(e = 20\) mm, the contact surface is at \(y = 0\). Both are clamped at \(x = 0\), at the free end a force \(F = 100\) N acts downwards. Each bar is divided into \(n\) equal frame elements (definition 12.17, Euler-Bernoulli beam with axial deformation) of length \(h = L/n\). Idealization: the glue is an infinitely stiff link without slip, a real glue has a finite shear stiffness and would give something in between. The linear model is fair, the stress at the clamp of the glued pair is \(F L\cdot 0{,}04\ \text{m}/I_{\mathrm{c}} = 4{,}7\) MPa, since 0,04 m is half the height of the pair.

We draw the wall with the two clamped bars and the pair of bars that slide, because nothing holds them together. At the free end acts the force \(F\). Both bars bend equally, since only the equal deflection joins them, and at the free end a slip therefore appears: the contact surface of the upper bar moves by \(e\varphi\) in one direction, that of the lower by \(e\varphi\) in the other, so together \(2e\varphi = 0{,}048\) mm. Below we draw the glued pair with the same wall and the same force, only that the sections at the nodes carry rigid links that hold the bars together. There is no slip, and the end deflects four times less. The deflections \(\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\) are in the ratio \(4 : 1\), as Steiner predicts: \(213\,333 \to 853\,333\) mm⁴.

In the free pair the multipoint constraint acts on the deflection only: \(v_{\text{up}} = v_{\text{low}}\) at every node, while the axial unknowns and the rotations of the two bars are free. The solution is unique (the matrix after clamping is positive definite) and therefore symmetric between the bars, which have the same \(EI\): they have the same rotation, and the system is a single beam with \(2EI\) under the force \(F\), which by theorem 12.14 is exact at the nodes. So the tip deflection is \(F L^3/(3\cdot 2EI) = 0{,}79719\) mm for every \(n\), as num-06.py computes.

The glued pair has three master unknowns at each node, six on both bars together, so the number of unknowns halves: at \(n = 4\) there are \(2\cdot 5\cdot 3 = 30\) unknowns of the bars and \(15\) master ones, \(12\) after clamping. The reduced matrix is positive definite (smallest eigenvalue \(6{,}57\cdot 10^{4}\), theorem 19.26, since after clamping the structure has no rigid motions left). The results:

\(n\) (elements per bar) tip deflection of the glued pair (mm) error (mm) error relative to \(0{,}19930\) mm
1 \(0{,}34877\) \(0{,}14947\) \(75{,}0\ \%\)
2 \(0{,}23667\) \(0{,}03737\) \(18{,}75\ \%\)
4 \(0{,}20864\) \(0{,}00934\) \(4{,}7\ \%\)
8 \(0{,}20163\) \(0{,}00234\) \(1{,}2\ \%\)
16 \(0{,}19988\) \(0{,}00058\) \(0{,}29\ \%\)
32 \(0{,}19944\) \(0{,}00015\) \(0{,}07\ \%\)

What do we notice? The tip deflection approaches the exact Steiner value from above, and with every halving of \(h\) the error shrinks by a factor of four (error column: \(0{,}14947 \to 0{,}03737 \to 0{,}00934\)). This is unusual: for the beam of chapter 12 the deflection at the nodes was exact for every \(n\) (theorem 12.14), here it is not, and the free pair kept that exactness. Why the glued pair lost it, what the error is and why a factor four, the next theorem shows.

Theorem 19.31 Glued cantilever with rigid links (zlepljena konzola iz togih povezav)

Let a cantilever of length \(L\) consist of two equal bars with \(EA\) and \(EI\), axes at \(y = \pm e\), each made of \(n\) equal frame elements of length \(h = L/n\) with nodes at \(x_{\mathrm{i}} = i\,h\). At node \(i\) there is the master node \(M_{\mathrm{i}}\) on \(y = 0\) with unknowns \((u_{\mathrm{i}}, v_{\mathrm{i}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{i}})\), and the bar nodes at \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) are tied to it by rigid links with offsets \((0, +e)\) and \((0, -e)\) (definition 19.28). Clamping: \(u_0 = v_0 = \varphi_0 = 0\). At \(M_{\mathrm{n}}\) a force \(F\) acts downwards, there are no other loads. Let \(r = EAe^2/EI\), \(EI_{\mathrm{c}} = 2\,(EI + EAe^2) = 2EI\,(1 + r)\), \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}} = -\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = -v_{\mathrm{i}}\). Then:

  1. \(u_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) for all \(i\).
  2. \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}} = \dfrac{F\,x_{\mathrm{i}}\,(2L - x_{\mathrm{i}})}{2EI_{\mathrm{c}}}\), which is the rotation of a cantilever with bending stiffness \(EI_{\mathrm{c}}\) by theorem 5.56, exact at every node.
  3. \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = \dfrac{F\,x_{\mathrm{i}}^2\,(3L - x_{\mathrm{i}})}{6EI_{\mathrm{c}}} + i\,\dfrac{F\,h^3}{24\,EI}\,\dfrac{r}{1 + r}\), so the tip deflection exceeds the exact one by \(\dfrac{F L^3}{24\,EI\,n^2}\,\dfrac{r}{1+r}\), relatively by \(\dfrac{r}{4n^2}\).
Proof

We must show three items. From the energy of the reduced system we get the axial unknowns, then the equilibrium at the nodes, then the rotations and at the end the deflection from the Hermite form of the element.

  1. By lemma 19.29 (\(a = 0\), \(b = \pm e\)) the unknowns of the upper bar at node \(i\) are \((u_{\mathrm{i}} - e\varphi_{\mathrm{i}},\ v_{\mathrm{i}},\ \varphi_{\mathrm{i}})\) and of the lower bar \((u_{\mathrm{i}} + e\varphi_{\mathrm{i}},\ v_{\mathrm{i}},\ \varphi_{\mathrm{i}})\). By theorem 19.26 the solution for the master unknowns is the solution of the symmetric positive definite system \(\mat T^\T\mat K\,\mat T\,\vek d_{\mathrm{m}} = \mat T^\T\vek f\), each of whose rows is the derivative with respect to an unknown of the function \(\Pi(\vek d_{\mathrm{m}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} U_{\mathrm{e}} + F\,v_{\mathrm{n}}\), where \(U_{\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the energy of the element (lemma 12.18, item 2) with the unknowns of the element expressed by the master ones, and \(F\,v_{\mathrm{n}}\) is the potential of the force \(F\) downwards (\(-F\) along \(y\), work \(-F\,v_{\mathrm{n}}\)).
  2. The energy of element \(j\) (between nodes \(j - 1\) and \(j\)) with both bars is by step 1 and lemma 12.18 (proof, step 1) the axial part \(\tfrac12\,\tfrac{EA}{h}\big[(\Delta u_{\mathrm{j}} - e\,\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}})^2 + (\Delta u_{\mathrm{j}} + e\,\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}})^2\big] = \tfrac{EA}{h}\,(\Delta u_{\mathrm{j}}^2 + e^2\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^2)\) and the bending part \(2\cdot\tfrac12\,EI\int_0^h v_{\mathrm{h}}''^2\,\mathrm{d}x = EI\int_0^h v_{\mathrm{h}}''^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), where \(\Delta u_{\mathrm{j}} = u_{\mathrm{j}} - u_{\mathrm{j}-1}\), \(\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{j}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1}\) and \(x\) is the distance from node \(j - 1\). The cross term between \(\Delta u_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\) cancels.
  3. The unknowns \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) occur only in the term \(\tfrac{EA}{h}\Delta u_{\mathrm{j}}^2\), a sum of squares that no force loads. The function \(\Pi\) is the sum of a function of the \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\) alone and a function of the \((v_{\mathrm{i}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{i}})\) alone, the first has its least value zero exactly at \(\Delta u_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) for all \(j\), and because \(u_0 = 0\) we get \(u_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) for all \(i\). This is item 1.
  4. Let \(M_{\mathrm{j}}(x) = EI\,v_{\mathrm{h}}''\) and \(V_{\mathrm{j}} = EI\,v_{\mathrm{h}}'''\) on element \(j\). The function \(v_{\mathrm{h}}\) is cubic (definition 12.17), so \(M_{\mathrm{j}}\) is linear, \(V_{\mathrm{j}}\) constant and \(M_{\mathrm{j}}' = V_{\mathrm{j}}\). By integration by parts \(\int_0^h EI\,v_{\mathrm{h}}''\,\delta v_{\mathrm{h}}''\,\mathrm{d}x = M_{\mathrm{j}}(h)\,\delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} - M_{\mathrm{j}}(0)\,\delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1} - V_{\mathrm{j}}\,(\delta v_{\mathrm{j}} - \delta v_{\mathrm{j}-1})\), since \(M_{\mathrm{j}}'' = 0\).
  5. We write the vanishing of the variation \(\delta\Pi\) with respect to \(\delta v_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\delta\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) (\(1 \le i \le n\)) by steps 2 and 4, with \(s = EAe^2/h\). At \(\delta v_{\mathrm{i}}\) (\(i < n\)) the coefficient is \(-2V_{\mathrm{i}} + 2V_{\mathrm{i}+1} = 0\), at \(\delta v_{\mathrm{n}}\) it is \(-2V_{\mathrm{n}} + F = 0\). So \(V_{\mathrm{j}} = F/2\) for every \(j\): each bar carries half the force. At \(\delta\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) (\(i < n\)) the coefficient is \(2\,[M_{\mathrm{i}}(h) + s\,\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}] - 2\,[M_{\mathrm{i}+1}(0) + s\,\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{i}+1}] = 0\), at \(\delta\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) it is \(2\,[M_{\mathrm{n}}(h) + s\,\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}] = 0\), since there is no couple at the end. Let \(m_{\mathrm{i}}\) be the common value of both expressions: \(m_{\mathrm{i}} = M_{\mathrm{i}}(h) + s\,\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{i}} = M_{\mathrm{i}+1}(0) + s\,\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{i}+1}\) for \(1 \le i < n\). At the ends we take the expression that exists: \(m_0 = M_1(0) + s\,\Delta\varphi_1\) and \(m_{\mathrm{n}} = M_{\mathrm{n}}(h) + s\,\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\).
  6. On element \(j\), \(M_{\mathrm{j}}(h) - M_{\mathrm{j}}(0) = V_{\mathrm{j}}\,h = Fh/2\) (steps 4, 5), so \(m_{\mathrm{j}} - m_{\mathrm{j}-1} = Fh/2\) and with \(m_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\), \(m_{\mathrm{j}} = -F\,(L - x_{\mathrm{j}})/2\). Because \(v_{\mathrm{h}}''\) is a linear function, \(\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \int_0^h v_{\mathrm{h}}''\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{h}{2EI}\,(M_{\mathrm{j}}(0) + M_{\mathrm{j}}(h)) = \tfrac{h}{2EI}\,(m_{\mathrm{j}-1} + m_{\mathrm{j}} - 2s\,\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}})\). With \(hs/EI = r\) we get \(\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\,(1 + r) = \tfrac{h}{2EI}\,(m_{\mathrm{j}-1} + m_{\mathrm{j}}) = -\tfrac{h}{2EI}\,F\,(L - \bar x_{\mathrm{j}})\) with \(\bar x_{\mathrm{j}} = \tfrac12(x_{\mathrm{j}-1} + x_{\mathrm{j}})\), so \(\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = -hF\,(L - \bar x_{\mathrm{j}})/EI_{\mathrm{c}}\).
  7. The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j} \le \mathrm{i}} h\,(L - \bar x_{\mathrm{j}})\) is the integral of the linear function \(L - x\) over \([0, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\), because the midpoint rule is exact for a linear function, and equals \(L\,x_{\mathrm{i}} - x_{\mathrm{i}}^2/2\). With \(\varphi_0 = 0\) we get \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}} = -F\,x_{\mathrm{i}}\,(2L - x_{\mathrm{i}})/(2EI_{\mathrm{c}})\), which is item 2 (the derivative of the deflection curve \(v(x) = -F\,x^2\,(3L - x)/(6EI)\) of theorem 5.56 is \(v'(x) = -F\,x\,(2L - x)/(2EI)\), which with \(EI_{\mathrm{c}}\) in place of \(EI\) is the same rotation at \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\)).
  8. Deflection: on a cubic piece \(v(x) = v_{\mathrm{j}-1} + \varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1}\,x + c_0\,x^2/2 + c_1\,x^3/6\), \(v'' = c_0 + c_1\,x\), we have \(v_{\mathrm{j}} - v_{\mathrm{j}-1} = h\varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + c_0\,h^2/2 + c_1\,h^3/6\) and \(\tfrac{h}{2}(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + \varphi_{\mathrm{j}}) = h\varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + c_0\,h^2/2 + c_1\,h^3/4\), so \(v_{\mathrm{j}} - v_{\mathrm{j}-1} = \tfrac{h}{2}(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + \varphi_{\mathrm{j}}) - c_1\,h^3/12\). For the elements, by steps 4 and 5, \(c_1\,h = (M_{\mathrm{j}}(h) - M_{\mathrm{j}}(0))/EI = Fh/(2EI)\), for the exact solution with \(EI_{\mathrm{c}}\) (theorem 5.56) \(c_1 = F/EI_{\mathrm{c}}\). The rotations are equal (step 7), so the increment of the deflection \(w\) is larger for the elements by \(\tfrac{Fh^3}{12}\,\big(\tfrac{1}{2EI} - \tfrac{1}{EI_{\mathrm{c}}}\big) = \tfrac{Fh^3}{24\,EI}\,\big(1 - \tfrac{1}{1+r}\big) = \tfrac{Fh^3}{24\,EI}\,\tfrac{r}{1+r}\), the same for every element.
  9. With \(w_0 = 0\) and \(i\) increments, item 3 follows. For \(i = n\) we have \(n\,h^3 = L^3/n^2\) and after division by the exact value \(F L^3/(3EI_{\mathrm{c}}) = F L^3/(6EI\,(1 + r))\) the relative error is \(\tfrac{(1+r)}{4n^2}\,\tfrac{r}{1+r} = \tfrac{r}{4n^2}\).

Source: The theorem and the proof are not from the sources. COOK §8.5 (PDF p. 295) describes only qualitatively that a beam-plate assembly is "too flexible" when the curvature varies and that it approaches the exact value with finer subdivision. The numbers are checked in num-06.py.

In our example \(r = EAe^2/EI = 800\cdot 400/106\,667 = 3{,}000\) and \(EI_{\mathrm{c}} = 8\,EI\). Item 3 gives the error \(F L^3/(32\,EI\,n^2)\), which is \(0{,}14947\), \(0{,}03737\), \(0{,}00934\), \(0{,}00234\), \(0{,}00058\), \(0{,}00015\) mm, equal to the column of the table to five places. The relative error is \(r/(4n^2) = 0{,}75/n^2\), so below \(1\,\%\) only from \(n \ge 9\). The rotations at the nodes are exact to \(10^{-16}\) rad, as the computation confirms (num-06.out).

The error grows with \(r\), that is with the Steiner term. At \(e = 0\) we have \(r = 0\), the links have no length and there is no error. Figure 19.20 shows the error on doubly logarithmic axes.

We draw the axes: on the horizontal one the number of elements \(n\) in doublings, on the vertical one the error \(|\delta_{\mathrm{n}} - \delta|\) in mm, where \(\delta_{\mathrm{n}}\) is the tip deflection with \(n\) elements per bar and \(\delta\) the exact one, both axes logarithmic. Each computation is placed as a point. The points lie on a line of slope \(-2\), which is the \(n^{-2}\) of the theorem. On the step from \(n = 8\) to \(n = 16\) the error falls to a quarter.

Why does theorem 12.14 not hold here? Its step 1 claims that every field of elements is an admissible virtual deflection, that is, a field belonging to the same model as the exact solution. For the glued pair the exact model is the common section: the axial displacement of each bar is \(\mp e\,v'(x)\) along its whole length, which is a quadratic function, because \(v\) is cubic. The field of elements has on an element a linear axial displacement of the bar (definition 12.17) and the rigid links demand \(\mp e\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) only at the nodes. Inside an element the bars can therefore still slip against each other. The difference between a quadratic and a linear function on an element is of order \(h^2\), and that is the reason for the factor four. The field of elements is not in the space of the common section, so Galerkin orthogonality (lemma 6.36) fails. The rotations are nevertheless exact, because they are determined by the moment equilibrium (steps 5 and 6), in which the link enters only as the stiffness \(EAe^2\) that the exact \(EI_{\mathrm{c}}\) already contains. The error is in the slope of the curvature \(c_1\): the shear force in an element is carried by the bars themselves by bending (\(V = F/2\) each), while in a common section it is carried mostly by the change of the axial forces (for \(r = 3\) three quarters, the bending of the bars only \(2EI/EI_{\mathrm{c}} = 1/(1 + r) = 1/4\)), and the increment of the deflection changes accordingly (step 8). COOK (PDF p. 295) says the same qualitatively: in pure bending the beam-plate assembly has the correct stiffness, when the curvature varies it is "too flexible", and finer subdivision brings the curvature on each element closer to constant and removes the error. Step 8 shows it in a formula: the increment of the deflection differs by \(h^3/12\) times the difference of the curvature slopes \(c_1\), and at constant moment both slopes are zero. Item 3 of the theorem says in addition how fast the error goes to zero and what it depends on.

Now Steiner. Theorem 19.31 obtained from the rigid link the bending stiffness \(EI_{\mathrm{c}} = 2\,(EI + EAe^2)\), and chapter 5 already had it from theorem 5.28. The agreement is a theorem, not a coincidence.

Corollary 19.32 Steiner's theorem from rigid links (Steinerjev izrek iz togih povezav)

For the glued cantilever of theorem 19.31, \(EI_{\mathrm{c}} = E\,I_{\mathrm{c}}\), where \(I_{\mathrm{c}} = 2\,(I + A\,e^2)\) is the second moment of the section of both bars together about the contact line \(y = 0\). The tip deflection tends with \(n \to \infty\) to \(F L^3/(3EI_{\mathrm{c}})\), by chapter 5 the deflection of a cantilever with a 20 mm × 80 mm section and \(I_{\mathrm{c}} = 853\,333\) mm⁴.

Proof

We must show the equality of the number \(EI_{\mathrm{c}}\) with the Steiner sum and the limit of item 3.

  1. Each bar has its centroid on its own axis, at distance \(e\) from the line \(y = 0\), area \(A\) and own second moment \(I\). By theorem 5.28 its second moment about \(y = 0\) is \(I + A\,e^2\). The moment of both together is their sum, \(I_{\mathrm{c}} = 2\,(I + A\,e^2)\).
  2. By theorem 19.31, \(EI_{\mathrm{c}} = 2\,(EI + EAe^2) = E\cdot 2\,(I + A\,e^2) = E\,I_{\mathrm{c}}\).
  3. The error of item 3 of the theorem is zero as \(n \to \infty\), because \(n^{-2}\) has limit zero, so the limit of the tip deflection is \(F L^3/(3EI_{\mathrm{c}})\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. Steiner's theorem and the deflection of a cantilever are from chapter 5.

So the link is Steiner's theorem at work: the term \(2EAe^2\) in \(EI_{\mathrm{c}}\) comes from the axial forces \(N = \mp EA\,e\,\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}/h\) of the two bars (step 2 of the proof of theorem 19.31), which form a couple with arm \(2e\) and moment \(2EAe^2\,\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}/h\). In the free pair there are no such forces.

Let us sum up what we saw and with what. The rigid link expresses the three unknowns of the dependent node by the three of the master (lemma 19.29), so it is a multipoint constraint (definition 19.30) and we eliminate it as in section 19.5. The glued pair showed that the link carries Steiner's term (corollary 19.32), and that the exactness of the deflection at the nodes from chapter 12 is lost with links while the rotation is kept (theorem 19.31, error \(r/(4n^2)\)). Limitations: as COOK says (PDF p. 296), a rigid link does not expand with temperature, and in dynamics a diagonal mass matrix is no longer diagonal after elimination. A similar link between a beam and a plate (an eccentric stiffener, COOK PDF p. 294) needs the plate elements of chapter 18, so we only mention it here.

Notation: the letter \(e\) here is the offset of the link, Euler's number is written \(\mathrm{e}\) (chapter 9). The letter \(F\) is a force, \(N\) the axial force (not the number of sectors in cyclic symmetry), \(\mat T\) the matrix of the transformation of unknowns, not the sign matrix of the space element and not the kinetic energy.

19.7 Coupling different elements

So far all elements that meet at a node have had the same unknowns. The bars of a truss have two at a node (the displacements \(u\) and \(v\)), the frame elements three (\(u\), \(v\) and the rotation \(\varphi\)). What happens when we have to attach a beam to a wall built of bars? Two elements meet that do not speak about the same quantities, so we call them dissimilar (različni elementi, COOK §8.5, PDF p. 292). Coupling (sklapljanje) means joining such elements into one system of equations. The word is from everyday language: as we couple two wagons so that they are pulled together, we couple two elements so that they move together.

The model is the following (figure 19.21). The wall is a block of five bars. Nodes \(1\) and \(4\) are clamped, both of their displacements are zero, nodes \(2\) and \(3\) are free and are joined by bars along the edges and along both diagonals. The bars have the cross-section \(20\ \text{mm}^2\) and the steel of chapter 12, \(E = 196\) GPa. This is a deliberately weak wall, so that the turning of its edge shows in the numbers. The distance between the free nodes is \(d = 0{,}2\) m. To the right edge we attach a beam of length \(1\) m with the cross-section \(20 \times 40\) mm as in chapter 12, \(EI = 20\,907\) N m\(^2\), \(EA = 1{,}568\cdot 10^{8}\) N, with one frame element (definition 12.17). The hollow node \(5\) is the start of the beam at the middle of the edge \(2\)-\(3\), it is not a node of the wall, node \(6\) is the end of the beam. The force \(F = 100\) N acts on it downward. The force has the letter \(F\) because \(P\) and \(S\) are reserved in this chapter for the mirror matrix (section 19.1).

We accept three idealizations. The bars are pinned and carry only axial force (chapter 7), the displacements are small (we get the bound for the rotation below) and the material is linearly elastic. The question is how to connect the unknowns \(u_5\), \(v_5\), \(\varphi_5\) of the beam with the unknowns \(u_2\), \(v_2\), \(u_3\), \(v_3\) of the wall, so that the system has a unique solution and the right stiffness. We go in three steps. First we check what a bar does to a frame node, since that is the simplest joint of different elements. Then we simply lay the beam on a node of the wall and see that it does not hold. At the end we write a constraint that does.

19.7.1 A bar at a frame node

Take a node of a frame (definition 5.90) where a frame element and a bar meet. The frame element comes from the left and has three unknowns at the node \(A\). The bar comes from the upper right and is attached at the point \(A\), so that its axis runs through this point (figure 19.22). Around the node we draw a small circle, as for a free body, and write into it the forces that the piece of beam and the bar exert on it. On the circle acts the force of the bar \(F_{\mathrm{p}}\) along its axis, and on the circle act the shear force \(Q\) and the moment \(M\) of the frame. The frame also acts on it with an axial force, which we do not draw, since like \(Q\) it acts at \(A\) and has no lever arm in the moments about \(A\). By the equilibrium of the circle, which the reader knows from school physics (the sum of forces and the sum of moments are zero, chapter 5), the moment of the bar does not enter: its force passes through the point \(A\), so it has zero lever arm. What this says in the language of matrices is told by the next lemma.

Lemma 19.33 A bar at a frame node is a hinge (palica v vozlišču okvirja je členek)

Let \(A\) be a node of a plane frame with the unknowns \(u_{\mathrm{A}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{A}}\), \(\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\) (definitions 5.90 and 12.17) and let a bar be attached at it whose axis passes through \(A\) (lemma 7.28). Let the connection table and the selection matrices of the elements be as in definition 7.11. Then:

  1. The matrix of the bar \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) in the space of all unknowns has the row and the column of the unknown \(\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\) equal to zero.
  2. The equation of the row \(\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\) of the assembled matrix contains only frame elements: the sum of the moments at the ends of the frame elements at \(A\) equals the given external couple at \(A\). The bar does not transmit a moment.
  3. The force of the bar on the node is \(\pm N\,\vek n\) along its axis and has zero moment about \(A\).
Proof

We must show that \(\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\) does not appear in the connection table of the bar, and from this obtain items 1 and 2 by the assembly theorem.

  1. By lemma 7.28 the bar carries only the displacements of its end points, that is four unknowns \(u\), \(v\) of each end. The connection table of the bar therefore does not contain \(\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\).
  2. By item 2 of lemma 7.12, \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) has nonzero entries only at the places \((I, J)\) where \(I\) and \(J\) are in the connection table of the element. The places \((\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}, J)\) and \((I, \varphi_{\mathrm{A}})\) are not in it, so the row and the column are zero. This is item 1.
  3. By item 1 of theorem 7.13, \((\mat K\,\vek d)_{\varphi_\mathrm{A}}\) is the sum over the elements whose table contains \(\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\). These are only frame elements, and the row of the equation \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f\) says that this sum equals \(f_{\varphi_\mathrm{A}}\). The moment of a frame element at its end is the third component of the forces of the surroundings on the end (lemma 12.18, item 1). This is item 2.
  4. By lemma 7.28 the force of the surroundings on the end of the bar is \(\pm N\,\vek n\) (the sign depends on the end) with the direction \(\vek n\) of the axis. The axis passes through \(A\), the lever arm is zero and the moment of the force about \(A\) is \(0\). This is item 3.

Source: COOK §8.5, figure 8.5-2a (PDF p. 293) says that the joint of a beam and plane elements without a rotation is a hinge and that no moment is transferred at the point \(A\). The proof is ours.

Let us test the lemma on a bar of the wall. The bar \(2\)-\(3\) is vertical, \(\vek n = (0, 1)\), \(L = d = 0{,}2\) m, \(EA = 196\ \text{GPa}\cdot 20\ \text{mm}^2 = 3{,}92\cdot 10^{6}\) N, so \(EA/L = 1{,}96\cdot 10^{7}\) N/m. By lemma 7.28 the nonzero block is \(\vek n\,\vek n^\T = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\), so the matrix of the bar, if its ends were frame nodes with three unknowns \((u, v, \varphi)\), has only four nonzero entries \(\pm 1{,}96\cdot 10^{7}\) N/m in the rows and columns of the vertical displacements \(v_2\), \(v_3\). The rows and columns of the rotations \(\varphi_2\), \(\varphi_3\) are zero, as item 1 says.

Where does the lemma fail? Take a bar that runs parallel to the axis of a beam and is attached to it off the axis, at the edge of the height \(40\) mm, so with the offset \(e = 20\) mm from the axis. With the bar force \(500\) N (the same number as we shall get below in the wall) its force acts along a line at the distance \(e\) from the point \(A\) and has the moment \(500 \cdot 0{,}020 = 10\) N m. The assumption of the lemma, that the axis of the bar runs through the node, does not hold, item 3 fails and the row \(\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\) gets a term that the matrix of the bar does not contain. Such joints are written with a rigid link (section 19.6).

19.7.2 A beam on a node without rotations

The simplest way to attach the beam would be to put its start into a node of the wall. So we replace node \(5\) by node \(2\): at node \(2\) the beam is attached so that it shares the displacements \(u_2\), \(v_2\) with the wall, and the rotation \(\varphi_5\) is its own new unknown, since the wall has no rotations (figure 19.23). There are then eight unknowns: four in the wall, \(\varphi_5\) and three at node \(6\).

Let us draw what this means. The wall and the clamp are as before, the beam starts at node \(2\). Let us turn it by a small angle \(\theta\) about this point, as the orange position shows: the end \(6\) moves to \(6'\). The bars of the wall do not change in this, since the nodes of the wall did not move. Whether such a motion really costs no energy and what follows from this is told by the next lemma.

Lemma 19.34 A beam on a node without rotations can turn (nosilec na vozlišču brez zasukov je vrtljiv)

Let \(A\) be a node that only bars have (two displacements) and let a frame element of length \(h\) and stiffnesses \(EA\), \(EI\) (definition 12.17) be attached at \(A\) so that it shares the displacements \(u\), \(v\) of the node, and its rotation \(\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\) is a new unknown that appears in the connection table only at this element. There are no other elements with the unknowns of the end of the beam, and no external couple acts at \(A\). Then:

  1. The moment at the start of the beam is zero, so the joint is a hinge.
  2. For every small angle \(\theta\) the displacement in which the nodes of the wall do not move and \((\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}, u_6, v_6, \varphi_6) = \theta\,(1,\ 0,\ h,\ 1)\) (the beam along the axis \(x\), end \(6\)) costs no energy.
  3. The matrix \(\mat K\) of the system is therefore singular, it necessarily has a zero eigenvalue.
Proof

We must show that the moment in the row \(\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\) is zero and that the turning of the rigid beam about \(A\) gives no energy, and then use the lemma on zero energy.

  1. The unknown \(\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\) is in the connection table only at this element, so by item 1 of theorem 7.13 the row \(\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\) of the system \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f\) says \((\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}})_3 = f_{\varphi_\mathrm{A}}\). There is no external couple at \(A\), so the moment at the end of the element is zero. This is item 1.
  2. Let the beam lie along the local axis \(\bar x \in [0, h]\) from \(A\) towards \(6\). By lemma 4.72, in a small rigid turn about \(A\) by \(\theta\) the point at the distance \(\bar x\) moves by \(\theta\,\bar x\) transversally and the cross-section turns by \(\theta\). So \(\bar u = 0\), \(\bar v(\bar x) = \theta\,\bar x\) and \(\varphi = \bar v' = \theta\) and the nodal displacements are \((0, 0, \theta, 0, \theta h, \theta)\).
  3. By definition 12.17 the field of the element is linear in \(\bar u\) and a Hermite polynomial of degree three in \(\bar v\), determined by the values and slopes at both ends. The line \(\bar v = \theta\,\bar x\) is a polynomial of degree at most three with the same four data \((0, \theta, \theta h, \theta)\), and the polynomial of degree at most three with these data is unique, so the field of the element is this line, \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) and \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}'' = 0\). The strain energy of the element \(\tfrac12\int_0^h (EA\,\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}'^2 + EI\,\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}''^2)\,\mathrm d\bar x\) (lemma 12.18, item 1, step 1) is therefore \(0\).
  4. The bars of the wall have zero elongations, since the displacements of the nodes of the wall are zero. By item 2 of theorem 7.13 the total energy \(\tfrac12\,\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d\) is the sum of the energies of the elements, so \(0\).
  5. The matrix \(\mat K\) is positive semidefinite (definition 7.15), since the energy of every element is nonnegative. By lemma 7.16, \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = 0\) gives \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek 0\) for a nonzero \(\vek d\). This is item 3.

Source: COOK §8.5, figure 8.5-2a (PDF p. 293): a joint without a rotation is a "hinge mechanism". The proof is ours.

Let us look at the numbers. The matrix of the eight unknowns has by computation (script num-07.py) the three smallest eigenvalues \(0\), \(4{,}18\cdot 10^{4}\) and \(3{,}66\cdot 10^{5}\), and the vector of the zero eigenvalue is at \(h = 1\) m \((\varphi_5, u_6, v_6, \varphi_6) = (1, 0, 1, 1)\,\theta\), as item 2 of the lemma predicts. The zero value does not change if we strengthen the wall: it is the same for bars with the cross-sections \(800\), \(100\) and \(20\ \text{mm}^2\). The equation \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek f\) with the force \(F = 100\) N at node \(6\) has no solution, since the load is not orthogonal to the zero vector: \(\vek f\cdot\vek d = -F\,h\,\theta \ne 0\). Orthogonality is needed, since a solution \(\vek d^*\) would give \(\vek d^\T\vek f = \vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d^* = (\mat K\,\vek d)^\T\vek d^* = 0\) by the symmetry of \(\mat K\) and lemma 1.101. This is the unbalanced moment \(F\,h = 100\) N m about node \(2\), which a hinge cannot take.

Let us also consider a nearby remedy: we set the rotation \(\varphi_5\) at node \(2\) to zero, because "the wall does not allow turning". The beam then gets a clamp and the system has a solution. For a rigid wall the tip deflection would be \(F\,h^3/(3EI) = 100 \cdot 1^3/(3 \cdot 20\,907) = 1{,}5944\) mm, for our weak wall with such a constraint \(1{,}6053\) mm, and the true value (below) is \(1{,}9103\) mm, so the deflection is \(16\,\%\) too small. A clamp that the wall cannot give makes the beam too stiff, since the wall has no rotations and the edge turns by \(2{,}8\cdot 10^{-4}\).

19.7.3 The rotation of an edge from two normal displacements

The beam must feel the rotation of the wall. The wall has on the edge \(2\)-\(3\) only the displacements of the nodes, but these two displacements can differ, and the difference tells how the edge turned. Let us draw it (figure 19.24). The edge \(2\)-\(3\) is a vertical segment of length \(d\) with the point \(5\) in the middle, and the beam is perpendicular to it. Let us turn the edge by a small angle \(\varphi\) counterclockwise about the point \(5\) (orange position). The upper node moves to the left, the lower to the right. The normal displacements \(u_2\) and \(u_3\) are horizontal and have opposite signs. By the rule of the small rigid displacement (lemma 4.72) the horizontal displacement of a point at the height \(y\) above the point \(5\) is \(-\varphi\,y\), so the rotation is \(\varphi = (u_3 - u_2)/d\).

The point \(5\) is an arbitrary point of the edge, not necessarily the middle. Let us write the general case and prove it.

Lemma 19.35 The rotation constraint from two normal displacements (vez zasuka in pomika iz dveh vozlišč zidu)

Let \(2\) and \(3\) be nodes of the wall lying on a vertical line at the distance \(d > 0\), node \(3\) below \(2\), and let \(5\) be a point between them at the height \(s\,d\) above \(3\), \(0 \le s \le 1\). Let the displacements \((u_2, v_2, u_3, v_3)\) of the nodes be small, which means that the rotation of the edge is \(|\varphi| \le 10^{-3}\). Then:

  1. In a small rigid displacement of the edge \(2\)-\(3\) with the displacement \((u_5, v_5)\) of the point \(5\) and the rotation \(\varphi\) counterclockwise we have, to first order in \(\varphi\),
    \[\begin{pmatrix} u_5 \\ v_5 \\ \varphi_5 \end{pmatrix} = \mat T_{\mathrm{w}} \begin{pmatrix} u_2 \\ v_2 \\ u_3 \\ v_3 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat T_{\mathrm{w}} = \begin{pmatrix} s & 0 & 1 - s & 0 \\ 0 & s & 0 & 1 - s \\ -1/d & 0 & 1/d & 0 \end{pmatrix} , \tag{19.10}\]
    where \(\varphi_5 = \varphi\).
  2. A force \(X\) in the horizontal direction, a force \(Y\) in the vertical direction and a couple \(M\) counterclockwise, all at the point \(5\) and collected in the column \(\mat F_5 = (X, Y, M)^\T\), are statically equivalent to forces at the nodes \(2\) and \(3\) with the horizontal components \(X_2 = s\,X - M/d\) and \(X_3 = (1 - s)\,X + M/d\) and the vertical ones \(Y_2 = s\,Y\), \(Y_3 = (1 - s)\,Y\). These four expressions are the entries of the column \(\mat T_{\mathrm{w}}^\T\,\mat F_5\).
Proof

We must show that equation (19.10) follows from the rigid displacement of the edge and that the statics of the edge gives the same column as \(\mat T_{\mathrm{w}}^\T\,\mat F_5\).

  1. By lemma 4.72 the displacement of the point with the vector \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) from the point \(5\) is \(\delta\vek a + \delta\boldsymbol\varphi\times\overrightarrow{OP}\). For the rotation \(\delta\boldsymbol\varphi = \varphi\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and the point \((0, y)\) we have \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} \times (0, y) = (-y, 0)\), so \(u = u_5 - \varphi\,y\) and \(v = v_5\).
  2. Node \(2\) is at the height \(y_2 = (1 - s)\,d\) above \(5\) and node \(3\) at the height \(y_3 = -s\,d\). By step 1, \(u_2 = u_5 - \varphi\,(1 - s)\,d\) and \(u_3 = u_5 + \varphi\,s\,d\), \(v_2 = v_3 = v_5\).
  3. Subtract: \(u_3 - u_2 = \varphi\,d\), so \(\varphi = (u_3 - u_2)/d\). Add \(s\) times the first and \((1-s)\) times the second equation of step 2: \(s\,u_2 + (1-s)\,u_3 = u_5 - \varphi\,s(1-s)d + \varphi\,(1-s)\,s\,d = u_5\). The same computation gives \(v_5 = s\,v_2 + (1-s)\,v_3\). This is equation (19.10).
  4. Two systems of forces are statically equivalent on a rigid body if they have the same resultant and the same moment about the same point (equilibrium of a rigid body, chapter 5). The sum of horizontal forces: \(X_2 + X_3 = X\). The moment about \(5\): the force \(X_2\) at the height \((1 - s)\,d\) has the moment \(-(1 - s)\,d\,X_2\), the force \(X_3\) at the height \(-s\,d\) has \(+s\,d\,X_3\), and the sum must be \(M\).
  5. From step 4: \(s\,d\,X_3 - (1-s)\,d\,X_2 = M\) and \(X_3 = X - X_2\) give \(X_2 = s\,X - M/d\) and \(X_3 = (1-s)\,X + M/d\). Statics determines the vertical forces only by their sum, \(Y_2 + Y_3 = Y\), and the division in the ratio \(s\) is the one that the interpolation in equation (19.10) gives (the second row of the matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{w}}\)). The column \(\mat T_{\mathrm{w}}^\T\,\mat F_5\) has, by the first and third rows of the matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{w}}\), exactly the entries \(s\,X - M/d\) and \((1-s)\,X + M/d\), and by the second row \(s\,Y\) and \((1 - s)\,Y\).

Source: COOK (8.5-3) (PDF p. 293): the rotation of node \(5\) is the difference of the normal displacements of nodes \(2\) and \(3\) divided by the distance, the translations are interpolated linearly. ONATE1 §9.3 (PDF pp. 334-335) likewise expresses the displacements of one element by the nodal displacements of the other. The proof from the rigid displacement is ours.

The proof showed that the relations (19.10) are exact for a rigid displacement of the edge (to first order) and that the same matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{w}}\), which turns the displacements of nodes \(2\) and \(3\) into the displacements of the end of the beam, carries the forces back when transposed. We now write the coupling of the wall and the beam as an elimination: the dependent unknowns \((u_5, v_5, \varphi_5)\) of the beam are expressed by the master unknowns of the wall by equation (19.10) (definition 19.25), and from the matrix of the beam \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) we get the matrix \(\mat T^\T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat T\) and add it to the wall (theorem 19.26). The theorem requires that every nonzero \(\vek d\) that satisfies the constraint has positive energy. This holds here. At zero energy no bar is stretched. Since nodes \(1\) and \(4\) are clamped, the elongations of the bars \(1\)-\(2\) and \(4\)-\(2\) are the components of the displacement of node \(2\) in two different directions, so node \(2\) stays at rest, and likewise node \(3\) with the bars \(4\)-\(3\) and \(1\)-\(3\). By the constraint (19.10) then \(u_5 = v_5 = \varphi_5 = 0\). The beam has zero energy only at \(\bar u_{\mathrm{h}}' = 0\) and \(\bar v_{\mathrm{h}}'' = 0\), that is in a rigid displacement, which is zero when the start neither moves nor turns, so the end \(6\) stays at rest too. The theorem therefore guarantees that the reduced matrix is positive definite and that the solution agrees with the multipliers.

The smallness of the rotation is an idealization that we must estimate. In a rigid turn by \(\varphi\) about the point \(5\) the exact horizontal displacement of the point at the height \(y\) is \(-y\,\sin\varphi\) and the vertical one \(y\,(\cos\varphi - 1)\), and the first order replaces them by \(-y\,\varphi\) and \(0\). The vertical error \(y\,(1 - \cos\varphi) \le y\,\varphi^2/2\) is, compared with the horizontal displacement \(y\,\varphi\), smaller by the factor \(\varphi/2\), so at \(|\varphi| \le 10^{-3}\) at most \(5\cdot 10^{-4}\). In the example below \(|\varphi| = 2{,}806\cdot 10^{-4}\) and for node \(2\) (\(y = d/2 = 0{,}1\) m) the vertical error is \(3{,}9\cdot 10^{-9}\) m, which is \(7\cdot 10^{-5}\) of the difference \(|u_3 - u_2| = 5{,}6\cdot 10^{-5}\) m.

Example 19.36 A beam on a wall of bars (nosilec na zidu iz palic)

For the model of figure 19.21 the matrix \(\mat T_{\mathrm{w}}\) at \(s = \tfrac12\) and \(d = 0{,}2\) m is

\[\mat T_{\mathrm{w}} = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac12 & 0 & \tfrac12 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac12 & 0 & \tfrac12 \\ -5 & 0 & 5 & 0 \end{pmatrix} ,\]

where the numbers in the third row are \(\mp 1/d\) in the unit \(\text{m}^{-1}\) and \(\varphi_5\) has no unit. There are \(4\) unknowns (the wall) and \(3\) (node \(6\)), \(7\) in all, as in COOK (PDF p. 293). The computation (num-07.py) gives: the smallest eigenvalue of the reduced matrix is \(1{,}52\cdot 10^{4}\), so it is positive definite as theorem 19.26 guarantees, the tip deflection is \(-1{,}9103\) mm, the rotation \(\varphi_5 = -2{,}806\cdot 10^{-4}\) and the displacement \(v_5 = -0{,}0353\) mm. The deflection is the sum of three parts: \(1{,}5944\) mm is the beam on a rigid wall, \(0{,}2806\) mm is the rotation of the edge times the length \(h = 1\) m, \(0{,}0353\) mm is the displacement of node \(5\) (the sum is \(1{,}9103\) mm). In the wall node \(2\) moves by \(u_2 = +0{,}02806\) mm and \(3\) by \(-0{,}02806\) mm: the upper fibre of the beam is stretched at the clamp, so node \(2\) is pulled out of the wall.

Statics checks the forces. The beam presses on the edge with the force \(100\) N downward and with the couple \(F\,h = 100\) N m clockwise, and the edge acts on it oppositely. The force of the surroundings on the end of the beam is therefore \(\mat F_5 = (X, Y, M) = (0, 100\ \text{N}, 100\ \text{N m})\), upward and counterclockwise. By lemma 19.35 (item 2, \(s = \tfrac12\)) the statically equivalent forces at nodes \(2\) and \(3\) are horizontal \(X_2 = -M/d = -500\) N and \(X_3 = +500\) N and vertical \(50\) N each, and the computation (num-07.py) gives the same column \(\mat T_{\mathrm{w}}^\T\,\mat F_5 = (-500, 50, 500, 50)\). The moment of these forces about the point \(5\) is \(-0{,}1\cdot(-500) - (-0{,}1)\cdot 500 = 100\) N m, so \(M\). These are the forces with which nodes \(2\) and \(3\) hold the beam. The beam acts on the nodes with the opposite forces: it pulls node \(2\) out of the wall with \(500\) N, pushes node \(3\) into it with \(500\) N and pulls both down with \(50\) N each, which agrees with the displacements \(u_2 > 0\) and \(u_3 < 0\). The wall takes the couple \(M\) as a pair of forces \(\pm 500\) N at the distance \(d\) and not as forces at one point.

What happens if we choose displacements that do not carry the rotation? For a beam we are used to the rotation being the difference of vertical displacements divided by the horizontal distance, \(\varphi \approx v'\). If we copy this habit to a vertical edge, we take \(\varphi_5 = (v_2 - v_3)/d\). In a rigid displacement of the edge \(v_2 = v_3\) at every rotation (step 2 of the proof of lemma 19.35), so this expression does not see the rotation, it records only the stretching of the edge. With it the computation gives the deflection \(-1{,}7170\) mm instead of \(-1{,}9103\) mm, so \(10\,\%\) too small, and the rotation \(\varphi_5 = -1{,}13\cdot 10^{-4}\) instead of \(-2{,}81\cdot 10^{-4}\). The error is smaller for a stronger wall and larger for a weaker one, since the wrong constraint underestimates the rotation of the edge, and for a weaker wall that rotation is a larger part of the deflection. With the bar cross-section \(800\ \text{mm}^2\) the error is by the same computation \(0{,}3\,\%\), with \(100\ \text{mm}^2\) \(2{,}3\,\%\) and with \(5\ \text{mm}^2\) \(27\,\%\). At a vertical edge the rotation is carried by the normal displacements \(u_2\) and \(u_3\), as figure 19.24 shows.

A last remark concerns the choice of the beam element. In this section we took the Euler-Bernoulli beam (definition 12.17), in which the rotation of the cross-section equals the slope of the axis, \(\varphi = \bar v'\). In the Timoshenko element (definition 12.31) the deflection and the tilt of the section \(\theta\) are independent unknowns, and the shear strain \(\gamma = v' - \theta\) can appear (definition 5.84). The constraint (19.10) ties the rotation of the cross-section to the rotation of the wall edge, since the section at the wall follows the edge, and that is the same unknown \(\varphi_5\) or \(\theta_5\) in both elements. The matrix \(\mat T\) is therefore the same, only the element matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) changes. In the Timoshenko element the section at the wall can yield in shear, in the Euler-Bernoulli one it cannot.

If the wall is made of plane or solid elements instead of bars, the idea stays the same: the displacements of the edge are interpolated from the nodes of the edge, the rotation is the difference of the normal displacements divided by the distance. How plane elements interpolate the displacements along an edge is treated in chapter 15. COOK (PDF p. 293) also knows another, ad hoc way (priložnostni način): the beam is extended into the wall by one or two elements that share the nodal displacements with the wall, while only the beam has rotations. The extension cannot turn rigidly without its nodes in the wall moving transversely to it, so the wall takes the moment by transverse forces at these nodes, much as by the pair of forces \(\pm 500\) N above. Since these forces are concentrated at single nodes, the stresses near the joint are not accurate, as COOK warns.

Let us sum up. A bar at a frame node gives a hinge (lemma 19.33), a beam on a single node without rotations can turn and the system is singular (lemma 19.34), a constraint that takes the rotation from two normal displacements (lemma 19.35) gives a system with a unique solution. Each of the three tells which unknowns can carry a moment. The elimination by theorem 19.26 is the same tool as for rigid links (section 19.6).

19.8 Periodicity: a row of equal cells

A steel beam of cross-section \(20 \times 40\) mm (\(EI = 20\,906{,}7\) N m², chapter 12) lies on many supports at equal distances and carries a uniform load \(q = 1000\) N/m downward. The distance between neighbouring supports is the span (razpon), \(l = 1\) m. What is the moment over a support in the middle of the row?

We build figure 19.25 as follows. First the beam, which continues on both sides, as the dotted ends show. Then the supports under it, one at each node, which allow no deflection. Above it the load \(q\), pointing down and ending on the beam, since the load pushes on the beam. Finally one span of length \(l\), outlined in blue, and its length.

With mirror symmetry (section 19.1) we would halve the beam, but half a row would remain, ten spans for twenty. The row has one more symmetry, which the mirror does not use. If we shift the beam together with its load by \(l\) to the right, we get the same beam with the same load. Why then should one span differ from its neighbour?

The reason is the same as for the mirror and comes from the equilibrium of the nodes. Each node is in equilibrium when the sum of forces and moments on it is zero (Newton's law). The shifted picture has the same nodes, the same neighbours on both sides and the same load, so it is in equilibrium too. If the equilibrium position is unique, it must equal its shifted copy. Every span therefore deforms like its neighbour. This is the claim we shall prove, but first we must say what the row is made of.

A row without an end is an idealization. A real row of supports has an end, where a different neighbouring structure or nothing supports it. How many spans from the end we must stay away for the idealization to be good, we shall compute at the end of the section. For now let the row run in both directions.

We draw the piece of row in figure 19.26 as follows. We start with one cell, which for a beam is one span. It is named so because the row is made of equal pieces, as a honeycomb is made of cells. Next to it are the neighbouring cells, drawn grey and dashed, because we do not compute them separately. The cell has a left joint \(A\) and a right joint \(B\), the edges where it touches its neighbours. The joint (stik) is so called because the two cells join there. On each there are nodes, drawn as dots, and in the cell an inner node \(\mathrm n\) with two segments to the dots on the joints. The two dots at \(A\) and \(B\) at the same height are homologous: one is the other shifted by the length \(l\). The name says that the nodes have the same place and the same role in their cells. The neighbour acts on the cell at each joint with a force, \(\vek F_{\mathrm{A}}\) at joint \(A\) and \(\vek F_{\mathrm{B}}\) at joint \(B\). Their directions are not known in advance, so they are drawn as a pull that starts at the node.

Definition 19.37 Row of equal cells (vrsta enakih celic)
Motivation

For a beam the cell is one span, but the same holds for a piece of a frame, a truss or a mesh of finite elements. We therefore define the row in general, with the matrices of the cell.

A row of equal cells (vrsta enakih celic) is a structure assembled by theorem 7.13 from cells numbered by the integers \(j \in \mathbb{Z}\), for which:

  1. Cell \(j\) has three groups of unknowns, in the same axes for all cells: inner \(\vek d_{\mathrm{n}}^j\), unknowns of the left joint \(\vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^j\) and unknowns of the right joint \(\vek d_{\mathrm{B}}^j\). Each group has the same number of components in every cell. The components prescribed by a support are prescribed in the same way in all cells and are not unknowns (theorem 7.18), their rows are not equations.
  2. The right joint of cell \(j\) is the left joint of cell \(j + 1\), so \(\vek d_{\mathrm{B}}^j = \vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^{j+1}\).
  3. All cells have the same stiffness matrix \(\mat K\) (definition 7.4, symmetric and positive semidefinite, definition 7.15) and the same column of equivalent forces \(\vek f\), in blocks by groups of unknowns:
    \[\mat K = \begin{pmatrix} \mat K_{\mathrm{nn}} & \mat K_{\mathrm{nA}} & \mat K_{\mathrm{nB}} \\ \mat K_{\mathrm{An}} & \mat K_{\mathrm{AA}} & \mat K_{\mathrm{AB}} \\ \mat K_{\mathrm{Bn}} & \mat K_{\mathrm{BA}} & \mat K_{\mathrm{BB}} \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \vek f = \begin{pmatrix} \vek f_{\mathrm{n}} \\ \vek f_{\mathrm{A}} \\ \vek f_{\mathrm{B}} \end{pmatrix} . \tag{19.11}\]
    By symmetry \(\mat K_{\mathrm{An}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{nA}}^\T\), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{Bn}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{nB}}^\T\), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{BA}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{AB}}^\T\).

A node at joint \(A\) and a node at joint \(B\) are homologous (homologni) if the second is the first shifted by \(l\). The length \(l\) after which the row repeats is the period (perioda) of the row.

Source: COOK §10.9, PDF pp. 368-369: repetitive symmetry, equal cells, joints \(AA'\) and \(BB'\) with nodes that correspond in number, position and kind, "homologous pairs". The division of the matrix \(\mat K\) of one cell into blocks with unknowns \(\mathrm n\), \(A\), \(B\) is after COOK (10.9-1), PDF p. 369, where the inner unknowns are \(\{\vek D_{\mathrm{I}}\}\). The row with integer indices \(j\), the infinite row and the column \(\vek f\) instead of \(\vek R\) are ours.

Notation: \(\mat K\) here is the matrix of one cell, not of the structure, and \(\vek f\) is the column of equivalent forces of the cell, as in theorem 7.13. The forces of the neighbours on the cell, as in chapter 7, are \(\vek F_{\mathrm{A}} = (\mat K\,\vek d)_{\mathrm{A}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(\vek F_{\mathrm{B}} = (\mat K\,\vek d)_{\mathrm{B}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{B}}\). For the transformation of unknowns we shall use \(\mat T\) (section 19.5). It is not the matrix of signs from lemma 12.22 and not the kinetic energy.

We write the rows of the equations of the row by theorem 7.13 (point 1): the force an unknown needs is the sum of the forces needed by the cells that contain it. An inner unknown is only in cell \(j\). The node of the joint between cells \(j\) and \(j + 1\) is in cell \(j\) at joint \(B\) and in cell \(j + 1\) at joint \(A\). Therefore

\[\begin{aligned} \mat K_{\mathrm{nn}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{n}}^j + \mat K_{\mathrm{nA}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^j + \mat K_{\mathrm{nB}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{B}}^j &= \vek f_{\mathrm{n}} , \\ \big(\mat K_{\mathrm{Bn}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{n}}^j + \mat K_{\mathrm{BA}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^j + \mat K_{\mathrm{BB}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{B}}^j\big) + \big(\mat K_{\mathrm{An}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{n}}^{j+1} + \mat K_{\mathrm{AA}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^{j+1} + \mat K_{\mathrm{AB}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{B}}^{j+1}\big) &= \vek f_{\mathrm{B}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{A}} , \end{aligned} \tag{19.12}\]

for every \(j\) and with \(\vek d_{\mathrm{B}}^j = \vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^{j+1}\).

We know what we want: to show that the two joints of a cell are equal, \(\vek d_{\mathrm{B}} = \vek d_{\mathrm{A}}\), and that the row is therefore solved on one cell. We take the transformation of unknowns that replaces both groups \(A\) and \(B\) by one,

\[\mat T = \begin{pmatrix} \mat I & \mat 0 \\ \mat 0 & \mat I \\ \mat 0 & \mat I \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \begin{pmatrix} \vek d_{\mathrm{n}} \\ \vek d_{\mathrm{A}} \\ \vek d_{\mathrm{B}} \end{pmatrix} = \mat T \begin{pmatrix} \vek d_{\mathrm{n}} \\ \vek d_0 \end{pmatrix} , \tag{19.13}\]

where \(\vek d_0 = \vek d_{\mathrm{A}} = \vek d_{\mathrm{B}}\) is the common joint. The last row with \(\mat I\) says \(\vek d_{\mathrm{B}} = \vek d_0\), the middle one \(\vek d_{\mathrm{A}} = \vek d_0\).

Theorem 19.38 Periodic cell (periodic cell)

Let a row of equal cells (definition 19.37) be given with the matrix \(\mat T\) of equation (19.13) and let

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{r}} = \mat T^\T \mat K\,\mat T = \begin{pmatrix} \mat K_{\mathrm{nn}} & \mat K_{\mathrm{nA}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{nB}} \\ \mat K_{\mathrm{An}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{Bn}} & \mat K_{\mathrm{AA}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{AB}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{BA}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{BB}} \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \vek f_{\mathrm{r}} = \mat T^\T \vek f = \begin{pmatrix} \vek f_{\mathrm{n}} \\ \vek f_{\mathrm{A}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{B}} \end{pmatrix} . \tag{19.14}\]
  1. The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{r}}\) is positive semidefinite.
  2. If the column \((\vek d_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek d_0)\) solves the system \(\mat K_{\mathrm{r}}\,(\vek d_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek d_0)^\T = \vek f_{\mathrm{r}}\), the family \(\vek d_{\mathrm{n}}^j = \vek d_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(\vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^j = \vek d_{\mathrm{B}}^j = \vek d_0\) for every \(j\) is a solution of equations (19.12). The forces of the neighbours on the cell are opposite, \(\vek F_{\mathrm{B}} = -\vek F_{\mathrm{A}}\).
  3. A solution of the row is bounded if there is a number \(C\) such that every component of every \(\vek d^j\) is at most \(C\) in absolute value. If the row has at most one bounded solution, every bounded solution of it is periodic, \(\vek d^{j+1} = \vek d^j\) for every \(j\), so \(\vek d_{\mathrm{B}} = \vek d_{\mathrm{A}}\) and it solves the system of point 2.
Proof

We must show three points. The first is a computation with a quadratic form, the second is substitution into the equations of the row, the third is an argument of uniqueness, as for the mirror.

  1. The matrix \(\mat T^\T\mat K\,\mat T\) is symmetric because \((\mat T^\T\mat K\,\mat T)^\T = \mat T^\T\mat K^\T\mat T = \mat T^\T\mat K\,\mat T\). For every column \(\vek y\) we have \(\vek y^\T\mat T^\T\mat K\,\mat T\,\vek y = (\mat T\vek y)^\T\mat K\,(\mat T\vek y) \ge 0\) because \(\mat K\) is positive semidefinite. Multiplying blocks we get the form in equation (19.14): \(\mat K\,\mat T\) has rows \((\mat K_{\mathrm{nn}},\ \mat K_{\mathrm{nA}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{nB}})\), \((\mat K_{\mathrm{An}},\ \mat K_{\mathrm{AA}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{AB}})\), \((\mat K_{\mathrm{Bn}},\ \mat K_{\mathrm{BA}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{BB}})\), and \(\mat T^\T\) adds the second and third rows. The same sum for \(\vek f\) gives \(\vek f_{\mathrm{r}}\).
  2. In equations (19.12) we insert \(\vek d_{\mathrm{n}}^j = \vek d_{\mathrm{n}}^{j+1} = \vek d_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^j = \vek d_{\mathrm{B}}^j = \vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^{j+1} = \vek d_{\mathrm{B}}^{j+1} = \vek d_0\). The first equation is the first row of the system \(\mat K_{\mathrm{r}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{r}}\) with \(\vek d_{\mathrm{r}} = (\vek d_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek d_0)\), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{nn}}\vek d_{\mathrm{n}} + (\mat K_{\mathrm{nA}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{nB}})\vek d_0 = \vek f_{\mathrm{n}}\). The second is the second row, \((\mat K_{\mathrm{Bn}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{An}})\vek d_{\mathrm{n}} + (\mat K_{\mathrm{BA}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{BB}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{AA}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{AB}})\vek d_0 = \vek f_{\mathrm{B}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{A}}\). Since there is no index \(j\) left in them, they hold for every \(j\).
  3. By the notation under the definition, the forces of the neighbours are \(\vek F_{\mathrm{A}} = (\mat K\,\vek d)_{\mathrm{A}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(\vek F_{\mathrm{B}} = (\mat K\,\vek d)_{\mathrm{B}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{B}}\) at \(\vek d = \mat T\,\vek d_{\mathrm{r}}\). Their sum is \((\mat K\,\vek d)_{\mathrm{A}} + (\mat K\,\vek d)_{\mathrm{B}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{A}} - \vek f_{\mathrm{B}}\), which is the second row of the system, and it is zero. Hence \(\vek F_{\mathrm{B}} = -\vek F_{\mathrm{A}}\).
  4. Let \((\vek d^j)\) be a bounded solution and \(\vek e^j = \vek d^{j+1}\) its shifted copy. It is bounded too (with the same \(C\)). The coefficients and the right-hand side of equations (19.12) do not contain \(j\), because all cells are equal (point 3 of the definition 19.37), so the equations for \(\vek e\) at index \(j\) are the equations for \(\vek d\) at index \(j + 1\), which hold, and also \(\vek e_{\mathrm{B}}^j = \vek d_{\mathrm{B}}^{j+1} = \vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^{j+2} = \vek e_{\mathrm{A}}^{j+1}\). The shifted copy is therefore a bounded solution, and by hypothesis \(\vek e = \vek d\), that is \(\vek d^{j+1} = \vek d^j\) for every \(j\).
  5. Hence \(\vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^j = \vek d_{\mathrm{B}}^{j-1} = \vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^{j-1}\) for every \(j\) by point 2 of the definition, so \(\vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^j\) does not depend on \(j\), and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{B}}^j = \vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^{j+1} = \vek d_{\mathrm{A}}^j\). Substitution into equations (19.12) gives, as in step 2, the system \(\mat K_{\mathrm{r}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek f_{\mathrm{r}}\).

Source: COOK §10.9, PDF pp. 368-369: the conditions \(\{\vek D_{\mathrm{B}}\} = \{\vek D_{\mathrm{A}}\}\) and \(\{\vek F_{\mathrm{B}}\} = -\{\vek F_{\mathrm{A}}\}\) (10.9-2), the transformation (10.9-3), the system (10.9-4). COOK writes the conditions down because the substructures are identical and does not prove them. The proof is ours, after the idea of mirror symmetry (theorem 19.6).

What have we shown? The problem of a row with infinitely many unknowns is equivalent to the problem of one cell, which has only \(\vek d_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\vek d_0\) as unknowns. The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{r}}\) equals the matrix of equation (10.9-4) in COOK, which is obtained from \(\mat K\) by the constraint \(\vek d_{\mathrm{B}} - \vek d_{\mathrm{A}} = \vek 0\) of definition 12.25, eliminated with the transformation \(\mat T\) (definition 19.25). The forces of the neighbours are opposite, which is the law of action and reaction for a node where two cells join, if there is no point force in it. One more thing from COOK: a load on a joint is entered only once, in \(\vek f_{\mathrm{A}}\) or in \(\vek f_{\mathrm{B}}\), otherwise the cell gets it twice, since the two terms in the second row of the system add up.

The hypothesis of a unique bounded solution is not self-evident, so we shall check it in the example. The theorem also does not say that a bounded solution exists. If the system of the cell has no solution, the row has no periodic solution.

Example 19.39 Continuous beam on equal spans (continuous beam on equal spans)

Back to the beam of figure 19.25. Model: Euler-Bernoulli beam with constant bending stiffness \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\) N m² (chapter 12), linearly elastic, with the axial force neglected in bending. The supports are rigid and at the nodes, the span is \(l = 1\) m, the load is \(q_0 = 1000\) N/m downward. We want the rotation \(\varphi\) over a support and the moment. The largest stress, \(|M|/W\) with section modulus \(W = I/(20\ \text{mm}) = 5333\) mm³ and the moment of step 4, is \(15{,}6\) MPa, below the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa of the steel of chapter 3, so the linear model is justified. By theorem 12.14 the nodal values are exact with one element per span.

  1. The cell is one span with one beam element (definition 12.3). The unknowns of the joints are deflection and rotation, \(\vek d_{\mathrm{A}} = (v_{\mathrm{A}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{A}})\) and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{B}} = (v_{\mathrm{B}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{B}})\). The supports prescribe \(v_{\mathrm{A}} = v_{\mathrm{B}} = 0\), so the unknowns are only the rotations \(\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}}\), and there are no inner unknowns.
  2. From equation (12.3) we take the rows and columns of the rotations, \(\mat K = (EI/l)\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\). The equivalent forces from equation (12.5) with load \(q = -q_0\) upward are \(\vek f = -q_0\,(l^2/12,\ -l^2/12) = (-83{,}33,\ +83{,}33)\) N m.
  3. The transformation \(\mat T = (1,\ 1)^\T\) gives by equation (19.14) \(\mat K_{\mathrm{r}} = (EI/l)(4 + 2 + 2 + 4) = 12\,EI/l = 250\,880\) N m and \(f_{\mathrm{r}} = -83{,}33 + 83{,}33 = 0\). The equation \(12\,EI/l\;\varphi = 0\) gives \(\varphi = 0\) (NumPy).
  4. The rotation over a support is therefore zero, and every span in the cell is a beam clamped at both ends.
