By corollary 12.16 with \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) the deflection is \(v = q\,s^2 (l - s)^2/(24\,EI)\) and the moment \(M = q\,(l^2 - 6\,l\,s + 6\,s^2)/12\) with \(q = -q_0\). Over a support (\(s = 0\) and \(s = l\)) \(M = -q_0 l^2/12 = -83{,}33\) N m (the upper fibres are in tension), at mid-span \(M = q_0 l^2/24 = 41{,}67\) N m, and the mid-span deflection is \(q_0 l^4/(384\,EI) = 0{,}1246\) mm downward.
  5. We check with two independent computations. Statics: the reaction of a support is the sum of the shear forces of the two neighbouring spans, \(2 \cdot q_0 l/2 = 1000\) N, and equals the load of two half spans. Mirror: the mirror through the middle of a span maps the loaded row onto itself, swaps \(A\) and \(B\) and reverses the sign of the rotation. The mirror image of a bounded solution is therefore again a bounded solution. Since there is only one (step 6), by the idea of theorem 19.6 \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}} = -\varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\), which together with periodicity \(\varphi_{\mathrm{B}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{A}}\) gives \(\varphi = 0\), like the system of the cell.
  6. We also check the hypothesis of point 3 of theorem 19.38. Every cell has the same \(\mat K\) and \(\vek f\). In the row equation for node \(j\) the equivalent pairs of the neighbouring spans are opposite, \(+83{,}33\) and \(-83{,}33\) N m, so the right-hand side is zero, and \((EI/l)\,(2\varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + 8\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} + 2\varphi_{\mathrm{j}+1}) = 0\), that is \(4\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} + \varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + \varphi_{\mathrm{j}+1} = 0\). Let \(\varphi\) be a bounded solution and \(S\) the supremum of the numbers \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}|\) (definition 1.30). From \(4|\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}| \le |\varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1}| + |\varphi_{\mathrm{j}+1}| \le 2S\) it follows that \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}| \le S/2\) for every \(j\), so \(S/2\) is an upper bound and \(S \le S/2\), that is \(S = 0\). The only bounded solution is \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\), and the hypothesis is satisfied. Twenty spans would give a system with \(21\) unknowns, the cell has one.

Source: COOK §10.9, PDF pp. 368-369: the cell as a substructure with \(\{\vek D_{\mathrm{B}}\} = \{\vek D_{\mathrm{A}}\}\). The example is ours, the value \(q l^2/12\) over a support and \(q l^2/24\) at mid-span is the moment of a beam clamped at both ends (COOK §2.9, PDF p. 63, equivalent forces with reversed sign).

Now the deflection and the moment in figure 19.25. The deflection is greatly magnified, at mid-span it is in fact \(0{,}1246\) mm. At every support it has a horizontal tangent, because \(\varphi = 0\), and so one arc passes into the next with the same tangent. The moment has a sharp peak downward at every support and a peak upward at mid-span, because the beam is in tension at the top over a support and at the bottom at mid-span.

The period in this case is one span. The theorem holds for a row without an end, but a real row has one. Let us test where the theorem stops being valid: first with a row that has an end.

Lemma 19.40 Influence of the end of a row (influence of the end of a row)

Let the beam of example 19.39 start at support \(0\) with a free rotation (simply supported end, moment zero) and continue with equal spans to infinity, the supports being at the nodes \(0, 1, 2, \dots\) With \(\rho = 2 - \sqrt3 = 0{,}2679\):

  1. The system of rotations \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\) has at most one bounded solution.
  2. This solution is \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \varphi_0\,(-\rho)^j\) with \(\varphi_0 = -q_0 l^3/(24\sqrt3\,EI)\).
  3. The moment over support \(j \ge 1\) is in absolute value
    \[|M_{\mathrm{j}}| = \frac{q_0 l^2}{12}\,\big(1 - (-\rho)^j\big) . \tag{19.15}\]
Proof

We must show three claims. We write the node equations, prove uniqueness as in the example, find the solution as a geometric sequence and insert it into the moment.

  1. By theorem 7.13 the row of node \(0\) is \((EI/l)(4\varphi_0 + 2\varphi_1) = -q_0 l^2/12\), and the row of node \(j \ge 1\) is \((EI/l)(2\varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + 8\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} + 2\varphi_{\mathrm{j}+1}) = 0\), because the equivalent pairs of neighbouring spans, \(+q_0 l^2/12\) and \(-q_0 l^2/12\), cancel (example 19.39, step 6).
  2. The difference \(\delta\) of two bounded solutions solves the homogeneous system, \(4\delta_0 + 2\delta_1 = 0\) and \(2\delta_{\mathrm{j}-1} + 8\delta_{\mathrm{j}} + 2\delta_{\mathrm{j}+1} = 0\). Let \(S\) be the supremum of the numbers \(|\delta_{\mathrm{j}}|\). The first row gives \(4|\delta_0| \le 2S\), the others \(8|\delta_{\mathrm{j}}| \le 4S\), so \(|\delta_{\mathrm{j}}| \le S/2\) for every \(j\), \(S \le S/2\) and \(S = 0\). This is point 1.
  3. Try \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \varphi_0\,r^j\). Row \(j \ge 1\), divided by \(2\varphi_0\,r^{j-1}\,EI/l\), gives \(1 + 4r + r^2 = 0\), so \(r = -2 \pm \sqrt3\). The sequence is bounded only for \(|r| < 1\), so \(r = -2 + \sqrt3 = -\rho\).
  4. The row of node \(0\) gives \((EI/l)(4 + 2r)\,\varphi_0 = -q_0 l^2/12\). Since \(4 + 2r = 2\sqrt3\), \(\varphi_0 = -q_0 l^3/(24\sqrt3\,EI)\). This proves point 2.
  5. The moment at the right end of span \(j - 1\), that is over support \(j\), is by point 1 of corollary 12.15 equal to the fourth force of the element, \(M_{\mathrm{j}} = (EI/l)(2\varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + 4\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}) - q_0 l^2/12\) (the fourth equivalent force is \(+q_0 l^2/12\)). With \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \varphi_0 r^j\) we have \(2\varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + 4\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \varphi_0\,r^{j-1}(2 + 4r)\), and from step 4 \((EI/l)\,\varphi_0 = -q_0 l^2/(12\,(4 + 2r))\).
  6. Hence \(M_{\mathrm{j}} = -(q_0 l^2/12)\big[1 + r^{j-1}(2 + 4r)/(4 + 2r)\big]\). The quotient is \((4\sqrt3 - 6)/(2\sqrt3) = 2 - \sqrt3 = \rho\), so \(M_{\mathrm{j}} = -(q_0 l^2/12)(1 + \rho\,(-\rho)^{j-1}) = -(q_0 l^2/12)(1 - (-\rho)^j)\). Since \(\rho < 1\), \(M_{\mathrm{j}} < 0\) and \(|M_{\mathrm{j}}|\) is equation (19.15).

Source: The lemma is ours, from theorem 7.13 and lemma 12.4. The behaviour of the end of a row (the influence falling geometrically, with a factor given by the node equations) is not treated in the sources, COOK (PDF p. 369, equation (10.9-2)) requires the condition \(\{\vek D_{\mathrm{B}}\} = \{\vek D_{\mathrm{A}}\}\) for the whole repetitive structure.

What does the lemma say about a beam with an end? At support \(j = 1\) the moment is \(|M_1| = 1{,}268 \cdot q_0 l^2/12 = 105{,}66\) N m, at \(j = 2\) it is \(0{,}928 \cdot 83{,}33 = 77{,}35\) N m, at \(j = 3\) it is \(1{,}019 \cdot 83{,}33 = 84{,}94\) N m. The value oscillates around the periodic value \(q_0 l^2/12 = 83{,}33\) N m and approaches it.

We build the figure as follows. The horizontal axis counts the supports \(j\) from the end, the vertical one is the moment divided by the periodic value \(q l^2/12\). The dashed line at \(1\) is the value given by the cell. The points are computed from equation (19.15), joined by segments so that the oscillation is visible, and the first four values are written out. The deviation is below \(1\) % at \(j = 4\), where \(\rho^4 = 0{,}0052\), and below \(0{,}01\) % at \(j = 7\), where \(\rho^7 = 9{,}9 \cdot 10^{-5}\).

Why is the first moment too large? The first span is simply supported at its end and cannot hold a moment, so the support must hold it. If the second span were infinitely stiff, the first span, clamped at one end and simply supported at the other, would have \(q_0 l^2/8 = 125\) N m over the support. This is the moment at \(n = 2\) in the table below. The actual value \(105{,}66\) N m lies between \(125\) and \(83{,}33\) N m, because the second span rotates somewhat.

Why does the deviation fall exactly by the factor \(0{,}268\) and change sign? The node equation says that the rotation of a support equals \(-1/4\) of the sum of the rotations of the neighbouring supports, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = -(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}-1} + \varphi_{\mathrm{j}+1})/4\). If the rotation of support \(j\) affected only the next support, its rotation would be \(-1/4\) of the rotation of support \(j\). The rotation \(\varphi\) of support \(j\) causes at the far end of the neighbouring span a moment \(2EI\varphi/l\) (half of the moment \(4EI\varphi/l\) at the near end), and support \(j + 1\) resists it with the stiffness \(8EI/l\) of both its spans, so the ratio is \(-2/8\). The reaction of the following support adds a correction. From \(1 + 4r + r^2 = 0\) we get \(r = -(1 + r^2)/4 = -0{,}25 \cdot 1{,}0718 = -0{,}2679\).

A real beam with \(n\) spans has an end on both sides. Support \(j\) from the left end is \(n - j\) from the right one. If we add the two influences, we get the estimate \(|M_{\mathrm{j}}| \approx (q_0 l^2/12)\big(1 - (-\rho)^j - (-\rho)^{n-j}\big)\), in which we neglect the influence passing from one end to the other, which is of order \(\rho^n\). The table compares the estimate with a finite element computation (NumPy).

\(n\) support \(j\) \(\lvert M_{\mathrm{j}}\rvert/(q_0 l^2)\), computed estimate
\(2\) \(1\) \(0{,}125000\) \(0{,}127992\)
\(3\) \(1\) \(0{,}100000\) \(0{,}099679\)
\(4\) \(2\) \(0{,}071429\) \(0{,}071367\)
\(5\) \(2\) \(0{,}078947\) \(0{,}078953\)
\(6\) \(3\) \(0{,}086538\) \(0{,}086540\)
\(8\) \(4\) \(0{,}082474\) \(0{,}082474\)
\(10\) \(5\) \(0{,}083564\) \(0{,}083564\)
\(20\) \(10\) \(0{,}083333\) \(0{,}083333\)

At \(n = 2\) and \(3\) the ends influence each other and the estimate deviates by \(3 \cdot 10^{-3}\) and \(3 \cdot 10^{-4}\), at \(n = 10\) by less than \(10^{-9}\). The periodic cell gives \(1/12 = 0{,}083333\). The computation reaches it to six digits only at \(n = 20\), at \(n = 5\) the error is \(5{,}3\) %, at \(n = 2\) it is \(50\) %. Conclusion: the periodic cell is valid in the interior of a long row. A support that is four spans from one end and far from the other has an error below \(1\) %. For a shorter row or near an end we must compute the whole row.

The second example that does not satisfy the theorem concerns not the end but the load. The hypothesis of equal load on all cells is essential in the theorem.

Take the same row with the load \(q_0\) only on every second span, as in figure 19.28. The same beam lies on the same supports, equally spaced. The load is on the first and third span, the second and fourth are empty. A cell with one span does not exist: every cell must have the same load, and only every second span has it. The period is therefore two spans, and the cell has two, the loaded one and the empty one.

Example 19.41 Load on every second span (load on every second span)

The cell has two elements and nodes \(0\), \(1\), \(2\) with rotations \(\varphi_0\), \(\varphi_1\), \(\varphi_2\), the deflection is zero everywhere. The first element is loaded.

  1. Joint: \(\varphi_2 = \varphi_0\), so \(\mat T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\). The matrix of a cell of two elements (theorem 7.13) is \((EI/l)\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 8 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\), the equivalent forces are \((-83{,}33,\ +83{,}33,\ 0)\) N m (only the first element is loaded).
  2. By equation (19.14) \(\mat K_{\mathrm{r}} = (EI/l)\begin{pmatrix} 8 & 4 \\ 4 & 8 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\vek f_{\mathrm{r}} = (-83{,}33,\ 83{,}33)\) N m. The mirror through the middle of the loaded span swaps nodes \(0\) and \(1\) and reverses the rotation, so \(\varphi_1 = -\varphi_0\). The first row is \((EI/l)(8 - 4)\,\varphi_0 = -83{,}33\) N m, so \(\varphi_0 = -83{,}33/(4 \cdot 20\,906{,}7) = -9{,}965 \cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(\varphi_1 = +9{,}965 \cdot 10^{-4}\). The second row gives the same, \(-4\,(EI/l)\,\varphi_0 = 83{,}33\) N m.
  3. The forces at the ends of the loaded span are \(F_2 = (EI/l)(4\varphi_0 + 2\varphi_1) + 83{,}33 = 2 \cdot 20\,906{,}7 \cdot (-9{,}965 \cdot 10^{-4}) + 83{,}33 = 41{,}67\) N m, so \(M(0) = -F_2 = -41{,}67\) N m, and the same on the right side. The unloaded span has equal moments at both ends and no load, so the moment in it is constant, \(-41{,}67\) N m. Over all supports the moment is \(-q_0 l^2/24 = -41{,}67\) N m, at mid-span of the loaded span \(q_0 l^2/8 - 41{,}67 = 83{,}33\) N m (statics of a simply supported span).
  4. The wrong conclusion with one span would give \(-83{,}33\) N m over a support and \(41{,}67\) N m at mid-span. The first is twice too large, the second twice too small. A computation of the whole beam with \(40\) spans gives \(-41{,}67\) N m over the middle supports and the rotation \(-9{,}965 \cdot 10^{-4}\) at the left end of the middle loaded span, as the cell does (NumPy).

Source: The example is ours, after theorem 19.38.

The period of the cell is therefore the period of the whole row, including the load, not only the shape. With equal load on every span one span is enough, with load on every second span we must take two. The same beam thus has two cells, depending on the load.

In composites, the repeating piece of material is called a unit cell (enotska celica). By the same idea, the behaviour of the whole material is computed from the behaviour of the cell. We do not treat this theory here and have no source for it in the books we use.

A shift of the row by one cell is a symmetry that leaves the solution unchanged. We shall use the same idea in section 19.9 for a rotation instead of a shift: the cells stand in a circle and each differs from its neighbour by a rotation, not by \(l\). Then theorem 19.38 will no longer be enough, because a rotation changes the axes of the unknowns, and we shall have to write the cells in their own axes.

19.9 Cyclic symmetry and the split into harmonics

A wheel with six spokes looks exactly as before after a turn by a sixth of a circle: the same spokes, the same steel, the same clamping. We press on the rim with a single radial force, say from hitting a kerb. The problem has 18 unknowns, since the rim has six nodes with three unknowns each. The turn by a sixth of a circle is a coincidence that mirror symmetry from section 19.1 does not know: a mirror swaps left and right, a turn does not. Does it help us reduce the problem to one sector of the wheel, and when? For a wheel with thirty-six spokes and a thousand elements per sector the problem would be thirty-six times smaller. The answer has two parts. When the load repeats on every sector, one sector is enough, which is how COOK proceeds (section 10.9, PDF p. 368-370). When the load is arbitrary, like our single force, one sector is not enough, but problems of the size of one sector still are, only there are more of them. The second part is not in the sources. We derive it from the discrete Fourier transform of chapter 9 and it is our derivation.

The model is the same wheel as in section 19.10. All members are straight steel beams with the cross-section \(20 \times 40\) mm as in chapter 12, \(E = 196\) GPa, \(EA = 1{,}568\cdot 10^{8}\) N, \(EI = 20\,907\) N m\(^2\), and each member is one frame element (definition 12.17). We make three idealizations. First: the hub is the point \(O\), rigidly clamped, while a real hub is elastic and the axle turns. Second: the spokes are bending beams and not cables, as on a bicycle wheel. Third: the rim is six straight beams with chord \(1\) m, while a real rim is a circular arc of length \(\pi/3 = 1{,}047\) m per sector, \(4{,}7\) % longer. The hexagon is mapped onto itself exactly by a turn by a sixth of a circle, so we chose it. The load acts only at nodes and there is none on the members, so by theorem 12.14 the displacements at the nodes of the frame model are exact. We compute linearly: the largest displacement is below \(3\) micrometres on a length of \(1\) m, a ratio of \(3\cdot 10^{-6}\), the largest rotation is \(0{,}94\) millionths of a radian and its square, the order of the neglected correction, is \(10^{-12}\).

We build figure 19.29 step by step. First the hub \(O\), clamped at the centre. Six spokes leave it and each ends in one of the six rim nodes, numbered \(0\) to \(5\) counterclockwise. Neighbouring nodes are joined by a rim beam. Every node has three unknowns, 18 in all. We divide the nodes into sectors. Sector \(0\) consists of node \(0\), the spoke that holds it and the rim beam up to node \(1\). Sectors \(1, \dots, 5\) are built the same way. A sector is thus a slice of the circle, like a piece of pie, and for our purposes it holds one piece of rim, one beam and one spoke. We chose the sectors so that each node lies in exactly one. The rim beam of sector \(0\) joins node \(0\) to node \(1\) of sector \(1\), so sectors \(0\) and \(1\) are neighbours, as are sectors \(5\) and \(0\).

We express the unknowns of a node in its own axes: the radial displacement \(r\) along the spoke outwards, the tangential displacement \(t\) perpendicular to it, and the rotation \(\varphi\). The axes of node \(j\) are turned by the angle \(j\alpha\) relative to the global axes, and at node \(1\) the axes \(r_1\), \(t_1\) are turned by the angle \(\alpha = 2\pi/N\) relative to the axes of node \(0\). Why local axes? Because then every sector looks the same: a spoke that runs radially has the same meaning and the same stiffness in local axes everywhere, and comparing sectors becomes comparing numbers.

Definition 19.42 Cyclic symmetry (ciklična simetrija)

Let \(N \ge 3\) be a natural number and \(O\) a point of the plane. A plane frame (definition 5.90), divided into frame elements (definition 12.17), is cyclically symmetric with \(N\) sectors about the point \(O\) (ciklično simetričen z \(N\) odseki) if its nodes are divided into \(N\) sectors (odseki) \(0, \dots, N-1\) of \(s\) nodes each, and under the rotation \(\rho\) about \(O\) by the angle \(\alpha = 2\pi/N\) counterclockwise three conditions hold.

  1. The rotation \(\rho\) takes the \(s\) nodes of sector \(j\) in order to the \(s\) nodes of sector \(j+1\) (sector numbers are counted modulo \(N\), so sector \(N-1\) goes to sector \(0\)).
  2. The rotation \(\rho\) takes elements to elements: if an element joins nodes \(a\) and \(b\), there is exactly one element that joins \(\rho a\) and \(\rho b\), with the same length, the same \(EA\) and the same \(EI\). Every element joins two nodes of the same sector or of two neighbouring sectors.
  3. If a component along an axis turned by \(j\alpha\) (below) is clamped at node \(a\), the same component along the axis turned by \((j+1)\alpha\) is clamped at node \(\rho a\).

The unknowns of sector \(j\) are the components of the displacements and rotations of its nodes in the axes that are the global axes turned by \(j\alpha\) counterclockwise (the axis rotation matrix \(\mat Q(j\alpha)\) of definition 2.37). They are collected in a column \(\hat{\vek d}_{\mathrm{j}}\) with \(n\) free unknowns. The axes of sector \(0\) are the global axes.

Source: COOK section 10.9 (PDF p. 368-369) and ONATE1 section 9.6.2 (PDF p. 348-349) describe identical sectors that fit together around a circle, and the displacements on the sector boundaries in their local axes. The definition in this form, with \(N\) sectors and a rotation \(\rho\), is ours, because the sources have no general definition.

The word cyclic comes from the Greek word for a circle: after \(N\) turns by \(2\pi/N\) we are back at the start, so the steps form a circle. A sector is a slice of a circle, like a piece of pie, hence the name. In our wheel \(N = 6\), \(s = 1\) (one node per sector), the clamping is the hub \(O\), which belongs to no sector and is not an unknown. Every rim node has all three unknowns free in local axes, so \(n = 3\). We assume further that the structure satisfies the hypotheses of theorem 12.20, so by that theorem \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is positive definite. For the wheel this holds because the hub \(O\) clamps all components.

How is the stiffness matrix arranged in these axes? Let \(\hat{\mat K}\) be the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) in the local axes of the sectors, with blocks \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{jl}}\) of order \(n\) (rows of sector \(j\), columns of sector \(l\)). Figure 19.30 shows the pattern for six sectors. The rows are the sectors \(j\), the columns the sectors \(l\), and every cell of the grid is one block of order \(n\). The block \((j, l)\) is non-zero only if sectors \(j\) and \(l\) are joined by an element, that is for \(l = j\) and for the neighbours \(l = j \pm 1\). The pattern is thus the diagonal, accompanied by one diagonal above it and one below it. The blocks along the diagonals are equal from row to row, a shift by one sector, in the figure the arrow, brings the same block. In the corners the pattern wraps around the circle: row \(5\) has the neighbour \(0\) to the right of the diagonal, and row \(0\) has the neighbour \(5\) on the left.

Lemma 19.43 Block circulant matrix (krožna bločna matrika)

Let a frame be cyclically symmetric with \(N \ge 3\) sectors (definition 19.42), let \(\hat{\mat K}\) be the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) in the local axes of the sectors (an \(Nn \times Nn\) matrix with blocks \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{jl}}\) of order \(n\)) and let \(\mat K_0 = \hat{\mat K}_{00}\) and \(\mat K_1 = \hat{\mat K}_{01}\) be blocks. Then:

  1. \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{j}+1, \mathrm{l}+1} = \hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{jl}}\) for all \(j\), \(l\) (indices modulo \(N\)).
  2. \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{jj}} = \mat K_0\) with \(\mat K_0\) symmetric, \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{j}, \mathrm{j}+1} = \mat K_1\), \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{j}+1, \mathrm{j}} = \mat K_1^\T\), and all other blocks are zero.
  3. The matrix \(\hat{\mat K}\) is symmetric and positive definite.
Proof

We must show that turning a sector by \(\alpha\) changes a stiffness block exactly as it changes the local axes, and that the two changes cancel. For an element we use lemma 12.18 on its stiffness matrix.

  1. Let \(\mat Q(\beta) = \begin{bmatrix}\cos\beta & \sin\beta \\ -\sin\beta & \cos\beta\end{bmatrix}\) be the rotation matrix of the axes by the angle \(\beta\) (equation (12.11), definition 2.37), \(\mat Z = \mathrm{diag}(\mat Q(\alpha), 1)\) a \(3 \times 3\) matrix and \(\tilde{\mat Z} = \mathrm{diag}(\mat Z, \mat Z)\). The matrix \(\mat Z\) is orthogonal, because \(\mat Q\) is orthogonal (definition 2.39).
  2. Let the element \(e\) be at the angle \(\alpha_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(e' = \rho e\) its image. By definition 19.42, item 2, \(e'\) has the same \(h\), \(EA\), \(EI\), hence the same local matrix \(\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\) (equation (12.12)), and the angle \(\alpha_{\mathrm{e}} + \alpha\). Since \(\mat Q(\beta_1 + \beta_2) = \mat Q(\beta_1)\mat Q(\beta_2)\) (the addition theorems for cosine and sine), \(\mat R_{\mathrm{e}'} = \mat R_{\mathrm{e}}\tilde{\mat Z}\) with \(\mat R\) from lemma 12.18. By item 2 of that lemma \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}'} = \mat R_{\mathrm{e}'}^\T\bar{\mat k}_{\mathrm{e}}\mat R_{\mathrm{e}'} = \tilde{\mat Z}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\tilde{\mat Z}\). For the node blocks \(a\), \(b\) of the element this means \([\mat k_{\mathrm{e}'}]_{\rho \mathrm{a},\rho \mathrm{b}} = \mat Z^\T[\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}]_{\mathrm{ab}}\mat Z\).
  3. The block \((a, b)\) of the matrix \(\mat K\) is by theorem 7.13 the sum of the blocks \([\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}]_{\mathrm{ab}}\) over all elements that have both nodes \(a\) and \(b\). By definition 19.42, item 2, the map \(e \mapsto \rho e\) is a bijection between the elements with nodes \(a\), \(b\) and the elements with nodes \(\rho a\), \(\rho b\). Hence \(\mat K_{\rho \mathrm{a}, \rho \mathrm{b}} = \mat Z^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{ab}}\mat Z\) (in global axes, before removing the clamped components). By item 3 of the definition clamped components map to clamped components, so from every sector we drop the rows and columns of the same components in local axes, and the blocks \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{jl}}\) keep the same shape for all sectors.
  4. Let \(\mat R_{\mathrm{j}}\) be the matrix that converts the global components of the nodes of sector \(j\) into local ones, \(\hat{\vek d}_{\mathrm{j}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{j}}\vek d_{\mathrm{j}}\), and let \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{s}} = \mathrm{diag}(\mat Z, \dots, \mat Z)\) with \(s\) blocks. The axes of sector \(j + 1\) are the axes of sector \(j\) turned by \(\alpha\), so \(\mat R_{\mathrm{j}+1} = \mat Z_{\mathrm{s}}\mat R_{\mathrm{j}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{j}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{s}}\) (rotations in the plane commute, step 4 of the proof of lemma 12.18) and \(\mat R_{\mathrm{N}} = \mat R_0\), since \(\alpha N = 2\pi\) and cosine and sine are periodic (lemma 8.10, item 4). The local block is \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{jl}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{j}}\mat K_{\mathrm{jl}}\mat R_{\mathrm{l}}^\T\), because energy is a scalar, \(\hat{\vek d}^\T\hat{\mat K}\hat{\vek d} = \vek d^\T\mat K\vek d\).
  5. From steps 3 and 4, \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{j}+1,\mathrm{l}+1} = \mat R_{\mathrm{j}+1}\mat K_{\mathrm{j}+1,\mathrm{l}+1}\mat R_{\mathrm{l}+1}^\T = \mat Z_{\mathrm{s}}\mat R_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{jl}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mat R_{\mathrm{l}}^\T\mat Z_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\). Since \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{s}}\) commutes with \(\mat R_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\mat R_{\mathrm{l}}\) and \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{s}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{s}}^\T = \mat I\), the \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{s}}\) cancel and what remains is \(\mat R_{\mathrm{j}}\mat K_{\mathrm{jl}}\mat R_{\mathrm{l}}^\T = \hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{jl}}\). This is item 1.
  6. Item 2 of the definition says that an element joins nodes of the same sector or of neighbouring sectors, so \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{jl}} = \mat 0\) if \(l\) differs from \(j\) by more than \(1\) modulo \(N\) (for \(N \ge 3\), \(j+1\) and \(j-1\) are different). By item 1, \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{jj}} = \hat{\mat K}_{00} = \mat K_0\) and \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{j},\mathrm{j}+1} = \hat{\mat K}_{01} = \mat K_1\). The matrix \(\mat K\) is symmetric (theorem 7.13), so \(\hat{\mat K} = \mat R\mat K\mat R^\T\) with \(\mat R = \mathrm{diag}(\mat R_0, \dots, \mat R_{\mathrm{N}-1})\) is symmetric (lemma 1.101), hence \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{j}+1,\mathrm{j}} = \hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{j},\mathrm{j}+1}^\T = \mat K_1^\T\) and \(\mat K_0 = \mat K_0^\T\).
  7. Since \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}\) is positive definite and \(\mat R\) is orthogonal, for \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\) also \(\vek x^\T\hat{\mat K}\vek x = (\mat R^\T\vek x)^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{ff}}(\mat R^\T\vek x) > 0\), because \(\mat R^\T\vek x \ne \vek 0\). This is item 3.

Source: COOK section 10.9 (PDF p. 369, equations 10.9-2 and 10.9-3) says that all sectors have the same stiffness matrix in their own axes and that pairs of nodes on the boundaries have the same displacements in local axes, ONATE1 (9.37) (PDF p. 349) the same. The proof that the block matrix is circulant is ours.

The lemma says where the regularity comes from: the turn rearranges the sectors and also the axes, and the two changes cancel. The block circulant matrix has its name because each block row arises from the previous one by a shift of one block, and at the end it wraps around the circle back to the start, like the numbers on a clock.

Let us look at the blocks of the wheel. Spoke \(0\) is the element from the clamped hub to node \(0\), rim element \(0\) joins node \(0\) to node \(1\), rim element \(5\) joins node \(5\) to node \(0\). At node \(0\) the local axes are the global ones. The spoke lies along the axis \(r\), so it contributes the axial stiffness \(EA/h = 1{,}568\cdot 10^{8}\) N/m in the direction \(r\) and the bending stiffness \(12EI/h^3 = 250\,880\) N/m in the direction \(t\). Both rim beams make an angle of \(60\) degrees with the direction \(r\), because the triangle of the hub and two neighbouring rim nodes is equilateral (both spokes and the chord are \(1\) m long). So each contributes \(\cos^2 60° = 0{,}25\) of its axial stiffness in the direction \(r\) and \(\sin^2 60° = 0{,}75\) in the direction \(t\) (equation (12.14)). For the block \(\mat K_0\) this gives \((\mat K_0)_{\mathrm{rr}} = EA/h + 2\,(0{,}25\,EA/h + 0{,}75\cdot 12EI/h^3) = 2{,}3558\cdot 10^{8}\) N/m. For \((\mat K_0)_{\mathrm{tt}} = 12EI/h^3 + 2\,(0{,}75\,EA/h + 0{,}25\cdot 12EI/h^3) = 2{,}3558\cdot 10^{8}\) N/m, equal to \((\mat K_0)_{\mathrm{rr}}\), because both sums are \(\tfrac32\,EA/h + 18\,EI/h^3\). For the rotation \((\mat K_0)_{\varphi\varphi} = 3\cdot 4EI/h = 250\,880\) N m, since each of the three beams at the node has stiffness \(4EI/h\) (matrix (12.12)). The remaining entries of the blocks we get the same way (NumPy). The block \(\mat K_1\) has all entries non-zero and is not symmetric, since the rim beam joins nodes \(0\) and \(1\), which have different axes. The blocks \(\hat{\mat K}_{02}\), \(\hat{\mat K}_{03}\), \(\hat{\mat K}_{04}\) are zero, because no element joins sector \(0\) to sectors \(2\), \(3\) or \(4\), as the empty cells of figure 19.30 show. Numerically the difference \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{j}+1,\mathrm{l}+1} - \hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{jl}}\) is at most \(1{,}8\cdot 10^{-7}\) N/m in all blocks, for the largest entry \(2{,}4\cdot 10^{8}\) N/m (rounding).

When is the solution the same on all sectors? The answer is as for mirror symmetry: if the turn preserves the structure and the load, it preserves the solution too, since the problem has only one solution.

Theorem 19.44 Cyclic load, one sector suffices (ciklična obremenitev, en odsek zadošča)

Let a frame be cyclically symmetric with \(N \ge 3\) sectors (definition 19.42), with blocks \(\mat K_0\), \(\mat K_1\) from lemma 19.43, and let the load be cyclic, that is the column of sector loads in local axes is the same for all sectors, \(\hat{\vek f}_{\mathrm{j}} = \hat{\vek f}_0\) for \(j = 0, \dots, N-1\). Then the system \(\hat{\mat K}\hat{\vek d} = \hat{\vek f}\) has exactly one solution, the solution is cyclic, \(\hat{\vek d}_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek u\) for every \(j\), and \(\vek u\) is the only solution of the system of order \(n\)

\[(\mat K_0 + \mat K_1 + \mat K_1^\T)\,\vek u = \hat{\vek f}_0 . \tag{19.16}\]

The matrix \(\mat K_0 + \mat K_1 + \mat K_1^\T\) is symmetric and positive definite.

Proof

We must show that the column with equal blocks solves the system if \(\vek u\) solves equation (19.16), and that this equation has a solution. Uniqueness then follows from lemma 19.43.

  1. The matrix \(\mat S = \mat K_0 + \mat K_1 + \mat K_1^\T\) is symmetric, because \(\mat K_0\) is symmetric and \((\mat K_1 + \mat K_1^\T)^\T = \mat K_1^\T + \mat K_1\) (lemma 1.101).
  2. Let \(\vek T = (\mat I, \dots, \mat I)^\T\) be the \(Nn \times n\) matrix with one identity block per sector (this \(\vek T\) is the transformation matrix \(\hat{\vek d} = \vek T\vek u\) of section 19.5 and is neither the matrix \(\mat T\) of lemma 12.22 nor the kinetic energy). By lemma 19.43, item 2, row \(j\) of the matrix \(\hat{\mat K}\) times \(\vek T\vek u\) is \(\mat K_1^\T\vek u + \mat K_0\vek u + \mat K_1\vek u = \mat S\vek u\) for every \(j\).
  3. For \(\vek u \ne \vek 0\), \((\vek T\vek u)^\T\hat{\mat K}(\vek T\vek u) = N\,\vek u^\T\mat S\vek u\), because the sum over all \(N\) rows gives by step 2 \(N\) times \(\vek u^\T\mat S\vek u\). The left side is positive, because \(\hat{\mat K}\) is positive definite and \(\vek T\vek u \ne \vek 0\) (lemma 19.43, item 3). So \(\mat S\) is positive definite, and the system \(\mat S\vek u = \hat{\vek f}_0\) has by theorem 6.29 exactly one solution.
  4. For this solution \(\vek u\), by step 2 row \(j\) of the system \(\hat{\mat K}(\vek T\vek u) = \hat{\vek f}\) is \(\mat S\vek u = \hat{\vek f}_0 = \hat{\vek f}_{\mathrm{j}}\), so \(\vek T\vek u\) solves the system. Since \(\hat{\mat K}\) is positive definite, the system has by theorem 6.29 exactly one solution, and it is \(\vek T\vek u\).

Source: COOK section 10.9 (PDF p. 369, equations 10.9-1 to 10.9-4): pairs of nodes on the boundaries \(AA'\) and \(BB'\) are tied by equal displacements in local axes and \(\mat T^\T\mat K\mat T\) is assembled. Our \(\mat S\vek u = \hat{\vek f}_0\) is the same equation, since \(\vek T^\T\hat{\mat K}\vek T = N\mat S\) and \(\vek T^\T\hat{\vek f} = N\hat{\vek f}_0\). Uniqueness as a consequence of positive definiteness is not from the source.

COOK requires equal displacements of the node pairs on the boundaries (PDF p. 369) and does not show that the solution obtained is really a solution of the whole structure. The proof above shows it: the solution with equal blocks is a solution and the only one. COOK also warns that the load of the nodes on a sector boundary must be listed on only one of the two boundaries \(AA'\) and \(BB'\), since otherwise the sector would receive twice the load (PDF p. 369). With us this cannot happen, because every node belongs to exactly one sector, and the load of a node is in the column \(\hat{\vek f}_{\mathrm{j}}\) of that sector.

What about our single force? The load \(\hat{\vek f}_0 = (-500, 0, 0)\) N at node \(0\) and nothing at the other nodes is not cyclic, since \(\hat{\vek f}_0 \ne \hat{\vek f}_1\). Theorem 19.44 does not apply here and the solution is not cyclic. But the load can be split into cyclic parts by the discrete Fourier transform (definition 9.102), which we know from chapter 9: there we split a periodic function into harmonics, here the column of sector loads, which is "periodic" in \(j\) with period \(N\). We expand the load of sector \(j\) by the number \(k\) and \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = \mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}k/N}\), which has \(|w_{\mathrm{k}}| = 1\) and \(w_{\mathrm{k}}^N = 1\) (theorem 9.29). The harmonic \(k\) is a load that is multiplied by the number \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\) from one sector to the next, so in one trip around the wheel it turns \(k\) times in the complex plane, which plays the same role as \(k\) oscillations per period in chapter 9. At \(k = 0\) the load is the same in all sectors, which is the cyclic load of theorem 19.44.

Figure 19.31 shows how our force splits. The single force \(F = 500\) N at node \(0\) equals the sum of four cyclically arranged parts. The harmonic \(k = 0\) is the force \(F/6 = 83{,}3\) N inwards at every node: the average of the load. The harmonics \(k = 1\) and \(5\) together give a radial load that varies as \(\tfrac{2F}{6}\cos(2\pi j/6)\) (\(167\) N inwards at node \(0\), \(83\) N inwards at nodes \(1\) and \(5\), \(83\) N outwards at nodes \(2\) and \(4\), \(167\) N outwards at node \(3\)). The harmonics \(2\) and \(4\) give \(\tfrac{2F}{6}\cos(2\pi\cdot 2j/6)\) and the harmonic \(3\) gives \(\tfrac{F}{6}(-1)^j\). At node \(0\) all parts add up to \(83{,}3 + 166{,}7 + 166{,}7 + 83{,}3 = 500\) N, and at node \(1\) to \(83{,}3 + 83{,}3 - 83{,}3 - 83{,}3 = 0\), since there is no force there.

For every harmonic \(k\) we must solve a smaller problem. Which one? Imagine a solution that is multiplied by \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\) from one sector to the next, \(\hat{\vek d}_{\mathrm{j}} = w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\,\vek U\) with a complex column \(\vek U\) of order \(n\). By lemma 19.43 row \(j\) of the system \(\hat{\mat K}\hat{\vek d} = \hat{\vek f}\) is \(\mat K_1^\T\hat{\vek d}_{\mathrm{j}-1} + \mat K_0\hat{\vek d}_{\mathrm{j}} + \mat K_1\hat{\vek d}_{\mathrm{j}+1} = w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\,(\bar w_{\mathrm{k}}\mat K_1^\T + \mat K_0 + w_{\mathrm{k}}\mat K_1)\vek U\), since \(w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j-1} = w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\,\bar w_{\mathrm{k}}\) (from \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\bar w_{\mathrm{k}} = |w_{\mathrm{k}}|^2 = 1\)). That is the phase \(w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\) times the matrix

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat K_0 + w_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mat K_1 + \bar w_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mat K_1^\T , \qquad w_{\mathrm{k}} = \mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}k/N} \tag{19.17}\]

of order \(n\) and the column \(\vek U\). At \(k = 0\) this is the matrix \(\mat K_0 + \mat K_1 + \mat K_1^\T\) of theorem 19.44. Beware of the notation: in this section \(k\) is not a stiffness but the number of the harmonic, and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\) at \(k = 0\) is not the block \(\mat K_0\) of the lemma but the sum of three blocks. The problem for one sector is thus \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\vek U = \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) with the load of the harmonic \(k\). Does it have a solution, and is the true answer real? We need complex columns for this, so first the properties of the matrix (19.17).

Lemma 19.45 The sector matrix is Hermitian and positive definite (odsekovna matrika je hermitska in pozitivno definitna)

In the setting of lemma 19.43 let \(k\) be an integer, \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = \mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}k/N}\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\) the matrix (19.17). For a complex matrix \(\mat M\) the conjugate transpose \(\mat M^*\) is the matrix with entries \(\overline{M_{\mathrm{lj}}}\), and \(\mat M\) is Hermitian (hermitska) if \(\mat M^* = \mat M\). For a complex column \(\vek z\), \(\vek z^*\) is the row of conjugate entries. Then:

  1. \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\) is Hermitian.
  2. For every non-zero complex column \(\vek z\) of order \(n\) the number \(\vek z^*\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\vek z\) is real and positive, so \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\) is invertible.
  3. \(\mat K_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = \overline{\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}}\) (conjugate entries) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}+\mathrm{N}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\).
Proof

We must show three items. For the second we use a complex column built from all the sectors with the phase \(w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\), and the positive definiteness of the matrix \(\hat{\mat K}\).

  1. The matrices \(\mat K_0\) and \(\mat K_1\) are real, so \((w_{\mathrm{k}}\mat K_1)^* = \bar w_{\mathrm{k}}\mat K_1^\T\) with the conjugate number \(\bar w_{\mathrm{k}}\) (definition 9.21) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}^* = \mat K_0^\T + \bar w_{\mathrm{k}}\mat K_1^\T + w_{\mathrm{k}}\mat K_1\) (the neighbouring terms swap roles). Since \(\mat K_0 = \mat K_0^\T\) (lemma 19.43, item 2), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}^* = \mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  2. Let \(\vek z \ne \vek 0\) and \(\vek Z\) a column of order \(Nn\) with blocks \(\vek Z_{\mathrm{j}} = w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\vek z\) for \(j = 0, \dots, N-1\). Since \(w_{\mathrm{k}}^N = 1\) (theorem 9.29, \(\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}k} = 1\)), \(\vek Z_{\mathrm{N}} = \vek Z_0\), so at \(j = 0\) the block \(\vek Z_{-1} = \vek Z_{\mathrm{N}-1} = w_{\mathrm{k}}^{-1}\vek z\) and at \(j = N-1\) the block \(\vek Z_{\mathrm{N}} = \vek z\), and the formula \(\vek Z_{\mathrm{j}\pm 1} = w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j\pm 1}\vek z\) holds for all \(j\). By lemma 19.43, \(\vek Z^*\hat{\mat K}\vek Z = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \vek Z_{\mathrm{j}}^*\big(\mat K_1^\T\vek Z_{\mathrm{j}-1} + \mat K_0\vek Z_{\mathrm{j}} + \mat K_1\vek Z_{\mathrm{j}+1}\big)\). The term \(j\) is \(\bar w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\,w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\,\vek z^*\big(\bar w_{\mathrm{k}}\mat K_1^\T + \mat K_0 + w_{\mathrm{k}}\mat K_1\big)\vek z\), and \(\bar w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j} = |w_{\mathrm{k}}|^{2j} = 1\) (theorem 9.29, item 2). Hence \(\vek Z^*\hat{\mat K}\vek Z = N\,\vek z^*\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\vek z\).
  3. Write \(\vek Z = \vek x + \mathrm{i}\vek y\) with real columns. Then \(\vek Z^*\hat{\mat K}\vek Z = \vek x^\T\hat{\mat K}\vek x + \vek y^\T\hat{\mat K}\vek y + \mathrm{i}\,(\vek x^\T\hat{\mat K}\vek y - \vek y^\T\hat{\mat K}\vek x)\) (lemma 9.20). The two numbers in the bracket are equal, because \(\vek y^\T\hat{\mat K}\vek x = (\vek y^\T\hat{\mat K}\vek x)^\T = \vek x^\T\hat{\mat K}\vek y\) (a number equals its transpose, \(\hat{\mat K}\) is symmetric), so the imaginary part is zero. At least one of \(\vek x\), \(\vek y\) is non-zero, because \(\vek Z \ne \vek 0\) (\(\vek Z_0 = \vek z\)), and \(\hat{\mat K}\) is positive definite, so the sum is positive. By step 2 \(\vek z^*\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\vek z\) is real and positive. If \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\vek z = \vek 0\), then \(\vek z^*\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\vek z = 0\), hence \(\vek z = \vek 0\), so \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\) is invertible.
  4. Since \(w_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = \mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}k/N} = \cos(2\pi k/N) - \mathrm{i}\sin(2\pi k/N) = \bar w_{\mathrm{k}}\) (theorem 9.29, item 1) and \(\mat K_0\), \(\mat K_1\) are real, \(\mat K_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = \mat K_0 + \bar w_{\mathrm{k}}\mat K_1 + w_{\mathrm{k}}\mat K_1^\T = \overline{\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}}\). Likewise \(w_{\mathrm{k}+\mathrm{N}} = w_{\mathrm{k}}\) gives \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}+\mathrm{N}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\).

Source: KREYSZIG section 8.5 (PDF p. 373) defines a Hermitian matrix by \(\bar{\mat A}^\T = \mat A\), says that it is named after Hermite, and that a real Hermitian matrix is symmetric. The lemma and its proof are ours.

The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\) thus has the properties of a stiffness matrix that we need: it is Hermitian, which is symmetry for a complex matrix, and positive definite, so the problem \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\vek U = \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) has exactly one solution. Now we can state the split in full.

Theorem 19.46 Split into harmonics (razcep po harmonikih)

In the setting of lemma 19.43 let \(\hat{\vek f}_0, \dots, \hat{\vek f}_{\mathrm{N}-1}\) be arbitrary real columns of order \(n\) (the sector loads in local axes) and

\[\vek F_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathrm{j}=0}^{N-1}\hat{\vek f}_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}jk/N} , \qquad k = 0, \dots, N-1 \tag{19.18}\]

their discrete Fourier transform in \(j\) (definition 9.102, for every component). Then:

  1. \(\hat{\vek f}_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=0}^{N-1} w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\,\vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) for every \(j\).
  2. For every \(k\) the system of order \(n\) \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\vek U_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) has exactly one solution \(\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  3. The solution of the system \(\hat{\mat K}\hat{\vek d} = \hat{\vek f}\) is \(\hat{\vek d}_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=0}^{N-1} w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\,\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}\), and it is real.
  4. \(\vek F_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = \overline{\vek F_{\mathrm{k}}}\) and \(\vek U_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = \overline{\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}}\) for \(0 < k < N\). So it suffices to solve the harmonics \(k = 0, \dots, \lfloor N/2\rfloor\), the harmonics \(0\) and (for even \(N\)) \(N/2\) are real, and every pair \(k\), \(N-k\) gives the real contribution \(2\,\mathrm{Re}\big(w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}\big)\).
Proof

We must show four items. The first follows from discrete orthogonality, the third from substitution into the system together with uniqueness, the fourth from conjugation.

  1. Substitute (19.18): \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\vek F_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac1N\sum_{\mathrm{i}}\hat{\vek f}_{\mathrm{i}}\sum_{\mathrm{k}=0}^{N-1}\mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}k(j-i)/N}\) (swapping the order of two finite sums). By lemma 9.103 the inner sum is \(N\) if \(N\) divides \(j - i\) and \(0\) otherwise. Since \(|j - i| < N\), this happens only at \(i = j\), and the sum is \(\hat{\vek f}_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  2. Item 2 is lemma 19.45, item 2: the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\) is invertible, so the system has the one solution \(\vek U_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{k}}^{-1}\vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  3. Let \(\hat{\vek d}_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}\). Row \(j\) of the system (lemma 19.43, item 2) is \(\mat K_1^\T\hat{\vek d}_{\mathrm{j}-1} + \mat K_0\hat{\vek d}_{\mathrm{j}} + \mat K_1\hat{\vek d}_{\mathrm{j}+1} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\,\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}\) (term by term as before the lemma, with \(w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j\pm1} = w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\pm1}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{k}}^{-1} = \bar w_{\mathrm{k}}\)). By item 2 this equals \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\vek F_{\mathrm{k}} = \hat{\vek f}_{\mathrm{j}}\) by item 1. So \(\hat{\vek d}\) solves the system. Let \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) be the real and imaginary parts of the column \(\hat{\vek d}\). Since \(\hat{\mat K}\) and \(\hat{\vek f}\) are real, \(\hat{\mat K}\vek a = \hat{\vek f}\) and \(\hat{\mat K}\vek b = \vek 0\). The second equation gives \(\vek b^\T\hat{\mat K}\vek b = 0\), and since \(\hat{\mat K}\) is positive definite, \(\vek b = \vek 0\). So \(\hat{\vek d} = \vek a\) is real, and by theorem 6.29 it is the only solution.
  4. Since \(\hat{\vek f}_{\mathrm{j}}\) is real and \(\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}j(N-k)/N} = \mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}jk/N}\) (theorem 9.29, item 1, and \(\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}j} = 1\)), \(\vek F_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = \overline{\vek F_{\mathrm{k}}}\). Conjugating the system \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\vek U_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) gives \(\overline{\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}}\,\overline{\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}} = \overline{\vek F_{\mathrm{k}}}\), that is by lemma 19.45, item 3, \(\mat K_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}}\overline{\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}}\). By item 2 this system has one solution, so \(\vek U_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = \overline{\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}}\). At \(k = 0\) and \(k = N/2\), \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = \pm 1\), so \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) are real and \(\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}\) is real. The terms \(k\) and \(N-k\) in the sum of item 3 at sector \(j\) are written \(w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\vek U_{\mathrm{k}} + \overline{w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}} = 2\,\mathrm{Re}\big(w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}\big)\).

Source: The split of the load and of the solution into harmonics on a cyclic structure is our derivation from the discrete Fourier transform (definition 9.102, chapter 9), because the sources of this section do not contain it. COOK section 14.4 (PDF p. 530-531) uses the same idea for bodies of revolution under arbitrary load: the load is written as a series of cosines and sines in the circumferential angle \(\theta\), each harmonic \(n\) is solved separately in the plane and the results are added.

The theorem says four things we shall need. The problem with \(18\) unknowns is replaced by six problems with three unknowns, of which by item 4 only four are needed (\(k = 0, 1, 2, 3\)), because \(k\) and \(6 - k\) are conjugates of each other. The solution is a sum of waves that turn by \(2\pi k/N\) from sector to sector, which at \(k = 1\) means one trip around and at \(k = 3\) a half turn per step. Since \(N\) sectors have only \(N\) different harmonics, the series does not reach arbitrarily high numbers: the harmonics \(k\) and \(k + N\) have the same values on the sectors, which is aliasing (corollary 9.104). For a continuous body, which COOK treats with a Fourier series in the angle (section 14.4), there is no aliasing, because the angle is continuous.

Example 19.47 A single force on the rim of the wheel (enojna sila na platišču kolesa)

The wheel of figure 19.29 has a radial force \(500\) N inwards at node \(0\), \(\hat{\vek f}_0 = (-500, 0, 0)\) (the component \(r\) is positive outwards, so inwards it is negative), and nothing at the other nodes (figure 19.31, top left). By equation (19.18) \(\vek F_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac16\,\hat{\vek f}_0 = (-83{,}33, 0, 0)\) N for every \(k = 0, \dots, 5\), since the only non-zero term has the factor \(\mathrm{e}^0 = 1\). The matrices \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\) are Hermitian and have positive eigenvalues, as lemma 19.45 requires. The smallest are \(3{,}26\cdot 10^{4}\), \(2{,}92\cdot 10^{5}\), \(2{,}09\cdot 10^{5}\) and \(1{,}67\cdot 10^{5}\) at \(k = 0, 1, 2, 3\) (numbers in SI units). The solutions \(\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}\) have a real radial displacement and by item 4 of theorem 19.46 are conjugate for \(k\) and \(6-k\), for example \(\vek U_1 = (-0{,}531, -0{,}530\,\mathrm{i}, -0{,}227\,\mathrm{i})\) and \(\vek U_5 = \overline{\vek U_1}\) (\(\mu\)m, \(\mu\)m, \(\mu\)rad):

\(k\) \(0\) \(1\) and \(5\) \(2\) and \(4\) \(3\)
\((\vek U_{\mathrm{k}})_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\mu\)m \(-0{,}266\) \(-0{,}531\) \(-0{,}530\) \(-0{,}529\)
contribution to \(r\) of node \(0\), \(\mu\)m \(-0{,}266\) \(-1{,}062\) \(-1{,}060\) \(-0{,}529\)

The contribution of a pair is twice the real part of \((\vek U_{\mathrm{k}})_{\mathrm{r}}\), because at node \(0\) the phase is \(w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,0} = 1\), and at \(k = 0\), \(3\) once. The sum is \(-2{,}916\ \mu\)m (before rounding the terms). The direct solution of the whole system with \(18\) unknowns gives the same: the difference at all six nodes and three components is at most \(1{,}4\cdot 10^{-19}\) m and the imaginary part of the sum is \(2\cdot 10^{-21}\) m (rounding, NumPy). At node \(1\) the same parts are \(-0{,}266\), \(-0{,}531\), \(+0{,}530\), \(+0{,}529\) with the phase factors \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the sum is \(+0{,}263\ \mu\)m, as the whole system gives. Figure 19.32 draws the radial displacements of the whole system as blue bars above the node numbers, on a horizontal axis with the scale one micrometre per centimetre. The bar of node \(0\) reaches \(2{,}92\ \mu\)m inwards, hence downwards, the other five are short and outwards.

Why is \(\vek U_0\) half of \(\vek U_3\) although the load \(\vek F_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the same? Because at \(k = 0\) the sector is about twice as stiff in the direction \(r\). Take the free body of node \(0\) in figure 19.29. At \(k = 0\) all the nodes move inwards by \(u\), the radius shrinks to \(R - u\) and the chord \(2(R - u)\sin 30° = R - u\) of the rim shrinks by \(u\). Each of the two rim beams is compressed by the force \(EA\,u/h\) along the chord and gives the radial component \(\cos 60°\cdot EA\,u/h\), so both together \(EA\,u/h\), and the spoke gives another \(EA\,u/h\). The radial stiffness is \(2\,EA/h = 3{,}136\cdot 10^{8}\) N/m, which is \((\mat K_{\mathrm{k}=0})_{\mathrm{rr}}\). At \(k = 3\) the nodes alternately move by \(-u\) and \(+u\): by the cosine rule the chord between a point at the radius \(R - u\) and the neighbouring one at the radius \(R + u\) at an angle of \(60°\) has length \(\sqrt{R^2 + 3u^2}\), so to first order it does not change, the rim does not resist and the stiffness is only that of the spoke, \(EA/h = 1{,}568\cdot 10^{8}\) N/m (\(1{,}576\cdot 10^{8}\) with the bending of the rim). The ratio of the stiffnesses is \(2{,}0\), as the table shows.

The split exists in the computation too, not only in the formulas: the sum of six problems with three unknowns gives the same as one problem with eighteen. But we also know what would happen if we proceeded like COOK and took only one sector with equal displacements on the boundaries.

Example 19.48 Two cases where the cyclic solution fails (dva primera, kjer ciklična rešitev ne drži)

Theorem 19.44 has two hypotheses, the cyclicity of the structure and the cyclicity of the load. Let us show what happens when each is missing.

  1. The load is not cyclic. The same wheel, the same force \(500\) N at node \(0\). The solution of one sector with equal displacements, equation (19.16) with \(\hat{\vek f}_0 = (-500, 0, 0)/6\), which is the harmonic \(k = 0\) alone, gives the radial displacement \(-0{,}266\ \mu\)m at all nodes, which is the orange dashed line in figure 19.32. The true displacement of node \(0\) is \(-2{,}916\ \mu\)m, which is \(10{,}98\) times larger, and elsewhere it is \(+0{,}26\ \mu\)m instead of \(-0{,}27\ \mu\)m, so of the opposite sign. The reason is in the table of example 19.47: at node \(0\) all six harmonics have the phase \(w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,0} = 1\) and add up, and the harmonic \(k = 0\) gives only \(9\) % of the sum. Elsewhere harmonics with different phases mostly cancel. The sector with equal displacements answers the question about the average load and not about a force at one place.
  2. The structure is not cyclic. Spoke \(3\) has half the width (\(10 \times 40\) mm), so \(EA/2\) and \(EI/2\), the rest is the same. At every node \(500/6 = 83{,}33\) N acts inwards, a cyclic load. The block \(\hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{j}+1,\mathrm{l}+1} - \hat{\mat K}_{\mathrm{jl}}\) has an entry \(7{,}8\cdot 10^{7}\) N/m, while the largest entry is \(2{,}4\cdot 10^{8}\) N/m, so the pattern is not circulant. The solution of one sector of a wheel with six equal spokes, \(-0{,}266\ \mu\)m, is still approximately right at five nodes (\(-0{,}245\ \mu\)m), but at node \(3\) the displacement is \(-0{,}49\ \mu\)m, which is \(1{,}8\) times larger, because the spoke there has half the axial stiffness. One spoke has spoiled the symmetry, and the theorem then claims nothing.

Two remarks complete the theorem. The first: COOK describes a trick (PDF p. 370). The sum of blocks in equation (19.16) arises by itself during assembly (theorem 7.13) if the homologous nodes \(0\) and \(1\) on the boundaries of the sector get the same number, and ONATE1 (section 9.6.2, PDF p. 348) recommends the same. The coordinates of the nodes in the computation of the element matrices are then still the true ones, and the displacements of the boundaries must be in local axes, as we did. The second: skew symmetry in COOK, figure 2.11-4 (PDF p. 70-71), where a half turn maps the structure onto itself, is the case \(N = 2\). Our definition requires \(N \ge 3\), because for \(N = 2\) the neighbours \(j - 1\) and \(j + 1\) are the same sector. Then all elements between the two sectors are collected in a single block \(\mat B = \hat{\mat K}_{01}\). By item 1 of lemma 19.43, which does not need \(N \ge 3\), \(\hat{\mat K}_{10} = \hat{\mat K}_{01}\), and by symmetry \(\hat{\mat K}_{10} = \hat{\mat K}_{01}^\T\), so \(\mat B\) is symmetric. The only harmonics are \(w_0 = 1\) and \(w_1 = -1\), and the sector matrices are \(\mat K_0 + \mat B\) and \(\mat K_0 - \mat B\) (not \(\mat K_0 \pm 2\mat B\), which equation (19.17) with \(\mat K_1 = \mat B\) would give). The harmonic \(0\) is a cyclic load, the second sector is a turned copy of the first, which is skew symmetry. The harmonic \(1\) has \(\hat{\vek d}_1 = -\hat{\vek d}_0\), which is skew antisymmetry: after the turn the loads reverse, as COOK describes next to figure 2.11-4b (PDF p. 71).

The wheel has, besides the turns, the mirror across spoke \(0\), which takes sector \(j\) to sector \(-j\) (section 19.1). In our result this is visible: \(u_{\mathrm{t}}\) at node \(1\) is \(+1{,}22\ \mu\)m and at node \(5\) it is \(-1{,}22\ \mu\)m, because the mirror reverses the direction \(t\) (theorem 19.6). In the harmonics the mirror shows in example 19.47: the radial component of every \(\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}\) is real, the tangential component and the rotation are imaginary, for instance \(\vek U_1 = (-0{,}531, -0{,}530\,\mathrm{i}, -0{,}227\,\mathrm{i})\). Item 4 of theorem 19.46, \(\vek U_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = \overline{\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}}\), holds for every real load, also an unsymmetric one. Only together with the mirror symmetry of the load does it say that \(\vek U_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}}\) has the same radial component as \(\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the opposite tangential component and rotation, which is the mirror \(t \to -t\) at the level of the harmonics. The next section (19.10) uses the same split for the natural frequencies of the wheel. What we have not proved: a wheel with a circular rim instead of a polygon and the loading of bodies of revolution by a series of cosines and sines (COOK sections 14.4 and 14.5, PDF p. 530-531) are only named. Plane and solid elements for such structures are in chapter 15.

19.10 Vibration of a cyclically symmetric structure

The wheel of section 19.9 has its hub at the point \(O\), rigidly clamped, six spokes of length \(1\) m and a rim of six straight beams with chord \(1\) m. All members are steel beams with a \(20 \times 40\) mm cross-section, as in chapter 12 (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³), and each member is one finite element. Sector \(j\) (\(j = 0, \dots, 5\)) is rim node \(j\) with the spoke and the rim beam attached to it. Its three unknowns are the radial displacement, the tangential displacement and the rotation, written in the axes of the sector, and we collect them in a column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{j}}\) (\(n = 3\)). For a static load, cyclic symmetry with the split into harmonics replaced one problem with \(18\) unknowns by six problems with three unknowns. Now we ask whether the same holds for vibration: which frequencies and shapes does the wheel have if we displace it from equilibrium and let go?

The model follows what holds for all vibration in chapter 10. The stiffness matrix \(\mat K\) is symmetric and positive definite because the hub is clamped (theorem 7.18), the mass matrix \(\mat M\) is symmetric and positive definite, and we look for eigenpairs \(\mat K\vek\varphi = \lambda\mat M\vek\varphi\) with \(\omega = \sqrt\lambda\) (definition 10.7). This is the undamped vibration of a model with one element per member. The frequencies we quote are those of this model and not directly those of a real wheel, since we did not estimate the error of the coarse mesh. The spokes are \(25\) times longer than the section height of \(40\) mm, so the beam model is appropriate.

In the axes of the sectors both matrices are block circulant by lemma 19.43. For \(\mat K\) this is the lemma, for \(\mat M\) the same proof holds, since the mass matrix is also assembled from identical sectors. Row \(j\) then has off the diagonal only the block \(\mat K_1^\T\) at sector \(j - 1\) and \(\mat K_1\) at sector \(j + 1\), and \(\mat K_0\) on the diagonal (all blocks are \(3 \times 3\) matrices, sector indices are taken modulo \(N = 6\), and \(\mat K_0\) is symmetric). We have \(\mat M_0\) and \(\mat M_1\) in the same way. For every \(k = 0, \dots, N - 1\) and \(w = \mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}k/N}\) let

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat K_0 + w\,\mat K_1 + \bar w\,\mat K_1^\T , \qquad \mat M_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat M_0 + w\,\mat M_1 + \bar w\,\mat M_1^\T , \tag{19.19}\]

the sector matrices of section 19.9 (in this section \(k\) is not a stiffness but the number of the harmonic, and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\) is not the entry \(k\)). We call \(k\) the harmonic because the pattern around the wheel is a discrete sine and cosine that repeats \(k\) times in one turn (definition 9.102).

For vibration the question is whether the wheel can carry waves that run around it, so that every sector equals its neighbour, only shifted in phase. The reason to try is the turn of the wheel: if we turn the wheel by one sector, we get a structure with the same stiffness and mass, hence by Newton's law the same equation of motion, and the turned mode is again a mode with the same frequency. Waves with a constant phase step are the columns that the turn merely multiplies by a number.

Theorem 19.49 Vibration of a cyclic structure by harmonics (nihanje ciklične konstrukcije po harmonikih)

Let \(N \ge 3\), and let the real block circulant matrices \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) (\(N \times N\) blocks of order \(n\)) have blocks \(\mat K_0, \mat K_1\) and \(\mat M_0, \mat M_1\) as above, with \(\mat K_0\) and \(\mat M_0\) symmetric and \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) symmetric positive definite. Let \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = \mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}k/N}\) and let \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\mat M_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the matrices of equation (19.19).

  1. For a number \(\lambda\) and a nonzero complex column \(\vek U\) with \(n\) entries, the column \(\vek d\) with blocks \(\vek d_{\mathrm{j}} = w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\,\vek U\) (\(j = 0, \dots, N - 1\)) solves \(\mat K\vek d = \lambda\mat M\vek d\) if and only if \((\mat K_{\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{k}})\,\vek U = \vek 0\).
  2. For every number \(\lambda\) the dimension of the space of solutions of \(\mat K\vek d = \lambda\mat M\vek d\) (the multiplicity of the eigenvalue \(\lambda\)) equals the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}=0}^{N-1}\dim\ker(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{k}})\). The eigenvalues of the wheel are therefore exactly the eigenvalues of the \(N\) sector problems together, with multiplicities added.
  3. All these values are real and positive. For \(k = 0\) and (for even \(N\)) \(k = N/2\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = \pm 1\) and \(\vek U\) can be taken real. For other \(k\) the real and imaginary parts \(\mathrm{Re}\,\vek d\) and \(\mathrm{Im}\,\vek d\) are real modes.
Proof

We have to show three points. In the first, the matrix \(\mat K\) acts on a wave as a multiplication. In the second, we split a wave into harmonics with the DFT (definition 9.102). The third follows from the chapter on eigenpairs.

  1. By the structure of a block circulant matrix, block \(j\) of the column \(\mat K\vek d\) is \((\mat K\vek d)_{\mathrm{j}} = \mat K_1^\T\vek d_{\mathrm{j}-1} + \mat K_0\vek d_{\mathrm{j}} + \mat K_1\vek d_{\mathrm{j}+1}\), indices modulo \(N\). For \(\vek d_{\mathrm{j}} = w^j\vek U\) we have \(\vek d_{\mathrm{j}\pm 1} = w^{\pm 1}w^j\vek U\), because \(w^N = \mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}k} = 1\) (theorem 9.29), so going around past \(N\) changes nothing, and \(w^{-1} = \bar w\) (\(|w| = 1\), lemma 9.20).
  2. Hence \((\mat K\vek d)_{\mathrm{j}} = w^j(\mat K_1^\T\bar w + \mat K_0 + \mat K_1 w)\vek U = w^j\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\vek U\) and likewise \((\mat M\vek d)_{\mathrm{j}} = w^j\mat M_{\mathrm{k}}\vek U\). The equation \(\mat K\vek d = \lambda\mat M\vek d\) is then \(w^j(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{k}})\vek U = \vek 0\) for every \(j\), and \(w^j \ne 0\) (theorem 9.29, item 2), which is point 1.
  3. Let \(\vek d\) be an arbitrary complex column with blocks \(\vek d_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\vek U_{\mathrm{k}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathrm{j}}w_{\mathrm{k}}^{-j}\vek d_{\mathrm{j}}\) (the DFT of each of the \(n\) entries, definition 9.102). Insert into \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\vek U_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{l}}\vek d_{\mathrm{l}}\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}k(j-l)/N}\). By lemma 9.103 the inner sum is \(N\) at \(l = j\) and zero for the other \(l \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}\), so \(\vek d_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\vek U_{\mathrm{k}}\). The map \(\vek d \mapsto (\vek U_0, \dots, \vek U_{\mathrm{N}-1})\) is therefore linear and invertible.
  4. Let \(\mat K\vek d = \lambda\mat M\vek d\). By step 2 and linearity, \((\mat K\vek d - \lambda\mat M\vek d)_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{k}})\vek U_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek 0\) for every \(j\). Multiply by \(w_{\mathrm{l}}^{-j}/N\) and sum over \(j\): by lemma 9.103 only the term \(k = l\) remains, so \((\mat K_{\mathrm{l}} - \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{l}})\vek U_{\mathrm{l}} = \vek 0\) for every \(l\). The solution \(\vek d\) is thus a sum of waves from point 1. Conversely, by point 1 and linearity every sum of waves with \(\vek U_{\mathrm{k}} \in \ker(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{k}})\) is a solution. The map of step 3 is therefore an invertible map of the space of solutions onto the sum of the spaces \(\ker(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{k}})\), and the two spaces have the same (complex) dimension. For real \(\lambda\) the matrix \(\mat K - \lambda\mat M\) is real, so the complex dimension of its kernel equals the real one, which is point 2.
  5. Let \(\lambda\) be an eigenvalue of sector problem \(k\) with vector \(\vek U \ne \vek 0\). By point 1 the wave \(\vek d\) is a nonzero solution of \(\mat K\vek d = \lambda\mat M\vek d\) and by lemma 10.18 \(\lambda\) is a real number. Let \(\vek d = \vek a + \mathrm{i}\,\vek b\) with real \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\). Since \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) are real and symmetric, \(\overline{\vek d}^{\T}\mat K\vek d = \vek a^\T\mat K\vek a + \vek b^\T\mat K\vek b > 0\) and likewise for \(\mat M\), so \(\overline{\vek d}^{\T}\mat K\vek d = \lambda\,\overline{\vek d}^{\T}\mat M\vek d\) gives \(\lambda > 0\).
  6. For \(k = 0\) and \(k = N/2\) we have \(w = \pm 1\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\mat M_{\mathrm{k}}\) are real, so the real matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{k}}\) with a nontrivial kernel has a real vector in its kernel. For other \(k\) the matrices \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\) and the number \(\lambda\) are real, so splitting \(\mat K\vek d = \lambda\mat M\vek d\) into real and imaginary parts gives \(\mat K\,\mathrm{Re}\,\vek d = \lambda\mat M\,\mathrm{Re}\,\vek d\) and the same for \(\mathrm{Im}\,\vek d\). Both are nonzero: with \(\mathrm{Re}\,\vek d = \vek 0\) the blocks \(\vek d_0 = \vek U\) and \(\vek d_1 = w\vek U\) would be purely imaginary, with \(\mathrm{Im}\,\vek d = \vek 0\) real, and in both cases \(w\) would be real (the quotient of corresponding nonzero entries), which is impossible for \(|w| = 1\) and \(w \ne \pm 1\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. The split of the vibration of a cyclic structure into harmonics is our derivation from the DFT of chapter 9 (a gap in the sources, section 19.9). COOK, PDF p. 448, only warns that most vibration modes of a shell of revolution have waves around the circumference.

The theorem says that the wheel's frequencies come from six smaller problems and that every frequency is real. How many frequencies there are and what the shapes look like, we show on the wheel.

Example 19.50 Frequencies of the wheel from six sectors (frekvence kolesa iz šestih odsekov)

For every \(k = 0, \dots, 5\) we solve the sector problem of size \(3\) (NumPy, outlines/ch-simetrija-vezi/num-10.py). The lowest three frequencies \(f = \omega/2\pi\) are in the table.

\(k\) first frequency (Hz) second frequency (Hz) third frequency (Hz)
0 \(17{,}044\) \(347{,}674\) \(1044{,}582\)
1 \(223{,}512\) \(536{,}826\) \(1221{,}490\)
2 \(152{,}907\) \(773{,}881\) \(1722{,}704\)
3 \(125{,}734\) \(821{,}531\) \(2081{,}798\)
4 \(152{,}907\) \(773{,}881\) \(1722{,}704\)
5 \(223{,}512\) \(536{,}826\) \(1221{,}490\)

The whole wheel has \(18\) unknowns, hence \(18\) frequencies. Solving the full model gives, in order of size, \(17{,}044\), \(125{,}734\), \(152{,}907\), \(152{,}907\), \(223{,}512\), \(223{,}512\), \(347{,}674\), \(536{,}826\), \(536{,}826\), \(773{,}881\), \(773{,}881\), \(821{,}531\), \(1044{,}582\), \(1221{,}490\), \(1221{,}490\), \(1722{,}704\), \(1722{,}704\), \(2081{,}798\) Hz. When we sort the six table rows by size, we get the same \(18\) numbers, with a largest difference of \(3 \cdot 10^{-12}\) Hz (rounding). This is the claim of point 2 of theorem 19.49 on numbers. The same holds for shapes: the column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{j}} = w^j\vek U\) from the sector problem solves the full problem with a relative residual of at most \(3 \cdot 10^{-13}\) for all six \(k\).

We build figure 19.33 row by row. Each row is one sector problem: row \(k = 0\) has dots at \(17{,}044\) and \(347{,}674\) Hz (the third, \(1044{,}582\) Hz, is off the figure). Rows \(k = 1\) and \(k = 5\) have dots at \(223{,}512\) and \(536{,}826\) Hz, that is at the same places. Rows \(k = 2\) and \(k = 4\) likewise have dots at \(152{,}907\) and \(773{,}881\) Hz. Only row \(k = 3\) has no partner, its dots are at \(125{,}734\) and \(821{,}531\) Hz. The axis under the rows is shared, so the dots can be compared by position. The agreement of rows \(k\) and \(6 - k\) is no accident, and corollary 19.51 explains it.

What do the shapes look like? Figure 19.34 shows, for each \(k\), the lowest shape of the sector problem, drawn as the deformed wheel.

We draw the wheel from above: the grey hexagon with its spokes is the wheel at rest, the blackwhite dot is the clamped hub. In panel \(k = 0\) we have \(w = 1\), every sector equals its neighbour, so the rim turns as a whole about the hub and the spokes bend. In panel \(k = 3\) we have \(w = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\pi} = -1\), so neighbouring sectors move in opposite directions and the pattern repeats three times around the wheel. The \(k = 1\) panels show the same wave twice, the first as the real part, the second as the imaginary part of the column \(\vek d\), and the \(k = 2\) panels likewise, with the first and the second mode. Why there are two pictures for one frequency at \(k = 1\) and \(k = 2\) is explained by the next corollary.

For our wheel, the agreement of frequencies \(k\) and \(6 - k\) is explained by mirror symmetry. Besides turns, the wheel also has the reflection across spoke \(0\) (section 19.1), which takes sector \(j\) to \(-j\). If a wave runs around the wheel in one direction, its mirror image runs in the other, so it has the phase step \(-2\pi k/N\), which is harmonic \(N - k\). The structure is the same after reflection, so the mirror wave is a mode with the same frequency. Since for \(k \ne 0, N/2\) the wave and its mirror image belong to the different harmonics \(k\) and \(N - k\), neither is a multiple of the other (step 3 of the proof of theorem 19.49), and they are two independent modes with the same frequency. The corollary shows more. Its proof by conjugation needs only that \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) are real, not mirror symmetry: the conjugate wave \(\overline{\vek d}\) runs around the wheel in the direction opposite to \(\vek d\), and since the matrices are real it is again a solution. So the frequencies \(k\) and \(N - k\) agree also for a cyclic structure without a mirror plane. We checked this on a wheel whose spokes are attached to a rigidly clamped ring of radius \(0{,}2\) m, each at a point turned by \(20^\circ\) in the same direction, so that it has no mirror plane: of the \(18\) frequencies again six are single and six double (outlines/finish-2026-11-16/ch-simetrija-vezi/check-10.py).

Corollary 19.51 Double frequencies of a cyclic structure (dvojne frekvence ciklične konstrukcije)

In the setting of theorem 19.49 let \(0 < k < N\) and \(2k \ne N\). Then \(\mat K_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = \overline{\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}}\) and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = \overline{\mat M_{\mathrm{k}}}\), and \(\ker(\mat K_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}}) = \overline{\ker(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{k}})}\) for every number \(\lambda\) (columns with conjugated entries). Every eigenvalue of sector problem \(k\) therefore has multiplicity at least \(2\) for the whole structure: if \(\vek d\) is a wave from point 1 of the theorem, then \(\mathrm{Re}\,\vek d\) and \(\mathrm{Im}\,\vek d\) are linearly independent real modes of the same frequency, and every linear combination of them is a mode.

Proof

We have to show the equality of matrices, the equality of kernels and the independence of two modes.

  1. From \(w_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = \mathrm{e}^{2\pi\mathrm{i}(N-k)/N} = \mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\mathrm{i}k/N} = \bar w_{\mathrm{k}}\) (theorem 9.29) and the reality of \(\mat K_0, \mat K_1, \mat M_0, \mat M_1\) it follows that \(\mat K_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = \mat K_0 + \bar w_{\mathrm{k}}\mat K_1 + w_{\mathrm{k}}\mat K_1^\T = \overline{\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}}\), and likewise for \(\mat M\).
  2. If \((\mat K_{\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{k}})\vek U = \vek 0\) and \(\lambda\) is real (point 3 of theorem 19.49), conjugating the equation gives \((\mat K_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\mat M_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}})\overline{\vek U} = \vek 0\), and conversely. The kernels have the same dimension.
  3. Since \(k\) and \(N - k\) are different classes modulo \(N\) (from \(2k \ne N\) and \(0 < k < N\)), by point 2 of theorem 19.49 both contribute to the multiplicity: \(\dim\ker_{\mathrm{k}} + \dim\ker_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}} = 2\dim\ker_{\mathrm{k}} \ge 2\).
  4. The wave \(\vek d\) belongs to the sum at \(k\), the wave \(\overline{\vek d}\) at \(N - k\) (its blocks are \(\bar w_{\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\overline{\vek U} = w_{\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{k}}^{\,j}\overline{\vek U}\)), so by step 3 of the theorem's proof they are linearly independent over \(\mathbb{C}\). Since \(\mathrm{Re}\,\vek d = (\vek d + \overline{\vek d})/2\) and \(\mathrm{Im}\,\vek d = (\vek d - \overline{\vek d})/(2\mathrm{i})\) (real and imaginary part: lemma 9.20) span the same space, \(\mathrm{Re}\,\vek d\) and \(\mathrm{Im}\,\vek d\) are also independent over \(\mathbb{C}\), hence over \(\mathbb{R}\). A linear combination is a mode because the equation \(\mat K\vek d = \lambda\mat M\vek d\) is linear.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. The mirror explanation follows theorem 19.18 on the modes of a mirror symmetric structure.

The points \(k = 0\) and \(k = N/2\) do not fall under the corollary, since there \(w = \pm 1\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{k}}\) is real, so the conjugate wave \(\overline{\vek d}\) is a wave of the same harmonic and gives no second independent mode. For the wheel these are two sector problems with three single frequencies each (rows \(k = 0\) and \(k = 3\) of figure 19.33). For all other \(k\) the frequencies are double: of the \(18\) frequencies, six are single and six are double (altogether \(12\) different values), and none is triple. That the double ones are exactly double is not stated by the corollary (the multiplicity is at least \(2\)), the list counts it: at \(152{,}907\) Hz the full model has two values that differ by \(5 \cdot 10^{-12}\) Hz, and no third in the list.

Example 19.52 The double frequency \(152{,}907\) Hz and the turned mode (dvojna frekvenca in zasukani način)

Take \(k = 2\) and the lowest vector \(\vek U\) of the sector problem, with its phase chosen so that its largest entry is real. Let \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{a}} = \mathrm{Re}\,\vek d\) and \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{b}} = \mathrm{Im}\,\vek d\). Both solve the full problem with a relative residual of \(3 \cdot 10^{-14}\), their \(\mat M\)-norms are equal (\(1{,}732\)) and \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{a}}^\T\mat M\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{b}} = 6 \cdot 10^{-16}\), so they are \(\mat M\)-orthogonal (definition 10.10). Turn the pattern \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{a}}\) by one sector, that is \(\vek d'_{\mathrm{j}} = (\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{a}})_{\mathrm{j}-1}\), where \((\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{a}})_{\mathrm{j}} = \mathrm{Re}(w^j\vek U)\) is block \(j\) of the column \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{a}}\). The wheel has the same stiffness and mass at every sector, so \(\vek d'\) is also a mode with the same frequency, and we express it with \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{b}}\). From \((\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{a}})_{\mathrm{j}-1} = \mathrm{Re}(w^{-1}w^j\vek U) = \cos\theta\,\mathrm{Re}(w^j\vek U) + \sin\theta\,\mathrm{Im}(w^j\vek U)\) with \(\theta = 2\pi k/N = 120^\circ\) (\(w^{-1} = \cos\theta - \mathrm{i}\sin\theta\)) it follows that

\[\vek d' = \cos 120^\circ\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{a}} + \sin 120^\circ\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{b}} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{a}} + \tfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{b}} , \tag{19.20}\]

which holds numerically with a largest difference of \(2 \cdot 10^{-15}\) for entries of size \(2{,}09\). By point 2 of theorem 19.49 the space of modes of this frequency is two-dimensional, since \(152{,}907\) Hz appears in the table only in rows \(k = 2\) and \(k = 4\), once each, and so it equals \(\mathrm{span}(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{a}}, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{b}})\). For a double eigenvalue, the computer returns an arbitrary column from this space: in our run, with radial components at the six rim nodes divided by the largest one, \(-0{,}044\), \(1\), \(-0{,}956\), \(-0{,}044\), \(1\), \(-0{,}956\), which is the combination with coefficients \(-0{,}577\) at \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(-0{,}022\) at \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{b}}\) (residual \(6 \cdot 10^{-14}\)). Such a shape is not mirror symmetric across spoke \(0\) although the wheel is, and it is no error: it is one mode of a two-dimensional space, and its shape depends on how the computation was carried out.

We build figure 19.35 from the left. The first panel is the mode \(\varphi_{\mathrm{a}}\), the deformed wheel in orange. The second panel is the mode \(\varphi_{\mathrm{b}}\), of the same frequency but with a different pattern. The third panel is the pattern of the first panel turned by \(60^\circ\) about the hub, and at the same time the sum \(-\tfrac12\varphi_{\mathrm{a}} + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\varphi_{\mathrm{b}}\) of equation (19.20). The turn gives no new independent mode, since the turned mode is only another combination of the same two. So at \(k = 2\) the wheel has two independent pictures and no third: there are many turns, but all lie in the same two-dimensional space.

One question remains that the result demands: what do we get if from section 19.9 we take only the sector with equal displacements at both edges, as COOK proposed (PDF pp. 368-370), that is \(k = 0\)?

Example 19.53 The sector with \(k = 0\) alone misses most modes (odsek le s \(k = 0\) zgreši večino načinov)

The sector with \(d_{\mathrm{B}} = d_{\mathrm{A}}\) is the sector problem for \(k = 0\) (matrix \(\mat K_0 + \mat K_1 + \mat K_1^\T\)). It gives three frequencies, row \(k = 0\) of figure 19.33: \(17{,}044\), \(347{,}674\) and \(1044{,}582\) Hz. Of the \(18\) frequencies of the wheel it finds \(3\). The lowest eight frequencies of the full model are \(17{,}044\), \(125{,}734\), \(152{,}907\), \(152{,}907\), \(223{,}512\), \(223{,}512\), \(347{,}674\) and \(536{,}826\) Hz, of which it finds \(2\) (\(17{,}044\) and \(347{,}674\)). The lowest frequency we do get, so the error might go unnoticed. The second frequency of the wheel is \(125{,}734\) Hz (\(k = 3\)), but from this sector we would read \(347{,}674\) Hz for the second one, which is \(2{,}765\) times too high. That the lowest frequency lies at \(k = 0\) is a property of this wheel. We did not compute another wheel, so we do not conclude that the lowest frequency is always at \(k = 0\). The sector with equal edges therefore suffices for a static load that is the same in all sectors, and for the lowest mode of this wheel, but not for vibration.

COOK (PDF p. 448) warns that most vibration modes of a shell of revolution have waves around the circumference, and this is the same difficulty. For vibration the sector with equal displacements at both edges is not enough, and we have to solve the sector problems for all \(k = 0, \dots, \lfloor N/2\rfloor\), since the remaining \(k\) are repeats by corollary 19.51. For \(N = 6\) these are four problems with \(3 \times 3\) complex matrices instead of one with \(18 \times 18\).

19.11 Connections

The abbreviations of subjects are the same as in section 1.19.

  • Mirror symmetry and its conditions: that a symmetric structure under a symmetric load gives a symmetric response is shown by theorem 19.4 for a body and by theorem 19.6 for a frame model. The second generalizes lemmas 7.36 and 7.38 of chapter 7, each of which held only for its own structure, to every frame model. Theorem 19.7 says what must hold on the plane of symmetry. This closes the promises of chapters 5 (symmetry of frames) and 11 (symmetry conditions of a body). A plane of symmetry that carries stiffness or load takes over only half of each, as in section 19.2 (lemma 19.9, which generalizes the half model of the bridge of lemma 7.39). A quarter of a plate with two symmetry edges was already used in section 18.9 (MK, AK), and a quarter of a plate with a hole with mirror conditions on the axis planes in section 17.9 (AK).
  • Symmetry in free vibration and buckling: theorem 19.18 splits the modes of a symmetric system into symmetric and antisymmetric ones, and its corollary 19.19 shows that the half model with symmetric conditions has exactly the symmetric modes, and the half model with antisymmetric conditions exactly the antisymmetric ones. The portal frame of section 19.4 has its lowest frequency, \(29{,}511\) Hz, in an antisymmetric mode and its lowest critical force, \(154{,}2\) kN, in the antisymmetric sway. The half model with symmetric conditions would give a lowest frequency of \(116{,}20\) Hz and a buckling force that is \(3{,}42\) times too large. For cyclic symmetry the same split is theorem 19.49, and its corollary 19.51 says that every frequency of harmonic \(k\) with \(k \ne 0\) and \(k \ne N/2\) has multiplicity at least \(2\) (section 19.10). A disk with \(N\) equal blades is cyclically symmetric, so the same split holds for it. Chapter 24 (DSK) does not use it, because there the disk is a rigid body or an axisymmetric rotating disk without blades.
  • Elimination of constraints, multipoint constraints and coupling of different elements: theorem 19.26 shows that the reduced matrix \(\mat T^\T\mat K\,\mat T\) gives the same solution as the multipliers of theorem 12.26 in chapter 12 and that the constraint forces \(\mat C^\T\vek\lambda\) follow from \(\mat K\vek d - \vek f\). The inclined support (lemma 19.27, figure 19.16) is the simplest case. Lemma 19.35 ties the rotation of a beam at a node of a mesh without rotations to two displacements, as figure 19.21 shows. When the mesh is made of plane or solid elements, which likewise have no rotations at a node, the same constraint is written for those elements. Their stiffness matrices were already derived in chapter 15 (AK). Guyan reduction, also called static condensation (statična kondenzacija), which eliminates part of the unknowns by static equilibrium, and substructures are treated in chapter 21 (DSK). There the reduced system has the same form \(\mat T^\T\mat K\,\mat T\), except that the columns of \(\mat T\) are not fixed by a support constraint but by a choice of shapes, for example static shapes in Guyan reduction.
  • Cyclic symmetry and loads without it: theorem 19.46 splits any load into harmonics by the discrete Fourier transform (definition 9.102) and solves each harmonic on one sector with the phase factor \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = \mathrm e^{2\pi\mathrm i k/N}\). This is our derivation, not from a source (the gap is described in section 19.9). COOK §14.4 (PDF p. 530-531) does the same for bodies of revolution under a load without axial symmetry: it expands the load in a Fourier series in the circumferential angle with sine and cosine terms, solves each term separately and adds the results. We do not prove that series here. The axisymmetric elements were already introduced in section 15.9 (AK), which only named loads without axial symmetry. The split into harmonics is the same idea for a structure of \(N\) equal sectors, with a finite sum of \(N\) harmonics instead of a series.
  • Periodicity: theorem 19.38 (section 19.8) allows a single span with equal boundary values for an infinite row of equal spans. For a finite row this holds only in the interior. The moment at the middle support is \(0{,}125\,ql^2\) for two spans, which is \(50\) % more than the cell value \(ql^2/12 = 0{,}08333\,ql^2\), for five spans the deviation is \(5{,}3\) %, and the cell value is reached to six digits only at 20 spans. From the end towards the interior the deviation decreases at every support by the factor \(2 - \sqrt3 \approx 0{,}268\) (lemma 19.40). Unit cells as a procedure for composite materials (homogenization) are only named, because the books we have contain no account of them.
  • Limits of the chapter: what is proved holds for a linear model in which the stiffness matrix and the load do not depend on the displacement. In nonlinear static problems, for example with large displacements or contact, a symmetry that is present when loading begins may later disappear (COOK PDF p. 71). The proof of theorem 19.4 fails there because it rests on the solution being unique, and a nonlinear problem can have several solutions. The chapter does not treat this. In buckling the two idealizations are a linear elastic model with axial forces that do not change up to buckling and beams with a small slope (section 19.4). At the sway load of \(154{,}2\) kN the stress in the column is \(192{,}7\) MPa, which is \(88\) % of the yield stress of \(220\) MPa, so the linear elastic model is at the edge of its validity. The cyclic split into harmonics and cyclic vibration are in none of the books we have, so they are proved in the chapter, not cited.
